Evergreen tree up to 30 m tall with characteristic peeling reddish bark; alternate dark waxy green oval leaves (15 cm); hanging clusters of white bell flowers; bright small red berries. Pacific madrone is an evergreen broadleaf tree of the Heath family (Ericaceae), native to the northwestern Coast Ranges of North America. Reaching heights of 6 to 30 m tall (6-30 m, or 6m to 30m or more depending on environmental conditions), trees feature single or multiple trunks from the base with rounded, spreading crowns, or a more shrublike habit. Young bark is chartreuse and smooth, aging to thin, smooth, deep brownish-red or cinnamon red bark that peels in large papery flakes away from the trunk and young branches to reveal an attractive, satiny green surface beneath that darkens with time to deep red. In midsummer, the exfoliated bark and shed leaves in shades of red to orange form a distinctive colorful carpet beneath the tree canopy (Saunders 1923).

Pacific madrone is a prolific seed producer, which produces seed every year from the age of three to five years. One pound of seeds will produce approximately 1,000 plants. Seedlings grow slowly and are highly susceptible to mortality. To start from seed, gather the fruits from the trees when they are ripe—generally from October to December.

These trees should only be planted in very well drained soils in areas with non-alkaline water. Although generally started from seed, Pacific madrone may also be propagated from cuttings, grafting, or layers. For best germination, use seeds that have been stratified by pre-chilling for one to two months at 2 to 5°C. Propagated by seed (stratified 1–2 months at 2–5°C) or sprouting from underground burls after fire/cutting.

Within managed conifer stands, Pacific madrone has been considered a “weedy” tree species. This is because it can out-compete replanting of timber species because of its ability to resprout from its stump or burl after disturbance. Interestingly, there is some evidence that Pacific madrone can facilitate growth of Douglas fir at some sites. In natural areas, the situation is reversed from that of timber production areas.

Perennial Grass, 30-120 cm height, blueish-green foliage and spike-like flowers. Inhabiting meadows and woodlands, as well as moist to dry slopes and open forests in lowland, montane, and subalpine zones.

Blue wildrye is a large perennial bunchgrass with an upright growth habit, featuring bluish-green foliage, spike-like flowers, and reaching heights of 30-180 cm with just a few stems per plant. Perennial, bluish, tufted grass from fibrous roots or short rhizomes; stems 30-180 cm tall, erect or slightly decumbent at the base, the nodes exposed and often covered with dense short hairs. Sheaths are smooth to rough, white-hairy close to the base, and often purplish at the stem-base. Leaf blades are lax, flat or slightly in-rolled, bluish-green with a white waxy coating, measuring 4-13 mm wide (ranging from 4-12 mm or 5–13 mm), rough on the nerves, sometimes hairy, and feature ear-shaped lobes up to 2.5 mm long at the leaf-bases that are often purple.

Flowering occurs in the late spring typically April to May in California. Further north, flowering typically occurs in June and July. Adequate moisture will promote good seed set, but even under adverse conditions of low moisture, seed will be produced in most years.

Seed is up to 8mm long, germinates easily, and has good seedling vigor. There are approximately 134,000 seeds/lb, and if planted at a rate of 1 lb./acre, there would be approximately 3 seeds/square feet.

‘Mariposa’ (CA) - Collected from a native stand near Mariposa, California at an elevation of 183 m above sea level. ‘Mariposa’ has shown a preference for loam to clay loam soils. It can persist on moderately deep road cut slopes.
Forage quality can be excellent when cut before the boot stage. It will not survive if grazed too heavily. Likewise, it is generally tolerant of mowing if not cut too short.

It is best grown for seed on well to moderately well drained, moist, medium textured soils. It establishes rapidly from seed but is short-lived. The species may also be less competitive with recently planted forest tree seedlings compared to certain introduced grasses. It establishes rapidly from seed but is relatively short-lived.

If dormancy is known or suspected, seed should have a TZ test to determine viability and then fall (Sept-Oct) sown or cold, moist stratified for 30-120 days.

Establishment of California oatgrass from seed can be problematic as the result of delayed germination and variable seed dormancy, as well as moderately slow seedling development combined with early competition from other species. Difficulties with reseeding Danthonia species were reported in the early to mid 1900’s when interest grew in reintroducing native perennial grasses on depleted or weedy grazing lands in California. Seed dormancy and germination: Evidence suggests the variable seed dormancy in California oatgrass is the result of either single or double (combined) dormancy.

In 2000, the NRCS Plant Materials Center at Corvallis, Oregon, the US Fish and Wildlife Service, and the Oregon Agricultural Experiment Station released Baskett Slough Germplasm California oatgrass, a selected class pre-variety (Darris and Lambert, 2000). The origin of this “natural” germplasm is the Baskett Slough National Wildlife Refuge in Polk County, Oregon.

Swards of native perennial grasses or grass-forb meadows containing California oatgrass can be improved and maintained with properly timed mowing, grazing, burning, herbicide applications, or combinations thereof. In California, the Pacific Northwest, and possibly other regions, doing nothing is often not an option in the long run because of ongoing and sometimes increasing competition from weedy annuals or invasive perennials, and the spread of shrubs or trees previously controlled or excluded by fire (Stromberg and Kephart 2003). Mowing is a viable option for controlling certain annual and perennial weeds as well as undesirable woody plants. For example, invasive perennial grasses such as tall oatgrass (Arrhenatherum elatius) are replacing native species on grasslands targeted for habitat conservation.

Seed is commercially available. Several other source identified populations of California oatgrass are periodically grown and sold as seed in Oregon and California. Native plant nurseries regularly produce plants of known origin in plugs and pots. Population genetics and seed transfer: Understanding patterns of genetic variation in California oatgrass across the landscape provides insight into adaptation and can help guide seed movement of populations within and among regions. In an analysis of data from a common garden study containing 66 populations (accessions) primarily from western Oregon and southwest Washington, plant vigor and seed abundance significantly correlated with winter precipitation, winter minimum temperature, and summer maximum temperature. However, for the subset of 33 Willamette Valley accessions, there were no significant correlations suggesting this region could be treated as a single seed zone for the species (Johnson undated). This makes it more likely for California oatgrass to have genetically distinct populations resulting in the need for smaller seed transfer zones compared to tree species. Knapp and Rice also noted seedlings from one population with narrower leaves came from a unique vernal pool location suggesting that restorationists should consider localized selection pressures when considering seed sources for a planting.

Few pest problems for California oatgrass have been recorded. However, it is one of many native grass hosts for the fungus (Gloeotinia temulenta) which causes blind seed disease, a potentially serious pest in ryegrass.

Few pest problems for California oatgrass have been recorded. The species can be infected by a nematode (Cynipanguina danthoniae) that causes leaf galls. Amme (1986) indicated that California oatgrass, along with other native grasses tested, appeared disease resistant during germination, transplanting, and growth in liners.

Heracleum maximum, commonly known as cow parsnip or hogweed, is a member of the carrot family (Apiaceae). Forms tall striking clusters of vegetation through summer by rhizome. Fireweed (Onagraceae) is a native, herbaceous rhizomatous perennial herb developing from widespread rootstocks and spreading roots typically within the top few inches of the ground surface, forming clonal colonies that bloom from June to September and attract native bees and leafcutter bees. Fireweed plants are protandrous (male reproductive organs mature before the female reproductive organs) and self-compatible (capable of self-fertilization) (Mosquin 1966). Flower anthers open, and disperse pollen, within 24 hours of the flower opening while the stigmas remain closed and the style strongly reflexed away from the anthers for 2 to 3 days, a process that promotes cross-pollination (Mosquin 1966).

The area of white brodiaea will require regular weeding and the use of a very weak solution of fertilizer twice only during the active growth in the spring. The corms can be kept from overcrowding by thinning them every three years. This involves picking off the cormlets and replanting them elsewhere in the garden. There are five major types of indigenous management activities conducted in California that were designed to ensure future corm production at traditional gathering sites: (1) conscious breaking off cormlets from the harvested parent corms and replanting them; (2) sparing whole plants; (3) harvesting the corms after plants have gone to seed and dumping the seeds on the ground; (4) burning areas; and (5) irrigation.

An erect or spreading Mediterranean-climate shrub 1-3 m tall with old branches possessing purplish-red bark and young twigs and stalks that are greyish-hairy and typically distinctly bristly with longer, scattered, glandular hairs. Leaves are alternate, evergreen, egg- or lance-shaped to elliptic, 2-5 cm long, 1-2.5 cm wide, narrowed at the tip, finely greyish-hairy particularly beneath, on stalks about 5 mm long. Belonging to the Heath Family (Ericaceae), hairy manzanita functions as an erect, much-branched evergreen shrub or small tree 1-3 m high with a broad, rounded, dense canopy, lacking a basal burl and thus unable to crown sprout after fire. Young twig bark is densely white-hirsute, while mature bark is smooth and dark red-brown.

The area planted in harvest brodiaea will require regular weeding and the use of a very weak solution of fertilizer twice only during the active growth in the spring. The corms can be kept from overcrowding by thinning them every three years. This involves picking off the cormlets and replanting them elsewhere in the garden. There are five major types of indigenous management activities conducted in California that were designed to ensure future corm production at traditional gathering sites: (1) conscious breaking off cormlets from the harvested parent corms and replanting them; (2) sparing whole plants; (3) harvesting the corms after plants have gone to seed and dumping the seeds in the hole; (4) burning areas; and (5) irrigation.

Seed is collected in midsummer from early June through late July. The seed is dark brown to black when mature and the pappus is white and expanded. The pappus can be removed with a hammer mill or brush machine, but pappus removal is not necessary for greenhouse propagation (Skinner 2004).

Bigflower agoseris can be seeded in spring or fall. It should be planted into a firm, weed-free seed bed at a depth of 3–6 mm. The recommended full stand seeding rate is 4 lbs pure live seed (PLS) per acre.

Bigflower agoseris should be used as a minor component of seed mixtures. Management strategies should be based on the key species in the established plant community. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment.
Seed of bigflower agoseris is available in limited quantities on the commercial market. Larger quantities of seed may be grown on a contract basis.

Bigleaf lupine can be hard-seeded, so physical or chemical scarification can improve uniformity of germination.

Prior to planting, reduction of the weed seed bank on site and proper field preparation is important. Bigleaf lupine, like many legumes, has hard - coated seeds, so will germinate unevenly if not scarified prior to sowing.

Scarified seeds or plugs should be started in moist to wet soils. The preferred planting method for seed production fields of this species is to plant plugs on wide row spacing (61–91.4 cm) to accommodate plant size and weed management strategies. Direct seeding is not recommended because weeds can out-compete seedlings in the spring.

There are a number of horticultural cultivars available commercially that are sometimes called bigleaf lupines but are actually crosses of L. polyphyllus with L. arboreus and possibly L. nootkatensis. These Russell Hybrids (named for British horticulturist George Russell) are sold under hybrid names such as Rainbow Lupins, Lupin Tutti Fruitti, and Band of Nobles (mixed), Chandelier (yellow), My Castle (red), Noble Maiden (white), The Chatelaine (pink), and The Governor (blue).

Planting in late fall, near a water source, or with irrigation is ideal for emerging L. polyphyllus seedlings. As they mature, however, the established plants are often very prolific and hearty and will not necessarily require irrigation throughout the dry season.

Tribes throughout the range of bigleaf lupine reportedly used different parts of the plant for medicinal or tonic purposes. The Salishan used it to make tonics and the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) ate the roots, fresh or steamed.

Red alder has two adaptations that allow the trees to colonize bare infertile substrates: (1) the roots have nodules that house symbiotic bacteria which fix nitrogen from the air contained in the pores of the soil, and (2) the seeds need sunlight to germinate. Actinomycetes (filamentous bacteria) in the genus Frankia invade alders through their root hairs and stimulate cell division, forming nodules on the roots Species of Frankia remove nitrogen from the air and ‘fix’ it in a form useful to plants. Red alder provides a home for the actinomycete, which in turn ‘leaks’ some of the nitrogen, making it available for the alder.

Found in woodlands, forests, floodplains, streambanks, clearcuts, slides, creeks, beaches, and riparian zones across lowland and montane zones, this taxon is common in coastal British Columbia, extending north to southeast Alaska and south to California. It is frequently associated with mixed evergreen and redwood forests, often forming communities with red alder trees. Red alder itself is primarily observed in moist areas within 200 kilometers of the Pacific Coast from Alaska to southern California at elevations below 762 meters, and ranges along streams and lakes from the Yukon Territory and British Columbia south through the Rocky Mountain region to Colorado and New Mexico, and along the Sierra Nevada to Lower California. Due to increased human disturbance such as logging, it has also successfully colonized upland areas.

A fast-growing, large, deciduous shrub inhabiting moist to wet sites in nutrient-rich soils, reaching 2-6 m in height. Conical clusters of small white flowers turn to an array of small red berries in early summer that are a favourite of many local birds. It features thick, soft, pithy, usually somewhat glaucous twigs, dark reddish-brown warty bark, and conical clusters of small white to creamy flowers that develop into clusters of small, shiny, red, waxy, pulpy berries (leaves, stems, and roots are poisonous) which are favored by local birds. Foliage is opposite, stalked, large, and compound, pinnately divided into 5-7 elliptic to lanceolate leaflets that are often asymmetric at the base, abruptly sharp-pointed at the tip, saw-toothed on the margins, and usually somewhat hairy beneath.

Redmaid seeds and greens were an important food source for many tribes in California including those whose territory neighbored the Salinan. The shiny black seeds were a major ingredient in pinole (from the Aztec word for seed flour, pinolli) and were valued for their high oil content. Small black oil-rich seeds gathered, parched, and ground into nutritious meal.

The seeds were separated by shaking or hitting the plants over the cleaned area or into a basket. Then they were placed into a tightly woven winnowing basket where they were tossed, allowing the moving air to remove any chaff. The seeds were then dried for storage or parched in a cooking basket along with hot coals.
Not only were the seeds used as ceremonial offerings, as evidenced by these burial sites, but also they are often mentioned in Chumash myths.
Dense stands can spread aggressively and crowd out surrounding vegetation if unmanaged.

Salmonberry (Rose Family, Rosaceae) is a moisture-loving, spring-blooming deciduous rhizomatous shrub, 1-4 m tall, often thicket-forming, with erect or arching stems. For best results, seed should be planted into a firm, weed-free seedbed, preferably with a drill that will ensure a uniform seed placement of about 6 mm. The small seed can be broadcast seeded, harrowed, and packed for good seed-soil contact; however, in dryland situations good precipitation at the time of germination is critical for emergence and establishment. The full seeding rate is 1.7 kg/ha PLS (2.0 lb/ac PLS), but this species would seldom be seeded in a pure stand. Seed of Sandberg bluegrass should be drilled at 6–19 mm deep depending upon soil type: 6 mm for fine, moist soils, 13 mm for medium textures, and 1.9 cm for coarse or dry soils. On semiarid lands, 3 pounds pure live seed (PLS) per acre is adequate.

Various "ecotypes" should be utilized within a reasonable geographic range from the original source, since available releases are primarily source identified or selected germplasm releases and have not been progeny tested to determine their range of adaptation and performance. Sandberg bluegrass will withstand heavy grazing and trampling, in part, because of its early maturity and apparent dormancy during the summer and fall grazing period. When planted in a native reclamation mix, it will be a minor component of the establishing plant community; therefore management should be based on other key species in the mixture. Any new planting should be deferred from livestock grazing until it is well established which may require 1 to 3 years.

Inhabiting woodlands, thickets, meadows, dry to mesic open rocky slopes, bluffs, gullies, forest margins, and open forests from the lowland to subalpine zones, this species is common throughout British Columbia, particularly in central and southern regions east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains. Its broader distribution extends north to Alaska, east to Alberta, and south to California, Nebraska, North Dakota, Colorado, and Arizona. It ranges from lower-elevation coniferous forests up to timberline, riparian zones, open or shaded disturbed sites, open woodlands, mountain shrublands, coulees, dry bluffs, and oak meadows, and is distributed along the Pacific coast from Alaska to California, eastward to Utah, Colorado, Iowa, Minnesota, Ontario, and Quebec, and north through the plains and prairies into the Northwest Territories of Canada.

Saskatoon has been artificially crossed with other species of serviceberry, and similar hybridization and intergradation also occurs in the field, particularly between saskatoon and low serviceberry (Amelanchier humilis Wieg.) Cultivars sold as Amelanchier alnifolia may actually be hybrids between A. alnifolia and other species of Amelanchier. Saskatoon reproduces from seed but more commonly by sprouting from the root crown and rhizomes and by layering.

Saskatoon in forests is fire-dependent, occurring in forests with fire regimes varying from frequent, low-severity fire (low-elevation forests) to infrequent, severe fire. It may persist in the understory for decades but eventually dies out with fire exclusion and canopy closure. After top-kill by light-to moderate-severity fire, saskatoon sprouts usually arise from the root crown or from shallowly buried rhizomes; sprouts arise from deeply buried rhizomes after even the most intense fire. Sasktoon cover and biomass production in western Montana may generally increase after fires in Douglas-fir/ninebark habitats, but browsing pressure from big game may slow the recovery.

A perennial forb and native member of the Ranunculaceae family, standing 15-50 cm tall (or stems measuring 15-40 (60) cm tall, extending from 15.2 cm to 0.8 m tall) with yellow flowers bearing 5 to 14 petals. Found in meadows and woodlands, specifically occupying moist to mesic meadows, grassy slopes, coastal bluffs, shores, clearings, and open forests from lowland to subalpine zones; common in coastal and northern British Columbia, infrequent elsewhere, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon, and Northwest Territories, east to Alberta, and south to California.

A perennial forb and native member of the Ranunculaceae family, standing 15-50 cm tall (or stems measuring 15-40 (60) cm tall, extending from 15.2 cm to 0.8 m tall) with yellow flowers bearing 5 to 14 petals. Perennial herb from a cluster of fibrous roots; stems 1 to several, erect or nearly so, 15-40 (60) cm tall, more or less hollow; plants variously hairy. Basal leaves are broadly egg-shaped, semi-circular, or kidney-shaped, measuring ¾ to 5.1 cm long by ¾ to 7.6 cm wide (specifically blades 1.5-5.5 cm long, 2-8 cm wide), deeply 3-lobed or -parted, with segments 1- to 2-times incised and ultimate segments oblong, elliptic, oblanceolate, or lanceolate, toothed, and tips pointed to rounded; leaf stalks are long, measuring 1 to several times the blade length. Stem leaves are alternate, fewer, stay low to the base, are more deeply dissected, shorter-stalked, and transition to 3- to 7-parted lower bracts and entire upper bracts.

Broadcast at a single species application rate of 6 to 7 pounds pure live seed (pls) per acre. Western buttercup has approximately 200,000 seeds per pound, so applying seed at a rate of one pound per acre will result in about 5 seeds per square foot. Field Establishment & Management: There are limited labeled herbicides appropriate for forb species in seed production; therefore, a weed free seedbed is very important. Germination begins 5 to 6 weeks after fall sowing. At the Corvallis PMC, fields are drill planted at a rate of 6 to 7 lb pls/acre at a depth of 3–6 mm with row spacing of 25.4–35.6 cm. When establishing a field with transplants, plugs can be planted as close as 0.3 m centers as plants do not take up much space, but row spacing should be planned to accommodate cultivation and harvest equipment.
There are no improved cultivars of western buttercup, but seed is sometimes available from commercial growers in the Pacific Northwest.

Thriving in meadows, rocky slopes, banks, and rockeries from lowland to montane zones, this plant grows in dry, rocky, or sandy soils requiring a minimum of 25 cm of precipitation at elevations from sea level to 3,050 m. Habitats include roadsides, coulees, bluffs, canyons, dry grasslands, thickets, and forests. It is common on Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland, and rare in south-central and southeastern British Columbia, with a regional range extending from British Columbia south to California and east to Nevada, Utah, Wyoming, and Montana. The species exhibits extensive genetic and phenotypic variation driven by polyploidy, encompassing diploid, tetraploid, hexaploid, and octoploid populations, with California serving as the geographic center of diversity containing 10 of the 12 recognized varieties.

Prairie sagewort, belonging to the Sunflower Family (Asteraceae), is a pleasantly fragrant, spreading perennial shrublet 10-40 cm tall (1-4 dm / 9.9–39.9 cm tall) arising from a stout stem-base or tough, woody crown, often shrubby at the base with several short, leafy offsets. Stems are ascending to erect, white or tawny, and woolly-hairy (whitish or grayish tomentose, having dense, velvety, fuzzy hairs). Basal leaves are few and soon deciduous. Stem leaves are silvery-silky hairy, tomentose, abundant, clustered toward the base and scattered along the stem; lower leaves are petiolate (short-stalked below, 12 mm / 13 mm long), becoming sessile or short-stalked above.

Perennial forb with hairy stems, 0.6–1.5 m tall; velvety opposite leaves to 15.2 cm; rose-colored star-shaped flowers in fuzzy umbel; horn-shaped fruits with silky seeds; sticky sap. Moist to mesic roadsides, ditches, streamsides, meadows, and grasslands in the steppe and montane zones; common in south-central and southeastern British Columbia; east to Manitoba and south to Missouri, Texas, and California; tolerant of moist soils in prairies, meadows, roadsides, streams, and ditches; drought-tolerant; western United States and Canada.

A member of the Milkweed Family (Asclepiadaceae), showy milkweed (Asclepias speciosa) is a hairy perennial forb and herb arising from a rhizome, reaching 0.6–1.5 m tall with erect to ascending stems 0.4-1.2 m tall that are woolly, greyish, or glabrous below, yielding sticky sap and milky juice. The velvety opposite leaves measure to 6 in (10-20 cm long), being simple, fleshy, persistent, and short-petioled with oblong or oval to elliptic or ovate blades, rounded or heart-shaped at the base (rarely cordate and clasping). Asclepias flowers resemble crowns arranged in fuzzy umbels, displaying rose-colored, star-shaped petals with a rose-purple reflexed corolla and hoods elevated above the corolla in pink, aging yellow, with horns exerted beyond the hoods. Edible shoots, buds, flowers, young seed pods, ground seeds. Pueblo people ate green milkweed pods and uncooked roots from one of the species that forms fleshy tubers underground. The young shoots, stems, flower buds, immature fruits, and roots of showy milkweed were boiled and eaten as a vegetable by various indigenous groups of eastern and mid-western America. In some areas the young leaves and stems were used as greens.

People have used milkweed for fiber, food, and medicine all over the United States and southern Canada. Sap used as antiseptic for cuts, ringworm, corns, calluses (Cheyenne). Seed decoction for snakebite (Paiute).

Stems used as cordage. Fibers from the stems of milkweed have been identified in prehistoric textiles in the Pueblo region. Tewa-speaking people of the Rio Grande still make string and rope from these fibers.

Occurs in dry grasslands, shrublands, and forest openings in the steppe and lower montane zones; frequent in south-central British Columbia, becoming less frequent eastward in southern British Columbia; extending east to southwestern Manitoba and south to Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. A perennial, strongly tufted grass from fibrous roots with hollow, minutely rough stems mostly (15) 20-40 cm tall (ranging from 24.1–90.2 cm / 25 to 90 cm in length); open sheaths; mostly basal blades 1-2 mm wide, 7-25 cm long (2.5–24.1 cm / 3.0 to 25 cm long, 1–2 mm / 0.07-0.2 cm wide), typically involute with flat bases, and minutely rough; and ligules scarcely 0.5 mm long, membranous, with frontal margins bearing hairs 2-3 mm long. Purple threeawn is a slender, densely cespitose perennial bunchgrass featuring a sparingly branched panicle inflorescence. Glumes are unequal with the lower glume shorter than the upper, colored light to dark brown or purple. Awns range from 6.1–14 cm (6.0 to 14 cm) in length, with the central awn thicker than the lateral awns.

An evergreen coniferous tree of the cypress family (Cupressaceae) thriving in moist and nutrient-rich soils, reaching 50 (-75) meters tall (historically cited up to 46–61 m / 60 m), often buttressed at the base with a conical to irregular crown; older individuals frequently exhibit multiple leaders and dead spike tops. Branches are arching with pendent, flattened branchlets arranged in fan-shaped sprays, while the aromatic wood features durable, clear grain and a drooping growing tip (leader). Bark is gray to reddish-brown, 10-25 mm thick, ridged and fissured, readily tearing off in long, thin strips. Leaves are evergreen, scale-like, sharply pointed, (1-) 3-6 mm long, somewhat overlapping and closely pressed to the stem in opposite alternating pairs (4 rows), glossy green above with white stripes on the lower surface, turning brown and shedding with age, and emit a spicy fragrance when crushed.

Cone production begins in open-grown trees of western red cedar at about 10-20 years of age but peak production occurs after 70-80 years and may continue for several centuries. Good seed crops are produced at intervals of 2-3 years.

In mixed-species and uneven-aged stands, western red cedars tolerate shady understory conditions and can maintain slow but acceptable growth rates over long periods. In timber harvest of these mixed-species stands, most of these trees are taken by clearcutting. Because of steep terrain, decay, and breakage, harvesting costs are high and lumber recovery is low. Because of its high susceptibility to windthrow in wet environments and in the moist sites where growth and yield are highest, western red cedars should not be left as scattered seed trees.

A deciduous shrub or small tree growing 1-8(-15) meters tall, rhizomatous and forming colonial thickets with smooth mottled brown/grey bark and straight main stems with spreading, ascending branches. Twigs are light brown, sparsely to moderately hairy, and sometimes glandular. Leaves are alternate, deciduous, nearly round to narrowly ovate or ovate-oblong, 4-10 cm long, with a heart-shaped or rounded base, blunt to broadly acute apex, often nearly angular and slightly lobed near the tip, and doubly serrate margins, usually pubescent on major veins and vein axils; petioles may bear glandular hairs. Male (staminate) and female (pistillate) flowers are separate, but both types present on each plant (the species monoecious); male flowers numerous in long, pendulous stalks (catkins) 4-6 cm long, in clusters of 2-3 near branch tips, appearing in the fall but opening the following spring; female flowers: several in a scaly bud, tiny and inconspicuous with only bright red stigma and styles protruding from the otherwise gray-brown buds, almost completely enclosed by bracts, near the end of the twigs.

A nitrogen-fixing deciduous shrub of the Elaeagnaceae family, featuring erect to spreading stems 1-2 m tall (or 0.9–4 m) with young brownish-scaled stems and older brownish, scaly branches. Leaves are opposite, entire, elliptic to narrowly egg-shaped (or oval), 1.5-6 cm long and 1-3 cm wide, greenish on the upper surface with whitish-silvery hairs, and white-scaly and brownish-scaly with rusty brown spots beneath. Inhabits marshes, lakeshores, and streams in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; common throughout British Columbia south of 56°N, becoming less frequent northward; ranging north to Alaska and Yukon Territory, east to Newfoundland, and south to Tennessee, Georgia, Texas, New Mexico, and California. Hardstem bulrush is found at low to mid elevations, generally below 2,300 m, in inundated to periodically wet areas of marshes, swamps, and meadows and along lake, reservoir, and pond shorelines.

Hardstem bulrush is a robust perennial rhizomatous wetland obligate species belonging to the Sedge Family (Cyperaceae), forming dense colonies and reaching up to 3-5 m (typically 100-300, up to 500 cm or 3 m) in height. Stems are circular in cross-section, tapered, firm, and not easily crushed between the fingers, measuring 1-2 cm thick and 1-3 m tall, in upright gray-green to dark-green stands. Leaves are few and short, borne mainly or entirely toward the bases, featuring prominent, well-developed sheaths and poorly developed or absent blades. The inflorescence is a terminal panicle of 3 to 10 spikes comprising up to 50 or more spikelets, each sessile or on a short pedicel, and exceeded by a 2.5 to 10 cm lateral bract.

Water Treatment/Erosion Control: Hardstem bulrush’s dense root mass makes this species an excellent choice for soil stabilization. Its above ground biomass provides protection from erosive wave action and stream currents that erode shorelines or stream banks. The rhizomatous root system also forms a matrix for many beneficial bacteria, making this plant an excellent choice for wastewater treatment (Hurd et al., 1994).
Not suited for heavy foot traffic; best planted in restoration beds, meadows, or borders.

There are no cultivars, improved, or selected materials of hardstem bulrush. Planting plugs (either from the greenhouse or wild transplants) is the surest way to establish a new stand of this species. Care should be taken not to collect plants from weedy areas as weeds can be relocated to the transplant site. Wild plants can be collected and transplanted directly into the desired site. If less than 4 dm² is removed from any 1 m² area (1 ft² in 1 yd²), the hole will fill in within one growing season. Hardstem bulrush reproduces sexually by seed and asexually through vegetative spread via rhizomes.

Water level in a wetland should be fluctuated from saturated conditions up to a maximum depth of 30 cm of standing water for establishing plants. The young plants can handle deeper water, but not for an extended period of time. This species can tolerate periods of drought and total inundation. It will spread into water depths of 1 to 1.5 m.
Common wildland collected seed is available from commercial sources (Native Seed Network).

Seed and young seeds edible. The young sprouts and shoots of hardstem bulrush can be eaten raw or cooked, and the rhizomes and unripe flower heads can be boiled as a vegetable. Hardstem bulrush rhizomes were also sundried and pounded into a kind of flour.
Hardstem bulrush has also been used by Native American tribes medicinally. The Cree used a poultice of stem pith to stop bleeding.
Stems used in basketry. Mat weaving (tule mats, bedding, wall partitions). Gathered stems woven into mats, widely traded among Coast Salish, Interior Salish, and Nuu-chah-nulth.
Navajo and Ramah tribes used the plant as a ceremonial emetic, and the Nlaka'pamux (Thompson) tribe placed ashes from burned stems on a newborn’s bleeding navel.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Pests are generally not a problem. Aphids will feed on the stems, but generally will not kill the plant.

Field mustard is an upright winter annual or biennial that is a member of the mustard family (Brassicaceae).

Cultivars with larger roots, commonly called forage turnip, have been a popular forage crop for livestock in Europe and Asia for at least 600 years (Undersander et al., 1991). Forage turnip is a useful crop for extending the fall grazing season for dairy cows and other livestock (Thomet and Kohler, 2003).

Good seed production requires cross pollination by various insects. One or two hives per acre can ensure good seed set (Duke, 1983). Seed production fields need to have proper isolation distances among varieties and all other forms of B. juncea, B. campestris, and B. napus.

Drill seed in the spring, late summer, or fall at a rate of 1.7–11.2 kg/ha and a depth of ½ to ¾ inch in rows 10.2–30.5 cm apart; alternately, broadcast at 9–15.7 kg/ha followed by cultipacking (Clark, 2007; Knodel and Olson, 2002). Field mustard has approximately 150,000 to 200,000 seeds per pound, so a seeding rate of one pound per acre will result in approximately 3 to 5 seeds per square foot.
Field mustard seed is generally available from commercial cover-crop suppliers, though quantities may be limited.

Soils should be tested prior to planting to determine fertilizer and lime requirements. When planted as a fall catch crop following a cash crop that has been well fertilized, additional fertilizer may not be needed. Lime should be added to correct pH to 5.5 to 6.8. Fertilizer applications, if required, should be banded at least 5.1 cm to the side and below the seed.

Common Fiddleneck is an annual forb and a member of the borage family (Boraginaceae), known for its distinctive helicoid cymes—coiled inflorescences, which are clusters of flowers arranged on a stem. With its vibrant orange-yellow blooms, it is both visually striking and pollinator-friendly. A slender, bristly-hairy native annual forb standing 15–80 cm tall from a taproot, bearing simple to branched stems. Alternate, lance-oblong to linear leaves (2–12 cm long, 0.5–2.5 cm wide) lead up to characteristic coiled scorpioid cymes of small, pale yellow tubular flowers (4–7 mm long) that uncurl as they bloom, yielding bumpy keeled nutlets.

Both species are associated with mixed warm desert shrub, creosote bush, sagebrush steppe, and pinyon-juniper communities in low valleys and foothills. Menzies’ fiddleneck has also been collected in higher-elevation plant communities including mountain brush and aspen-fir communities (Welsh et al., 2003). Bristly fiddleneck is widespread, occurring in all western states from New Mexico north to Idaho and into British Columbia (USDA NRCS, 2023).

Tilley et al. (2023) recommend wearing protective gear to minimize or prevent eye, skin, and inhalation hazards from fiddleneck bristles. Seed can be collected by clipping stems just below the inflorescence or using a racquet and hopper. Raquet and hopper methods allow for multiple harvests and require less hands-on removal of stems.

Tilley et al. (2023) found no significant difference in germination in three different soil types (fine sandy loam, loam, and clay loam). They did find significantly fewer seeds emerged from depths of 1 and 2 cm compared to surface sown seeds. This may indicate a possible light requirement for germination agreeing with Forbis (2010), or it may be the result of low seedling vigor.

Fiddleneck seed is currently difficult to obtain on the commercial market and wildland collection is often the only means of obtaining seed. Seed should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

Bristly and Menzies’ fiddleneck are early seral colonizers. They are typically abundant on disturbed sites for the first few years following disturbance and then reduce in density making way for later seral, longer-lived species. Occasionally these species can form persistent stands, especially under management where succession is interrupted.

Soft-stem bulrush (Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani) is a large, wetland-inhabiting perennial sedge belonging to the Sedge Family (Cyperaceae), sometimes growing in water up to 2 m deep and reaching up to 2-3 m (50-200 cm or more, up to ten feet) in height. Perennial herb from long rhizomes; stems nearly round in cross-section, tapered, smooth, easily crushed between the fingers, 50-200 cm tall or more. Leaves are few, restricted to the base (reaching about 1/2 the length of the stems); sheaths are brown to straw-coloured or mottled brownish, and reddish near the base; blades are usually lacking or numbering 1 or 2, when present C-shaped to flattened top to bottom, much shorter than the sheaths, with margins often minutely rough. Blossoms are borne in an open inflorescence of many stalked, budlike spikelets, covered by reddish brown scales below the top of the stem (Tiner 1987).

The plant arises from long rhizomes with nearly round, tapered, smooth stems that are easily crushed between the fingers.

Hookedspur violet is a common native perennial forb of the violet family (Violaceae) featuring short to elongate, slender rhizomes and growing to approximately 10.2 cm in height. Perennial herb arising from a rhizome, lacking stolons, with stems absent in spring but developing ascending, usually hairy aerial stems 2-10 cm tall as the season progresses. Basal leaves are egg-shaped to heart-shaped with blunt-toothed margins, blades 0.5-4 cm long that are smooth or hairy, and stalks 5-7 cm long. Plants typically produce round to oval 5.1 cm leaves from branched, hairy stems.

Hookedspur violet was used in traditional medicine by the Blackfoot, Nuxalk (Bella Coola) and Tolowa tribes. Leaves and roots were used to treat stomach problems and asthma in children, and as a cataplasm to treat soreness and swelling. In addition, the Southern Dakelh (Carrier), and S'Klallam (Klallam) used the plant as an analgesic and gastrointestinal aid, and the Makah tribe used it as a gynecological aid.

Susceptibility to heart rot and decay is one of the more important factors in management of grand fir. Centers of decay are closely related to logging scars, frost cracks, broken tops, and other mechanical injuries. Grand fir is thin-barked and sensitive to fire – ground fires in moist creek bottoms are highly damaging but trees on dry hillsides are more resistant, largely because of a deeper root system and thicker bark. Control of fires in the drier southern parts of the Northwest has allowed an increase in range of grand fir over the last 50 years.

Late successional, shade-tolerant tree growing in tight clusters ("tree islands"); mature height 4.8 to 7.0 m; seeds passively dispersed by wind/gravity. Inhabits moist to mesic slopes across montane to alpine zones; common in British Columbia in and east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, locally frequent on Vancouver Island; ranges north to south Alaska and Yukon, east to southwestern Alberta, and south to Oregon, northern Nevada, Arizona, and New Mexico.

A cold-hardy, spire-topped subalpine conifer typically growing 15–35 m tall (occasionally up to 50 m in sheltered forests, or forming stunted krummholz mats at timberline). Characterized by smooth, grayish-white bark studded with resin blisters and stiff branches that curve upward. The blunt needles span 1.8–3 cm, displaying a waxy bluish-green hue with stomata across both faces. Upright seed cones measure 6–12 cm in length, clustered near the treetop in deep velvety purple.

Periodic thinning increases the yield and size of individual trees, but the fir component of subalpine spruce-fir stands is likely to be greatly reduced by repeated thinning, so that the stand at the time of final harvest will be almost pure Spruce. In the Cascades, the European balsam woolly adelgid has caused significant mortality to subalpine fir, virtually eliminating it from some stands in Oregon and southern Washington. Windthrow is a common problem in subalpine fir, presumably because of its relatively shallow root system. Pruning should be kept to a minimum, for when older branches are removed, new growth seldom develops and, consequently, the trees become ragged and unkempt.

Silver maple is found on stream banks, flood plains, and lake edges where it grows best on better-drained, moist alluvial soils, at elevations of 30-600 meters. Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.

Silver maple inhabits most of the eastern half of the United States and immediately adjacent Canada, excluding major portions of the Gulf and Atlantic coastal plains. Its natural range extends from Maine, New Brunswick, and southern Quebec, west to Minnesota, southeastern South Dakota, eastern Nebraska, Kansas, and Oklahoma, and south to Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, northwestern Florida, and central Georgia. It is relatively uncommon in the southern portion of its range and absent at higher elevations in the Appalachians; its abundance in natural habitats has declined due to the conversion of bottomland forests for agriculture, while increasing in urban areas as a result of planting.
Vancouver Island; Gulf Islands; Lower Mainland; West of Cascade Crest

Silver maple is susceptible to fire damage because of its thin bark, soft wood, and shallow/surface roots; surface fires kill seedlings and saplings and wound larger trees, exacerbating the tendency to rot. Prescribed fire is not recommended where silver maple is a desirable species.

Due to the abundance of plump, nutritious seed produced by Indian ricegrass, it is considered an excellent food source for birds, such as morning doves, pheasants, and songbirds.

‘Nezpar’ Indian ricegrass was originally collected in 1935 from a site south of White Bird, Idaho by the Washington Plant Materials Center (PMC) staff. It was selected from 152 accessions for its vegetative characteristics and low seed dormancy by the Idaho PMC and released in 1978.

Indian ricegrass establishes slowly and new seedings should not be grazed until at least late summer or fall of the second growing season. It makes its initial growth in early spring and matures seed by mid summer. New stands should not be grazed until the plants are reproducing by seed. Indian ricegrass benefits from grazing use if it is moderately grazed in winter and early spring.

Foundation and registered seed is available through the appropriate state Crop Improvement Association or commercial sources to grow certified seed. It is noted for its large erect plant type, robust stems, abundant leaves, medium to small dark nearly hairless elongated seeds (< 50 percent dormant seeds), and good to excellent seedling vigor. Certified seed is available, and Aberdeen PMC maintains breeder seed. It is considered very drought tolerant, has good seedling vigor, forage, seed yields, and is long lived. Certified seed is available, and Los Lunas PMC maintains breeder seed. Its more acute angle of glumes helps retain seed longer and protects it from seed shatter caused by wind and/or rain. Columbia needlegrass occurs in western North America east to Saskatchewan and Texas, inhabiting openings in upper sagebrush zones, mountain brush, pinyon-juniper, and aspen-fir communities at higher elevations from 1,640 m to 2,400 m, where it is known to form dense stands on open hillsides. It has been known to form dense stands on open hillsides.

A native perennial bunchgrass with erect culms generally measuring 30–60 cm tall (occasionally taller). Basal foliage is narrow and flat to rolled (0.5–5 mm wide), bearing a slender, purplish-tinted contracted panicle with hairy lemmas and distinctive twice-bent awns 20–30 mm in length. Columbia needlegrass is a native perennial bunchgrass with culms typically ranging from 30 to 60 cm tall but larger specimens approaching 3 m tall have been documented (Welsh et al. 2003). Foliage is mostly basal with blades flat to rolled, 0.5-5 mm wide.

Seed can be removed from plant material with a hammermill or brush machine. Seed is cleaned using an air-screen cleaner with 1.40 mm top screen and solid bottom screen and light air. Seed should be stored in cool-dry conditions with temperatures of approximately 10° C (10°C) and relative humidity of 20 to 30%.

The full stand rate for an estimated 50 seeds per square foot would be approximately 1 to 2 lbs/ac. The actual seeding rate should be adjusted to reflect the desired percentage of the overall mix. Seed should be planted at or just below the soil surface, to no more than 3 mm depth.

Nettleleaf giant hyssop should be used as a minor component of pollinator and restoration seed mixtures. Management strategies should be based on the key species in the established plant community. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment.

Limited quantities of wildland collected seed may be available from commercial sources. Commercially available seed sources should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

Erosion control/reclamation: Crested wheatgrass is well adapted for stabilization of disturbed soils in semi-arid sites (Hull, 1974). It establishes quickly and competes well against other aggressive introduced plants during the establishment period. Crested wheatgrass competes better against introduced winter annual species such as cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) and medusahead (Taeniatherum caput-medusae) than most native species because it germinates earlier and grows more rapidly at colder temperatures. Drought tolerance, fibrous root systems, and excellent seedling vigor make crested wheatgrass suited for soil stabilization and reclamation in areas receiving 230 mm or more annual precipitation. These grasses can be used in urban areas where irrigation water is limited to provide ground cover, weed control and to stabilize ditch banks, dikes, pipelines, power lines, and roadsides. In areas above 350 mm annual precipitation, ‘Roadcrest’ and ‘Ephraim’ may exhibit their rhizomatous traits and make excellent low maintenance turf when broadcast seeded to establish lawns. Planted over vast burned areas for soil conservation and erosion control.

Small rodents eat crested wheatgrass seeds. Deer, antelope, and elk graze it, especially in spring and fall.

Seed production of crested wheatgrasses has been very successful under cultivated conditions. Row spacings of 0.6 to 1.0 m under irrigation and 1.0 m under dryland conditions with >350 mm annual precipitation are recommended.

Crested wheatgrass should be seeded with a drill at a depth of 13 mm (½ in) or less on medium to fine textured soils and 25 mm or less on coarse textured soils. The recommended single species seeding rate is 5.6 kg/ha (5 lb/ac) Pure Live Seed (PLS) or 215 PLS/m2 (20 PLS/ft2). If used as a component of a mix, adjust the seeding rate to the percent of mix desired. The recommended seeding rate for seed production in 1.0 m row spacing is 3.1 kg/ha (2.8 lb/ac).

New stands of crested wheatgrass should not be grazed until they are firmly established and have started to produce seed heads. Six inches of new growth should be attained in spring before grazing is allowed in established stands. Three inches of stubble should remain at the end of the grazing season to maintain the long-term health of the plant. In addition, leaving three inches or more stubble going into the winter will result in a 10 to 14 day earlier growth period or “green-up” the following spring.

Foundation and Registered seed are available through the appropriate state Crop Improvement Association or commercial sources to grow certified seed. Douglas has larger seed than other crested wheatgrasses and has excellent seedling vigor. Certified seed is available. ARS in Logan, Utah maintains breeder and foundation seed. It is a good seed producer. Aberdeen PMC maintains breeder and foundation seed. It is a good seed producer and has good lodging resistance. Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada Research Station, Swift Current, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, maintains breeder and foundation seed. Common seed is available, but certified seed is not available. Plants are uniform, erect, with heavy, awnless seeds. The seed heads are dense and compressed. Nordan has good seedling vigor and seed quality, and long-term forage yields are equal to the newer varieties. ARS at the Great Plains Research Laboratory maintains breeder and foundation seed. Summit has not persisted in the seed market because of production issues (Robins & Jensen, 2020). Agri-Food Canada, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, maintains breeder and foundation seed. USDA ARS Logan, Utah maintains breeder and foundation seed. It was selected for improved seedling establishment under harsh dryland conditions and is intended for use on arid and semiarid rangelands. It is intended to replace Hycrest for reseeding sites on heavier soils receiving less than 380 mm annual precipitation.

There are no serious disease problems in crested wheatgrass; however, it is a host of black grass bugs (Irbisia and Labops spp.), which prefer wheatgrasses. Heavily infested plants have reduced green leaf area and appear frosted, yellow or straw colored. Damage can reduce forage yield, plant height and seedhead production.

Inhabits dry to mesic roadsides, fields, and waste places in the lowland and montane zones; common throughout British Columbia; introduced from Europe. Redtop has been cultivated and planted extensively throughout North America and has been widely naturalized in numerous habitats, occurring in areas with shallow water, wet meadows, and stream banks from sea level to 2438 m (Monsen et al., 2004). Redtop can be found growing in pure stands or with other wetland and wet meadow species such as sedges, rushes, and other grasses, and is also common in riparian areas growing in association with cottonwood, alder, and willow species. Native to Eurasia and North Africa, redtop was introduced to North America in the 18th century as a lawn, meadow, and pasture grass (Monsen et al., 2004) and has since become naturalized and widely distributed throughout the United States and Canada, growing better in the moist mountain areas of the West and humid areas of the Northeast than in the warmer climates of the southern states.
Meadow; Rock Garden; Rain Garden / Wetland

Erosion control: Redtop is commonly used for erosion control in plantings along riparian zones and wetlands. It germinates very rapidly and performs well on acidic low fertility soils. Its root system is well suited for holding soils on wetlands, waterways, ditchbanks and burned or cutover-timberland (Wasser, 1982). Revegetation: This species has been used to recapture sites which are very acid to land affected with heavy metals and poor soil quality such as mine spoils. It has been shown to have a higher tolerance of acidic soils than Kentucky bluegrass (Balasko et al., 1995).

Stands should be combined or swathed when plants are in the hard dough stage. Seed shatters readily, so delaying harvest can significantly reduce yields.

Redtop can be established by seed, sprigs, or sod. For seeding, plant at a depth of 0–6 mm into a smooth, firm, well-drained, weed free seed bed. For turf plantings, seed at a rate of approximately 1 lb/1000 ft². Seed production fields should be soil tested before planting to determine soil nutrient levels and fertilizer needs.

There are several released materials of the stoloniferous creeping bentgrass, which are used readily as lawn and golf course varieties. There is currently only one known released variety of redtop. ‘Streaker’ redtop was released in 1982 by Jacklin Seed Company and Lofts Seed.

Stands of redtop should not be grazed until the plants are at least 20.3 cm tall. Pasture mixes will need to be grazed closely in a rotation to keep plants producing palatable regrowth on wet and sub-irrigated sites. Redtop should not be grazed closer than three inches (USDA NRCS, 1995). Cut hay in early flowering stage for best quality.

It was chosen from among 21 lots of seed which were evaluated for uniformity, vigor, seed yield and mechanical purity and cleanliness. It’s intended use is for overseeding of dormant warm season grasses.

Redtop is known to develop ergot which can lead to livestock poisoning (Ontario, 2010). This species can also develop leaf rusts, spotting and snow mold, but these have generally not been a problem (Wasser, 1982). Redtop is an introduced species that can displace native vegetation.

Redtop has been described as weedy or invasive in some states and European countries. It may become weedy or invasive in some regions or habitats and may displace desirable vegetation if not properly managed.

A delicate mountain bunchgrass standing 12–35 cm tall from fibrous root systems with loosely scattered tufts. Leaves are slender and short (1–5 cm long, 0.5–2 mm wide), flat initially and rolling inward with age. Stems terminate in open, diffuse purplish panicles with delicate capillary branchlets. Perennial grass from fibrous roots, with scattered shoots; stems 12-35 cm tall.

Sitka alder grows on soils that vary from infertile mineral to rich humus covered substrates, highly acidic to neutral pH (3.3-7.5), and coarse to medium texture (rocky, gravelly, loamy sands, sandy loams, silts, loams) (Hauessler et al., 1990; Mitchell, 1968). Thriving on moist slopes, streambanks, avalanche tracks, bogs, and fens across all zones; ssp. crispa is frequent in northern British Columbia, while ssp. sinuata is common throughout southern British Columbia, becoming less frequent and transitional to ssp. crispa in northern British Columbia; circumboreal, extending east to Quebec and south to North Carolina, Minnesota, Colorado, and California. Sitka alder is a thicket forming, pioneer, early-seral, and mid-seral species. It is well recognized as an ecologically important species for natural colonization and stabilization of landslide chutes, steep slopes, rock slides, stream banks, areas of flood deposition and scour, and exposed mineral soils following glacial retreat, avalanches, road building, logging, fire, soil slumping, and other drastic disturbances. Typical habitat for Sitka alder includes moist montane woods, rocky or sandy coasts (Alaska), stream banks, bogs, fens, lakeshores, moist talus slopes, the edges of moist meadows, and the north face of rocky outcrops or other shady aspects (Elias, 1980).

The catkins of Sitka alder can be eaten raw or cooked but have a bitter taste (Plants for a Future, 2011). Apparently, young buds and inner bark are edible as well, but the bark will cause vomiting if not dried or aged first.

A decoction of stems was apparently drunk as a remedy for colds or dried stems were placed in the nose or chewed for the same reason (Turner, et al., 1990). Sitka and green alder had several medicinal uses. Pistillate catkins of Sitka alder were crushed and eaten raw for treating gonorrhea. The inner bark or ointments made from it were used to treat skin problems such as wounds, skin ulcers, and swellings.
The bark was a source of red or brown dye which was used to color wool and tanned animal skins. Alder was burned as firewood and preferred for smoking fish.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Sitka alder is a thicket forming, pioneer, early-seral, and mid-seral species. It is well recognized as an ecologically important species for natural colonization and stabilization of landslide chutes, steep slopes, rock slides, stream banks, areas of flood deposition and scour, and exposed mineral soils following glacial retreat, avalanches, road building, logging, fire, soil slumping, and other drastic disturbances.

Sitka alder (Betulaceae family) is a deciduous shrub or small tree that grows to a height of 1-6 m in the mountains and 4-12 m at lower elevations. Initially fast growing, its habit is freely branching at the base, upright to bent, and multi-stemmed with a rounded, open crown. In the wild, crooked or leaning specimens are usually the result of avalanches, slides, or snowpress. Life expectancy is 25 to 50 years under typical growing conditions (Elias, 1980).

Erosion control and reclamation: Sitka alder is a valuable shrub for slope and stream bank stabilization and general erosion control on disturbed, nutrient poor sites. It can be planted for acid, coal, placer, and copper mine spoil reclamation, soil enrichment, and other land rehabilitation efforts where an easy to establish, deciduous shrub is desired (Uchytil, 1989). The species may also be useful in hedgerows, the shrub row of field windbreaks, and other conservation buffers.

Sitka alder grows on soils that vary from infertile mineral to rich humus covered substrates, highly acidic to neutral pH (3.3-7.5), and coarse to medium texture (rocky, gravelly, loamy sands, sandy loams, silts, loams) (Hauessler et al., 1990; Mitchell, 1968). It also does well in heavier clay loam soils that are nutritionally poor but moist (Plants for a Future, 2011).

Typical habitat for Sitka alder includes moist montane woods, rocky or sandy coasts (Alaska), stream banks, bogs, fens, lakeshores, moist talus slopes, the edges of moist meadows, and the north face of rocky outcrops or other shady aspects (Elias, 1980). Sitka alder freely interbreeds with green alder (A. viridis ssp. fruticosa) and intermediate types can be found in British Columbia (Hauessler et al., 1990).

The catkins of Sitka alder can be eaten raw or cooked but have a bitter taste (Plants for a Future, 2011). Apparently, young buds and inner bark are edible as well, but the bark will cause vomiting if not dried or aged first.

A decoction of stems was apparently drunk as a remedy for colds or dried stems were placed in the nose or chewed for the same reason (Turner, et al., 1990). Sitka and green alder had several medicinal uses. Pistillate catkins of Sitka alder were crushed and eaten raw for treating gonorrhea. The inner bark or ointments made from it were used to treat skin problems such as wounds, skin ulcers, and swellings.

This plant is native to the colder regions of Europe and Asia. It ranges naturally from the British Isles in the west to Siberia in the east going as far south as Turkey and Italy and possibly China. Records indicate that creeping foxtail was introduced into the United States around the end of the 19th century. At the time, it was little used by farmers who lacked the specialized equipment to plant and harvest its small fluffy seeds.

Erosion control: Creeping foxtail’s vigorous rhizome production (up to 120 cm crown diameter/year) and water tolerance make it well suited to erosion control and stream bank stabilization. Creeping foxtail can tolerate both high water levels and periods of drought, it can be used on earthen dams where water levels fluctuate. It survives in a broad range of pH, making it suitable for mine spoils, saline seeps (tolerant to ECs of 12) bogs and acidic roadways.

Seed production practices for creeping foxtail are more involved and difficult than those of most other forage grasses. Harvest timing is critical for a good yield, and seed cleaning requires more time and equipment than for most other grass species. Stands should be planted in wide-spaced 91.4–121.9 cm rows, but rhizomes cause sod binding and row closing.
Creeping foxtail establishment techniques are similar to those for other forage grasses. For best results the seedbed should be weed free, moist and firmly packed.

Young seedlings are small and weak. Growth is slow for the first 4 to 6 weeks even under irrigated conditions. Rhizomes can emerge as early as 8 weeks. With the emergence of rhizomes, growth is rapid.

Foundation seed is available through the appropriate state Crop Improvement Association or commercial sources to grow certified seed. Certified seed is available. Powdery mildew (Erysiphe cruciferarum) infection of desert madwort has been reported in Turkey and Romania. Desert madwort is weedy on disturbed sites and can displace desired native vegetation if not properly managed. For example, the presence of desert madwort in the Gardiner Basin of Yellowstone National Park, Montana has made it nearly impossible for native plants to establish. Plants should not be intentionally propagated because, once established, desert madwort may become invasive. Plants typically flower in early spring to mid-summer, with seeds being dispersed by mid-summer. Seed production is greatest in climates of harsh, cold winters and hot, dry summers. | Host insect damage: Idaea rusticata: on leaves; Selania malcolmiae: in shoots; Tatochila autodice: on leaves

The species is tolerant of most soil textures and occurs from near sea level to subalpine altitudes. It is found on open, dry rocky slopes to partially shaded sites with moist, deep soils but prefers moist, well-drained, acid soil and full sun or partial shade (Dirr 1983). Plants of Amelanchier alnifolia can even be grown in granitic mine spoil and produce reasonable growth, but not on pyritic spoil (Voeller and others 1998). This plant is generally not tolerant of saline soils and high water tables.

Pacific serviceberry is reported as a component of Quercus garryana, prairie, mixed conifer, and Pseudotsuga menziesii/Pinus contora/Berberis nervosa/Spirea betulifolia plant communities (Franklin and Dryness 1973).

Tilley et al. (2023) recommend wearing protective gear to minimize or prevent eye, skin, and inhalation hazards from fiddleneck bristles. Seed can be collected by clipping stems just below the inflorescence or using a racquet and hopper. Raquet and hopper methods allow for multiple harvests and require less hands-on removal of stems.

Tilley et al. (2023) found no significant difference in germination in three different soil types (fine sandy loam, loam, and clay loam). They did find significantly fewer seeds emerged from depths of 1 and 2 cm compared to surface sown seeds. This may indicate a possible light requirement for germination agreeing with Forbis (2010), or it may be the result of low seedling vigor.

Bristly and Menzies’ fiddleneck are early seral colonizers. They are typically abundant on disturbed sites for the first few years following disturbance and then reduce in density making way for later seral, longer-lived species. Occasionally these species can form persistent stands, especially under management where succession is interrupted.

Fiddleneck seed is currently difficult to obtain on the commercial market and wildland collection is often the only means of obtaining seed. Seed should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

Indian hemp plants are not widely available. Transplanting bare rootstock or collecting seed for direct reseeding into the ground will be necessary in most areas. Use of plants which have been traditionally used by the ancestors of that place, and which are adapted to the climate, soils, and site conditions of that place, is optimum.

When used for fiber, Indian hemp is collected in the autumn after the leaves have begun to senesce or dry up and the stalks turn a deep reddish brown color. Plants are cut at the base of the stem. Cutting the plants appears to stimulate new growth in the spring; so as many stalks as possible are cut. Plants are then split open and the fibers removed and processed into cordage.
Apocynum cannabinum is available from native plant nurseries within its range.

Indian hemp could be dried, crushed, and then snuffed for coughs in head colds. The root was made into a tea and was used to help a baby’s cold, earache, headache, nervousness, dizziness, worms and insanity. It acts as a vaso-constrictor, slows and strengthens the heartbeat, and raises blood pressure. Root tea used cautiously for heart palpitations and cardiac disorders.

The fibers are then twisted into string, which provides cordage. String, thread, rope, baskets, snares, netting, and clothing were made from the bast fibers of the Indian hemp plant because they are so silky yet strong. Strong fibre bark, twine, and woven products (bags, mats, fishnets) widely traded as exchange medium. Fibers woven into large gathering bags holding up to four dry gallons of bulbs. Blackburn and Anderson (1993) quote Craig Bates of the Yosemite Museum that it takes approximately five stalks of milkweed or Indian hemp to manufacture one foot of cordage.

Cordage was then used to make tump straps, belts, netted bags, hairnets, and ceremonial regalia (capes, skirts, and head-dresses). It is carried with great pride as part of ceremonial regalia, the twined handbag emphasizing the distinct cultural heritage of the person who carries it.

Tall oatgrass is genetically tetraploid and is wind pollinated, although self-fertilization may occur. Due to the uneven timing of seed ripening and seed shattering, seed harvest has proven difficult. There are approximately 150,000 to 189,000 seeds per pound of tall oatgrass.

Ensure the seedbed is firm and free of weeds. For best results, seed in the spring as seedlings are not winter hardy. Recommended seeding rates range from 5 to 8 pounds Pure Live Seed (PLS) lbs per acre.

There are two tall oatgrass cultivars released in the United States. ‘Tualatin’ from Oregon State University was released for improved seed retention and ‘Ruffner’ from USDA’s Plant Materials Center in West Virginia was released for use as a cool season forage.
During the establishment year, control of broadleaf weeds is recommended to increase the success of the stand.
These plant materials may be available from commercial seed producers.

Douglas’ sagewort seeds germinate at relatively cool temperatures to coincide with fall precipitation. Direct seeding can be done throughout the late fall and winter on prepared sites at a seeding rate of 2.5 kg/ha drilled at a depth of ¼ inch, or 3.4 kg/ha broadcast. At Elkhorn Slough on the central California Coast field plantings were generally most successful in the early spring (ESNERR, 2001).
Cultivars should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

White sage is a white-woolly, perennial aromatic herb in the Sunflower Family (Asteraceae) with a strong odor of sagebrush, arising from creeping rhizomes with erect, simple or clustered stems 0.3-1.0 m tall (3-7 dm / 1-2 1/4 ft tall) bearing white matted hairs. Stem leaves are alternate, numerous, lanceolate to oblanceolate or elliptic, 3-9 cm long (or 3-11 cm / 3.2–11.4 cm long) and 10-21 mm wide (up to 1.5 cm / 14 mm wide), with dense white matted hairs on both sides or loosely woolly to green and glabrate above. Leaf margins are entire to deeply or irregularly lobed or toothed, with lobes sometimes again toothed or irregularly lobed. Small, tight, greenish flower heads cluster among leaves near stem ends from August through September, yielding dry, smooth, broadly cylindrical achenes.

Other tribes who used white sage include the Arapaho, Comanche, Gros Ventre, Creek, Navaho, Tewa, and Ute (Nickerson 1966, Carlson and, Denig 1855, Elmore 1944), Robbins et al. 1916, The Dakota and other tribes used white sage tea for stomach troubles and many other ailments. The Cheyenne used the crushed leaves as snuff for sinus attacks, nosebleeds, and headaches. The Kiowa made a bitter drink from white sage, which they used to reduce phlegm and to relieve a variety of lung and stomach complaints Usually, they chewed the stem and leaves and swallowed the juice. They used a strong tea as an astringent for eczema and as a deodorant and an antiperspirant for underarms and feet. The Omaha used the leaves in a tea for bathing and used the powdered leaves to stop nosebleeds. Both the Pawnee and the Bannock women drank Artemisia ludoviciana tea during their moon time, or menstrual periods (Dunbar 1880).

Burning white sage and “smudge sticks” (the process of harvesting sage stems and tying the stem together into a “smudge stick”), was and is used for cleansing and purification, White sage or “man sage” was perhaps the most important ceremonial plant of the Cheyenne. The sage was spread along the borders and on the altar in almost every ceremonial lodge (including the stone peoples lodge or sweat lodge) with the flowering end toward the fire.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

The Kiowa made a bitter drink from white sage, which they used to reduce phlegm and to relieve a variety of lung and stomach complaints Usually, they chewed the stem and leaves and swallowed the juice. They used a strong tea as an astringent for eczema and as a deodorant and an antiperspirant for underarms and feet. The Omaha used the leaves in a tea for bathing and used the powdered leaves to stop nosebleeds. Both the Pawnee and the Bannock women drank Artemisia ludoviciana tea during their moon time, or menstrual periods (Dunbar 1880).

Burning white sage and “smudge sticks” (the process of harvesting sage stems and tying the stem together into a “smudge stick”), was and is used for cleansing and purification, White sage or “man sage” was perhaps the most important ceremonial plant of the Cheyenne. The sage was spread along the borders and on the altar in almost every ceremonial lodge (including the stone peoples lodge or sweat lodge) with the flowering end toward the fire.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Revegetation/reclamation: Because of its wide range of adaptation and ease of establishment, big sagebrush can be a very important species for use in revegetation efforts. Seedlings are able to compete with grasses and forbs as well as other shrubs allowing it to be used as a component of a wide range of seed mixes. Seedlings are very easy to establish when planted correctly and can be drill seeded or broadcast with near equal levels of success. Because sagebrush plants spread readily by seed, it can be seeded at relatively low rates and allowed to spread by natural recruitment. Big sagebrush plants provide many additional benefits to the plant community. The dense canopy protects understory herbaceous plants from grazing. Healthy sagebrush communities provide a multi-tiered ecosystem with high levels of biodiversity. Big sagebrush plants also have a two-part root system with a deep tap root and a shallow, diffuse root system. Numerous studies have shown sagebrush plants create “hydraulic lift” where deep soil moisture is brought to near the soil surface by the tap root system during the day and then released into the upper soil at night. This water is then available to the diffuse root system of big sagebrush as well as to the roots of other understory plants. Sagebrush plants also increase water retention by trapping and holding windblown snow. Big sagebrush subspecies are often useful indicators of soil characteristics. Generally, a subspecies indicates the soils at a site, thus proper identification of big sagebrush at a subspecific level can provide useful information on soils and ecological site characteristics. In some areas, however, such as those with glacial deposits, a separation based on soil characteristics is considerably more complex.

The vast majority of big sagebrush seed used in revegetation is wildland collected material. Seed collection occurs in late fall to early winter (early October through the end of December) depending on the subspecies. Seed of big sagebrush are best adapted to germinate in habitats with ecological conditions approximating those of the seed collection site. Seed source and subspecies should always be seriously considered prior to seeding. It may be necessary to use seed from more than one subspecies in a given revegetation project to ensure adequate establishment in all habitats.
‘Hobble Creek’ mountain big sagebrush was released by the Utah Agricultural Experiment Station, Utah State University and the USDA Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station in 1987.

Historically, sagebrush communities have been poorly managed, mostly in attempts to reduce or eliminate sagebrush stands to increase forage production for livestock. Recently, however, the value of sagebrush to the western rangelands is being recognized, and practices are evolving to better manage healthy and productive sagebrush communities. Contrary to long standing beliefs, studies show that complete sagebrush removal negatively affects biodiversity and has little long term affect on perennial grass production. Indeed, several studies indicate that forage production may actually decline when sagebrush is completely removed or controlled.

Persistent fruit, hips, cones, or dried seedheads add late-season visual interest and winter wildlife forage.

Dry slopes and shrublands in the steppe zone; locally frequent in extreme south-central British Columbia; south to Colorado and California. This species commonly occurs in dry plains and hills of the sagebrush steppe and grassland communities, often in association with big sagebrush (A. tridentata), bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), and Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda).

This perennial, mildly aromatic, evergreen shrub grows 20-80 cm tall, with threetip sage characterized as a medium-sized shrub reaching 0.9–1.8 m tall with silvery green herbage. Stems solitary or branched from the base with shredding, grey or light brown bark when older or with a dense, grooved, white-woolly hairiness on the twigs, 20-80 cm tall. The principal leaves are short-stalked, grey-hairy, 0.5-3.0 cm long, and deeply divided into 3 linear or narrowly lanceolate lobes which may sometimes be 3-cleft, or with some leaves linear and entire; overall leaves are distinctly three-cleft with linear lobes (Welsh et al., 2003).

Edible, possibly medicinal root. The root is analgesic and antihaemorrhagic and can be chewed or used as a tea to treat chest and back pains, coughs and spiting up of blood. A poultice made from the chewed root has also been used to treat cuts.
Not safe for ingestion by children, pets, or livestock.

Canadian milkvetch looks similar to some closely related poisonous locoweeds, so its use is not recommended unless positive identification can be made. Many members of this genus contain a poison that affects cattle. They become affected with a sort of insanity, a slow poisoning that can cause death within a period of months or even a year or two.

Short-toothed Canada milkvetch seed should be scarified before planting. It has potential for high incidence of hard seed in the order of 85 to 90 percent. Scarified seed of good quality should germinate at a range of 85 to 90 percent or more.

Currently, there are no known cultivars of short-toothed Canada milkvetch on the commercial market. The Pullman Washington Plant Materials Center has a selection of short-toothed Canada milkvetch that is scheduled for release.
Seed production hinges on successful cross pollination of flowers by insects. Careful thought should be given to this fact when applying pesticides in the vicinity of Canada milkvetch plants.

Average seed yields range from 400-600 lb/ac in Montana and Wyoming. Yields as high as 1000 lb/ac have been recorded. Dryland yields average between 100 and 200 lb/ac.

Cicer milkvetch seed has an extremely hard seed coat which results in low germination of untreated seed. Seed coats respond well to mechanical or chemical scarification which facilitates air and water imbibition and allows germination.

Cicer milkvetch is a long lived perennial, and stands normally improve with age due to the proliferation of plants via rhizomes. Leaves and stems stay green and succulent later into fall than alfalfa, but spring growth starts 14 to 28 days later than alfalfa. Growth rates increase with rising temperatures. To control weeds during establishment mow weeds to an 20.3 cm height to keep weeds from overtopping cicer milkvetch seedlings and to reduce weed seed.

Clones and breeder seed are maintained by the USDA-ARS, Fort Collins, CO. Oxley II was developed for improved seedling vigor and forage yield.
