Found in dry sagebrush flats and grassy slopes within steppe and lower montane zones; rare in south-central and southeastern British Columbia, extending south to Washington, north-central Oregon, and Mexico. Basalt milkvetch occurs in juniper and sagebrush plant communities in arid to semi-arid sites across western North America (Welsh et al., 2003), as well as in ponderosa pine forests and chaparral ecosystems (Johnson et al., 2008). It is possibly one of the most widely distributed species of Astragalus (Isley, 1998), spanning from northern Mexico to southern British Columbia (Bhattarai, 2007) at elevations from 200 to 2,500 m in sites receiving 12.7–76.2 cm of annual precipitation (Bhattarai, 2007). The species is locally abundant in the Columbia Basin and Great Basin, particularly within the Owyhee Desert, Snake River Plains, and the Lahontan Basin through the Humboldt River valley (Cronquist et al., 1989).

Restoration: Basalt milkvetch is one of the few native legumes that is adapted for use in restoration in the semi-arid west. As a legume, it has the ability to add nitrogen to rangeland plantings, and it is known to resprout readily after fire making it a valuable species for the fire-prone west. Basalt milkvetch is safe to be used in grazing areas. Unlike many milkvetch and locoweed species, basalt milkvetch does not pose any threat to livestock from toxicity. Basalt milkvetch can also produce new shoots from lateral roots; which may help basalt milkvetch persist under grazing (Bhattarai, 2007).

Reliable seed production of basalt milkvetch has been problematic. The upright stems of basalt milkvetch make seed much easier to harvest than low-growing Astragalus species; however, high rates of plant mortality in test plots in Utah had significant effects on seed production.

Basalt milkvetch has physical seed dormancy due to a hard seed coat which inhibits water imbibition (Shock, 2008). Jones et al. (2016) found that scarification for 6 seconds with a Forsberg Line debearder (Fred Forsberg & Sons, Inc., Thief River Falls, MN) modified with four internal paddles and lined with medium-grit emery paper increased tetrazolium imbibition by 8.6%, yet the percentage of hard seed was still very high following scarification (74.7%). Shock (2008) found that lightly mechanically scarifying the seed for 7.5 seconds in a hand-made scarifier with 220-grit sandpaper significantly improved germination when compared to a non-scarified control or seed that was scarified for 15 or 30 seconds. High density plantings using transplanted tubelings are often chosen over direct seeding due to poor establishment from seed.

NBR-1 Germplasm basalt milkvetch was released in 2008 by the USDA-ARS Forage and Range Research Lab in cooperation with the Utah Agricultural Experiment Station and Utah State University. It is intended for conservation uses including post-fire reclamation, rangeland restoration, wildlife habitat improvement and plant diversity enhancement in the Northern Basin and Range Ecoregion (Johnson et al., 2008). The I-49 strain of rhizobium from Nitragin Company (Milwaukee, WI) was found to create the highest nodule weight and number of nodules among six accessions of basalt milkvetch from CA, OR, NV, ID and BC (Bhattarai, 2007). Greenhouse trials involving a single accession of basalt milkvetch indicated that plants inoculated with I-49 also developed a higher nitrogen pool and greater number of nodules compared to other tested rhizobium strains (Bhattarai, 2007).

Basalt milkvetch should be used as a minor component of restoration seed mixtures. Management strategies should be based on the key species in the established plant community. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment.

Fourwing saltbush begins growth in mid to late spring. Seed matures 3 to 4 months after flowering. It typically spreads via seed distribution, and may also root sprout following wildfire or layer if covered with sand.

'Marana' fourwing saltbush was released in 1979 by the NRCS Plant Materials Center in Lockeford, California. Plant spacing should be 1.8–2.4 m within row and 2.4–3 m between rows. Planting one male plant for every 5 female plants is recommended.

Fourwing saltbush is palatable to cattle, sheep and deer season long. It provides nutritious winter browse on many areas and is a good fall and winter browse plant for bighorn sheep, antelope, and elk. In new plantings, utilizing good seedbed and weed control techniques should enhance establishment and reduce competition with other plants. In interseedings, plant competition should be reduced by chemical, scalping, furrowing or other techniques that help control existing vegetation and weeds.

Inhabiting dry grassy slopes in the montane zone; rare in northeastern British Columbia, known exclusively from Clayhurst Crossing, Peace River; extending east to Saskatchewan and south to Idaho, Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, and Arizona. Gardner’s saltbush inhabits drylands, salt desert shrub ecosystems, mixed grasslands among sagebrush, saltbush, and greasewood species, and occurs in pure stands (Nord et al., 1968).

A perennial semishrub with a woody base arising from a taproot, featuring erect or spreading, freely branched stems 10-60 cm tall, with the lower one-third less herbaceous than the upper two-thirds and capable of developing adventitious roots; leaves are alternate, opposite, or subopposite, petiolate or sessile, narrowly spoon-shaped to oblong, linear, oblanceolate, obovate, spatulate, or orbiculate, 2-5 cm long, 2-12 mm wide, narrowed gradually to a short stalk or sometimes unstalked, with cuneate bases, simple entire margins, and densely greyish-scurfy surfaces. Inflorescence is a spike or panicle, 2.5–25.4 cm high with yellow or brown clustered flowers that are less than ¼ inch long, sessile or on a stalk (Robson, 2008). Seeds develop July through August, are teardrop-shaped, tan or brown in color, short in length and less than 1/10 of an inch wide (Robson, 2008). Gardner’s saltbush is a warm-season perennial subshrub or shrub-forb that can grow to 50.8 cm tall (Jacobs, 2001).

Drill seeding is an effective method for establishing Gardner’s saltbush. Seed should be dormant planted, after November 1 in Bridger, Montana, though spring plantings in April or May are possible (Carlson et al., 1984). For a full stand, 3 Pure Live Seeds (PLS) should be planted per square foot or linear foot or 1 PLS lb/acre (USDA-NRCS, 2013). Full stand seed production entails dormant fall drill seeding of de-winged seeds at 3 PLS per linear foot at approximately ½ inch in depth.
Plant selections (cultivars, germplasms, and seed sources) should be chosen based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

Minimizing soil surface disturbance is the best management approach for Gardner’s saltbush. Newly seeded Gardner’s saltbush sites should be protected from livestock grazing for three or more years. Once established, grazing can occur when plants are dormant, but should cease before spring plant growth ensues. Gardner’s saltbush should not be grazed heavily as weedy and invasive species such as halogeton (Halogeton glomeratus) and cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) can replace it. Irrigate to keep soil moisture above 50% field capacity.
There are no known Gardner’s saltbush seed sources for conservation purposes.

Inhabiting dry grassy slopes in the montane zone; rare in northeastern British Columbia, known exclusively from Clayhurst Crossing, Peace River; extending east to Saskatchewan and south to Idaho, Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, and Arizona. Gardner’s saltbush grows in drylands, salt desert shrub ecosystems, in mixed grasslands among sagebrush, saltbush and greasewood species and in pure stands (Nord et al., 1968).

A perennial semishrub with a woody base, featuring erect or spreading, freely branched stems 10-60 cm tall and alternate, narrowly spoon-shaped to oblong leaves 2-5 cm long and 2-12 mm wide that narrow gradually to a short stalk or are sometimes unstalked, densely greyish-scurfy, and usually smooth-margined. Gardner’s saltbush is a warm-season perennial subshrub or shrub-forb that can grow to 50.8 cm tall (Jacobs, 2001; McArthur & Monsen, 2004). Leaves are simple with entire margins and a cuneate base (Robson, 2008).

Inhabiting dry grassy slopes in the montane zone; rare in northeastern British Columbia, known exclusively from Clayhurst Crossing, Peace River; extending east to Saskatchewan and south to Idaho, Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, and Arizona. Gardner’s saltbush grows in drylands, salt desert shrub ecosystems, in mixed grasslands among sagebrush, saltbush and greasewood species and in pure stands (Nord et al., 1968). It is considered a principal component of salt-desert shrub ranges (Blaisdell & Holmgren, 1984; McArthur & Monsen, 2004). Gardner’s saltbush grows in semi-arid to temperate climates from 884–2560 m in elevation on ridgetops, slopes, uplands, canyon bottoms, rolling plains and in disturbed areas (McArthur & Monsen, 2004; Rocky Mountain Herbarium, 2008; Flora of North America, 2021).
Not suited for heavy foot traffic; best planted in restoration beds, meadows, or borders.

Drill seeding is an effective method for establishing Gardner’s saltbush. Seed should be dormant planted, after November 1 in Bridger, Montana, though spring plantings in April or May are possible (Carlson et al., 1984). For a full stand, 3 Pure Live Seeds (PLS) should be planted per square foot or linear foot or 1 PLS lb/acre (USDA-NRCS, 2013).

There are no known Gardner’s saltbush seed sources for conservation purposes. Plant selections (cultivars, germplasms, and seed sources) should be chosen based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

Coyotebrush is found in several habitats including Coastal Strand, Northern Coastal Scrub, Coastal Sage Scrub, Chaparral, Foothill Woodland, Mixed Evergreen Forest, Closed-cone Pine Forest (Calflora, 1997).

Coyotebrush is a native, perennial, evergreen shrub in the Asteraceae family with either an erect, rounded or procumbent habit. It ranges in height from 0.3–3.7 m, depending upon the subspecies and location (Bogler, Robbins et al., 1970). The stems are dark brown, hairless and shiny; they may be scurfy and are usually resinous and sticky. Leaves are alternate and either lacking or with a short petiole, they are broadly ovate or wedge shaped from ½ to 2.5 cm long.

Erosion Control and Habitat Restoration: Coyotebrush has been successfully used for erosion control. For sloping areas, B. pilularis. Ssp. pilularis, is a good choice due to its low growing and spreading habit (Steinberg, 2002). In areas adjacent to established coyotebrush stands recruitment can be spontaneous from wind dispersed seeds. Coyotebrush habitat can act as a nurse crop for tree species and is useful for restoration of oak woodlands.

Coyotebrush has low palatability and nutritional value for grazers and browsers, cattle will graze it if nothing else is available but will more likely trample the plants.

Seed can be collected with a cloth spread around and under the coyotebrush. The seed should be dried in a warm ventilated room or in the sun without wind. Sometimes the tufts of hair on the seed (known as the pappus) are removed before planting.

Coyotebrush is tolerant of a wide range of soil types including alkaline soils, clay and sandy soils, and some plants tolerate serpentine soils. The seeds have no stratification or temperature requirement and will germinate on mineral soil (Olsen, 1974). Seeds mature in late fall through winter and are wind dispersed, so this is the best time to establish a planting.
There are also several named cultivars including B. pilularis. Ssp. pilularis, 'Pigeon Point', which is a vigorous, long lasting cultivar with dark green foliage that grows 0.3 m tall by 3.7 m wide.
Coyotebrush can be pruned to a desired shape, or it can be coppiced, cut back to 15.2 cm in height and will sprout from the base.
The wide distribution, ease of vegetative propagation and successful production from seed results in locally adapted plant materials being available from local nurseries.

There is a report of an infusion of coyotebrush used as a general remedy by the Costanoan Indians. A decoction prepared from the leaves was a remedy for poison oak rash used by the Chumash Indians on the Santa Ynez Reservation in the late 1950s.
Chestnut (1902) reported that the Indians of Mendocino County had formerly used the brittle stems of coyotebrush as arrows.

A perennial herb featuring large, arrow-shaped basal leaves and bright yellow sunflower-like blooms. Inhabiting dry grasslands, shrublands, and open forests in steppe and montane zones, including meadows, shrublands, grasslands, and subalpine to alpine zones such as Neskonlith Meadows; common in southern British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, extending east to Alberta, south to South Dakota, Colorado, and California, and occurring throughout western North America to Arizona; commonly associated with sagebrush communities—including basin big sagebrush, mountain big sagebrush, threetip sagebrush, and infrequently Wyoming big sagebrush—as well as mountain shrub, pinyon-juniper, ponderosa pine, Douglas fir, and aspen plant communities on open hillsides and prairies at mid to upper elevations.

Arrowleaf balsamroot is a long-lived perennial forb native to western North America, featuring a deep taproot and woody stem-base with ascending, few to several, minutely glandular and short-woolly stems 20-80 cm tall. The taproots can reach 2.7 m long and 10 cm in diameter, with deep lateral roots running horizontally for 60 to 100 cm. The sagittate leaves are mostly all basal and petiolate, 5 to 45 cm long and 1.5 to 15 cm wide, silvery especially beneath with fine, close, felt-like woolly hairs, becoming green with age, and entire; upper stem leaves are smaller, lanceolate to spoon-shaped, and linear to elliptic. Several flower stems arise from the root crown to a height of 15 to 80 cm, bearing a solitary floral head with bright yellow sunflower-like blooms comprising 8 to 25 ray flowers with 20 to 60 mm long petals surrounding a disk 12 to 25 mm in diameter, with both ray and disk flowers fertile.

Arrowleaf balsamroot is a long-lived perennial forb native to western North America, featuring a deep taproot and woody stem-base with ascending, few to several, minutely glandular and short-woolly stems 20-80 cm tall.

Basal leaves long-stalked, the blades mostly triangular, 10-50 cm long, 10-20 cm wide, silvery, especially beneath, with fine, close, felt-like woolly hairs, green with age, entire; stem leaves several, lanceolate to spoon-shaped, greatly reduced.

Heads possess ray and disk flowers and are solitary or rarely few, with the disk measuring 2.5 cm or more and any lateral heads being smaller; involucral bracts are lanceolate to oblong-lanceolate, slightly woolly, with the outer ones 1-2.5 cm long, herbaceous, and exceeding the inner ones; ray flowers number 8-25, commonly 13 or 21 in a terminal head, are yellow, 2.5-4.0 cm long, and soon deciduous; disk flowers measure 6-8 mm long and are yellow.

Seed of arrowleaf balsamroot requires stratification for germination (Chambers and others, 2006; Young and Evans, 1979). Seed should be sown into containers to a depth of 0.6 to 1.3 cm and lightly covered with pea gravel and then placed outdoors in late fall or early winter for natural stratification.

Arrowleaf balsamroot should be drilled seeded into a weed free seed bed in late fall. Seeding depth should be set to 0.6 to 1.3 cm. Broadcast seeding can be successful if the seed is subsequently covered.
There are currently no commercial releases of arrowleaf balsamroot.

Arrowleaf balsamroot should be used as a minor component of seed mixtures. Management strategies should be based on the key species in the established plant community. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment (Ogle and others, 2011a; Stevens and Monsen, 2004).
Wildland collected seed is available from commercial sources.

Inhabiting shores, marshes, wet meadows, and ditches in steppe and montane zones; frequent throughout British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains; ranging north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to Quebec, and south to Maine, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California; known to occur in the presence of gravitational water, either permanently or for extended periods during the growing season, particularly within the three wettest drainage regimes.

American sloughgrass is a cool-season annual or short-lived perennial grass commonly found in shallow marshes or sloughs, often possessing stolons and a shallow root system supporting an erect, hollow, leafy stem up to 100 cm tall. Sheaths are open; blades are mostly 5-10 mm wide and flat; ligules are 6-11 mm long, pointed, entire or commonly with jagged margins, usually folded back in growth, and hairy. Basal leaves contain cross veins intersecting longitudinal veins at right angles to form rectangles. The spikelets have very short pedicels and are arranged on only one side of the panicle branches (Reeder, 1953).

Boe and Evans (1981) reported that panicles of American sloughgrass bagged to prevent cross pollination exhibited 100% seed set.

Propagation of American sloughgrass via seed is the preferred method since there aren’t any dormancy restrictions that inhibit rapid and uniform germination. The planting site should be prepared and tilled to discourage weeds during the establishment period. The best planting times in the Great Plains are late fall, to allow fall establishment, or a dormant seeding, which would promote early spring establishment.
‘Egan’ American sloughgrass was named and released as a cultivar by the Alaska Plant Materials Center at Palmer, Alaska in 1986. The original seed collection was made by James R.

Beal (1896) pointed out that Beckmannia syzigachne was a forage grass of some prominence west of the Mississippi River. It is palatable to livestock and is frequently hayed or grazed. Forage nutritional data. National Academy of Science, 1971 indicated it is high in protein and nonstructural carbohydrates.

The original seed collection was made by James R. The seed was harvested from a single plant growing on a gravel road fill site off Steese Highway in Gold Stream Valley, North of Fairbanks, Alaska. Breeder and Foundation seed production will be maintained by the Alaska Plant Materials Center. Foundation class seed will be available from the Alaska Seed Growers, Inc. to seed growers for the production of Certified class seed (Alaska Plant Materials Center, 1986).

The Alaska Plant Materials Center has found that if ‘Egan’ is grown on upland farm land without irrigation, the plants will be stressed to the point of disease onset.

Inhabiting dry grasslands in the steppe zone, this species is rare in south-central and southeastern British Columbia, ranging east to southern Manitoba and south to Maine, New York, South Carolina, Missouri, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. Blue grama performs best in the drier regions of the northern and southern Great Plains and the southwestern United States, naturally occurring in mixed stands—primarily with buffalograss (Bouteloua dactyloides), needle-and-thread (Hesperostipa comata), western wheatgrass (Pascopyrum smithii), and green needlegrass (Nassella viridula)—in shortgrass prairie settings, while also associating with species such as prairie sandreed and sand sagebrush in sandier habitats. Blue grama is most effective when grown in the dryer parts of the northern and southern Great Plains and southwestern region of the U.S. It naturally grows in mixed stands, primarily with buffalograss (Bouteloua dactyloides), needle-and-thread (Hesperostipa comata), western wheatgrass (Pascopyrum smithii), and green needlegrass (Nassella viridula)in a short grass prairie setting. It will be associated with other species such as prairie sandreed and sand sagebrush in a sandier habitat.

It is also used in surface mine re-vegetation plantings.

A highly palatable grass for livestock on a year long basis.

To consistently produce grass seed of any species the most important first step is to obtain a uniform, clean stand of grass. Skips and thin spots in the row invite weeds and other competing species which will cause trouble later. Weeds must be controlled the year of seeding and in subsequent years.

Proper seedbed preparation is always necessary when trying to establish any native grass or wildflower species. For the best results seed of blue grama should be drilled on a firm and weed free seed bed with a depth band and packer wheel equipped native grass drill. Depth of seeding should be ¼ to ½ inch.
‘Lovington’ was released as a cultivar in 1963 by New Mexico AES and the Los Lunas Plant Materials Center. The original source of the material was a field harvest in 1944 near Lovington, New Mexico.

Once established this grass is palatable to livestock year around. Growing points of this grass are low and near the grounds surface, thus close grazing by livestock can be allowed. To obtain the best forage yields, grazing should be deferred once every two to three years. Blue grama cures well on the stem making it a good grass for deferred grazing during its dormant period.

It has uniform size, leafiness, excellent seedling vigor and fast establishment characteristics. The material was screened initially for heavier caryopsis weights, increased seedling vigor and greater emergence from deeper soil depths. Its intended use was for rangeland improvement and go back cropland seeding in southern and central Great Plains.

Cultivars with larger roots, commonly called forage turnip, have been a popular forage crop for livestock in Europe and Asia for at least 600 years (Undersander et al., 1991). Forage turnip is a useful crop for extending the fall grazing season for dairy cows and other livestock (Thomet and Kohler, 2003).

Good seed production requires cross pollination by various insects. One or two hives per acre can ensure good seed set (Duke, 1983). Seed production fields need to have proper i solation distances among varieties and all other forms of B. juncea, B. campestris, and B. napus.

Drill seed in the spring, late summer, or fall at a rate of 1.7–11.2 kg/ha and a depth of ½ to ¾ inch in rows 10.2–30.5 cm apart; alternately, broadcast at 9–15.7 kg/ha followed by cultipacking (Clark, 2007; Hannaway and Larson, 2004; Knodel and Olson, 2002).
Cultivated from seed. Field mustard seed is generally available from commercial sources, but quantities may be limited, so it is best to check with seed suppliers a few months prior to planting.

Widely adopted and grown in gardens as food. Cooked and eaten as a staple root vegetable. Field mustard roots and leaves were used as food by many Native American tribes following introduction of the plant by white settlers.
Various parts of the plant have been used as a folk remedy for different types of cancer, either by boiling the mashed stems and leaves, powdering the seeds, or making a salve from the flowers.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Cheatgrass is one of the most widespread introduced annual grasses in North America, occurring in all 50 states as well as in most Canadian provinces and parts of Mexico. Annual grass from fibrous roots, possessing more or less densely hairy stems with fine, soft, short to moderately long and straight hairs, standing (10) 20-50 (70) cm tall; sheaths soft-hairy; leaf blades 2-3 (4) mm wide, flat, hairy with fine, soft, short to moderately long, straight hairs; leaf-bases lacking ear-shaped lobes; ligules jagged, 1.2-3 mm long. Belonging to the grass family (Poaceae), cheatgrass functions as an annual or winter annual, softly downy to short-hairy throughout, generally 10-60 cm tall with stems solitary or in a few-stemmed tuft. Leaf blades extend up to 20 cm long, flat, relatively narrow, usually 2-5 mm wide, and generally long-ciliate near the base.

Occurring in dry to mesic roadsides, disturbed sites, waste places, meadows, grasslands, and shrublands in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; common in southern BC, rare elsewhere; introduced from Eurasia and North Africa. Cheatgrass is one of the most widespread introduced annual grasses in North America, occurring in all 50 states as well as in most Canadian provinces and parts of Mexico. It is most common where annual rainfall ranges from 15-55 cm and autumn rainfall ranges from 5-12 cm (Peepers 1984). It acts as a weed of roadsides, cropland, hayland, pastureland, rangeland, and waste places, usually occurring on dry, sometimes weakly alkaline, clayey to loamy to sandy or gravelly soils. Cheatgrass is especially common in the western states, including the Columbia Basin, Snake River Basin, and the Great Basin (Morrow & Stahlman 1984). During periods of multiple year drought, it may almost disappear from the plant community only to return in very lush stands as moisture conditions improve.

Bluejoint is a tall, erect, cool-season perennial grass of the grass family (Poaceae) found in wet meadows and prairies, arising from fibrous roots and rhizomes that produce a hummocky, uneven natural stand appearance. Stems are 60-150 cm tall (reaching 1 to 2 meters), smooth, bearing 3 to 8 nodes, and often branching above. Sheath summits range from smooth to strongly hairy. The lax, usually flat leaf blades are rough on both surfaces, often glaucous above, measuring 5-30 cm long and mostly 3-8 mm wide, with an elongated and very narrow appearance and a bluish-green color.

‘Sourdough’ bluejoint reedgrass is a cultivar developed by the Alaska Experiment Station for revegetation uses. Collections (36) from the interior, western and south central Alaska were combined into a synthetic population to produce ‘Sourdough’.

Because unfertilized bluejoint is intolerant of heavy grazing or repeated harvests, harvesting should be restricted to a single event per year. To maintain adequate stands of bluejoint, harvest should be performed before flowering and only on alternate years. McKendrick et al. (1977) noted that fertilized stands (1-2 tons dry matter / acre) of bluejoint produced three times more forage than did unfertilized stands (0.5 tons dry matter / acre). Mitchell (1974) found that fertilized stands produced crude leaf protein of 12-20% dry weight during mid-June harvests.

Calamovilfa is a genus native to North America and contains five individual species. Calamovilfa closely resembles Calamagrostis and Ammophila in gross morphological characteristics, and was placed close to them in the tribe Agrostideae by Hitchcock (1951). Reeder and Ellingson (1960) pointed out that Calamovilfa differs from these genera in several important embryo characteristics, types of lodicules, leaf anatomy, and chromosome size and number.

Propagation of Calamovilfa longifolia is accomplished by seed and vegetative means. Maun (1981) studied germination and seedling establishment on Lake Huron sand dunes at Pinery Provincial Park, Ontario. Seedling establishment is considered risky on sand dunes where high soil surface temperatures, low nutrient supply, low moisture availability, and erosion can limit seedling establishment and growth.

‘Goshen’ prairie sandreed was cooperatively named and released by the Soil Conservation Service Plant Materials Center, Bridger, Montana and the Montana and Wyoming Agriculture Experiment Stations in 1976 (Scheetz and Lohmiller, 1978). The original germplasm was collected near Torrington, Wyoming in 1959.

Mullahey et al. (1991) found that a June and August defoliation of prairie sandreed over a three year period produced the greatest dry matter yield compare to other treatments and the control. Generally annual dry matter yields declined for all defoliation treatments and the control during the three year study. Burlaff (1971) concluded that the concentration of crude protein in prairie sandreed declined with increased maturity of the forage. Dry matter digestibility also declined with advanced maturity of the plants.

An assembly of 48 accessions was collected in 1968 from Kansas, Nebraska, and South Dakota and established in a space plant nursery at Manhattan, Kansas. The top ranked accessions from the nursery were provided to L.C. Selections from the nursery were evaluated for vigor, forage production and rust tolerance. Seed production is average for the species.

Redmaid seeds and greens were an important food source for many tribes in California including those whose territory neighbored the Salinan. The shiny black seeds were a major ingredient in pinole (from the Aztec word for seed flour, pinolli) and were valued for their high oil content. The parched seeds were pulverized in bedrock mortars into an oily meal, which was then prepared into balls and cakes.

The seeds were separated by shaking or hitting the plants over the cleaned area or into a basket. Then they were placed into a tightly woven winnowing basket where they were tossed, allowing the moving air to remove any chaff. The seeds were then dried for storage or parched in a cooking basket along with hot coals.
Not only were the seeds used as ceremonial offerings, as evidenced by these burial sites, but also they are often mentioned in Chumash myths.

Great camas differs from common camas (Camassia quamash ssp. breviflora) in the following ways: the flowers are regular, with tepals that twist together after anthesis and remain over the ovary; anthers are dull yellow to violet; the plant is larger, with longer flower stalks and bigger bulbs; and there is a fine, waxy powder on the leaves.

Great camas can be propagated from seeds or bulbs; shade tolerance, moisture requirement, and preferred planting depth may differ among specific phenotypes. Great camas is frequently found in areas with soil moisture persisting throughout most of the growing season.

Its preferred habitat includes shady environments, such as those that occur along riparian zones or under moderately dense deciduous forest canopies in western Oregon. Minor surface soil loosening adjacent to established plants may enhance natural seed regeneration.

Cultivars of Leichtlin’s camas are widely available in the flower bulb industry. One cultivar, Camassia leichtlinii ‘Alba’, is white (or bluish-white), while ‘Caerulea’ has light blue flowers, and ‘Plena’ has double greenish yellow blooms (Brenzel 1995). ‘Blauwe Donau’ is described as having sea-lavender-violet flowers and lilac anthers. ‘Lady Eve Price’ has campanula-violet flowers with each segment having a darker colored methyl-violet central stripe. ‘Semiplena’ has large, semi-double, creamy-white flowers.

Camas was considered to be one of the most important bulbs to local California natives. Except for choice varieties of dried salmon, no other food item was more widely traded. People traveled great distances to harvest the bulbs and there is some suggestion that plants were dispersed beyond their range by transplanting.
Traditionally utilized by Nez Perce as cough medicine (boiled juice mixed with honey). Death camas used with extreme caution in a mix with other medicines. Gynecological aid to induce labor.
The bulbs were dug with a pointed digging stick.

This species has utility for erosion control, constructed wetland system applications, wildlife food and cover, wetland creation and restoration, and for increasing plant diversity in wetland and riparian communities. Its dense root mass (214 cm of roots/cm3 of soil) makes this species resistant to soil compaction and erosion. It also makes it an excellent choice for soil stabilization in wetland and riparian sites. Nebraska sedge is used extensively in bioengineering techniques, because of its root system. The rhizomes also form a matrix for many beneficial bacteria making this plant an excellent choice for wastewater treatment.

Fox sedge occurs near water on moist open ground in swamps, prairie swales, lowland forests, wet ditches, ravines, and along the margins of marshes, springs, lakes, and ponds, often associated with soft rush, wool grass, bulrush, various sedges, brome grass, Virginia wild rye, oxeye daisy, boneset, Joe-Pye weed, ironweed, golden alexanders, sneezeweed, and monkeyflower. Buckbrush is one of the primary shrub species in the chaparral ecosystem. It is commonly found on dry, rocky slopes and ridges along with associated shrub species including chamise (Adenostoma fasciculatum) and whiteleaf manzanita (Arctostaphylos viscida) (Baker, 1982). In some places, Ceanothus cuneatus outcompetes other shrub species to form dense, impenetrable thickets (McMinn, 1939).

Buckbrush shrubs contain a significant amount of woody material and several California tribes including the Kawaiisu and the Miwok used this species for firewood. The Kawaiisu used the straight twigs of this shrub as the foreshafts for two-piece arrows. The arrows were created by stripping and sharpening the Ceanothus twigs and fitting them inside sections of hollow Carrizo grass of “cane”.

Yellow star-thistle prefers deep loamy soils with south-facing slopes and 30.5–63.5 cm or more of annual rainfall with a bimodal distribution in the fall and spring. It favors perennial bunchgrass communities dominated by bluebunch wheatgrass, Idaho fescue, and Sandberg's bluegrass.

The rosette of yellow star-thistle lies close to the ground and produces six to 28 deeply lobed leaves that range from 2.5–20.3 cm (2.5 to 20 centimeters) long and are generally less than 5.1 cm (5 centimeters) wide. The rigidly branched, winged flowering stems average about 0.6 m (60 centimeters) tall, but range from 10.2 cm (10 centimeters) to 1.5 m (1.5 meters), depending on environmental conditions. The stem leaves are entire without lobes, linear in shape, and are vested with woolly hairs that persist through the growing season. Flower heads are solitary on the ends of short stems and have many bright yellow flowers.

Yellow star-thistle is a listed noxious weed and is invasive in many western states. Yellow star-thistle is one of the more invasive weeds of the Intermountain West and Pacific Northwest. A report from 2003 estimated that yellow star-thistle has infested nearly 15 million acres in 17 western states. Yellow star-thistle is problematic on canyon lands, rangelands, pastures, roadsides, and disturbed areas. Its rapid growth rate and aggressive resource acquisition make it competitive in native plant communities.

Inhabits dry sandy or rocky slopes, grasslands, shrublands, scree, and talus slopes across steppe to alpine zones; common in southern British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains; extending east to Missouri and south to Arizona, Nevada, and California. The species occurs in diverse plant communities including shadscale, sagebrush steppe, pinyon-juniper, mountain brush, and pine-fir forests in areas receiving 25.4–152.4 cm of annual precipitation (USDA-NRCS, 2009).

Douglas’ dustymaiden is a biennial or short-lived perennial forb (Asteraceae) developing from a taproot and basal rosette, featuring ascending to erect, sparsely to densely woolly stems (sometimes glandular in the inflorescence) measuring 10-60 cm tall. Basal leaves are 1-3 pinnately cut, 2-12 cm long, and stalked with contorted, curled ultimate segments, while stem leaves are reduced and become unstalked upwards. Cytogeographic studies of the Chaenactis douglasii complex reveal chromosome counts of 2n = 12, 13, 14, 15, 18, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 37, and ca. 38, with diploids primarily in Pacific and Rocky Mountain ranges and polyploids on intervening plateaus in correlation with geologic substrate age.

Heads discoid, typically several arranged in a flat-topped inflorescence, or with lateral branches overtopping the central axis; involucres 7-17 mm tall; involucral bracts narrowly oblanceolate, glandular or glandular-hairy; disk flowers 50-70, white, sometimes pinkish.
Achenes 6-8 mm long, densely stiff-hairy; pappus of 10-16 unequal scales.
Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Taproot); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.

Douglas’ dustymaiden is adapted to a wide range of soil conditions ranging from acidic to moderately basic. The species is found growing in medium to coarse textured well drained soils with a pH of 4.2 to 7.9 and electrical conductivity of 0.06 to 2.5 dS/m (Borden and Black, 2005). Douglas’ dustymaiden requires full exposure to sunlight and a minimum 25.4 cm rooting depth (USDA-NRCS, 2009).
Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.

Douglas’ dustymaiden can be used as part of a native forb component in wildland seedings to increase biodiversity, improve wildlife habitat, and provide food for numerous birds. Important insect-foraging habitat for sage-grouse broods.
Small Mammals. Seeds feed small mammals.
Seed should be planted in late fall into slightly roughened soil and then lightly packed.

Parkinson and DeBolt (2005) reported 12% germination from 30 day cold moist stratification at 4° C (4°C); however no tetrazolium tests were conducted to determine seed viability prior to the experiment.

Seed can be surface sown in greenhouse containers in spring and transplanted when plants are large enough to disturb. A common garden study comparing 15 populations of Douglas’ dustymaiden from Idaho, Utah and Nevada had establishment percentages ranging from 66 to 98% (Tilley and St. John, 2010) from seed that was field-planted in November and allowed to undergo natural stratification.

Currently there are no releases of this species. Aberdeen Plant Materials Center assembled collections of Douglas’ dustymaiden in 2007 and began evaluating populations in a common garden study in 2008. Seed production fields of Douglas’ dustymaiden can be planted into weed barrier fabric at 23 to 30 cm spacing. Plants grown in weed barrier fabric at Aberdeen, Idaho (an 20.3–30.5 cm mean annual rainfall zone) required no supplemental irrigation (Tilley and St. John, 2010).
When planted in a native reclamation mix, it will be a minor component of the establishing plant community; therefore management should be based on other key species in the mixture.

Leatherleaf (Ericaceae) is a low, evergreen shrub 0.3-1.5 meters tall with erect, branching stems that are short white-hairy and sometimes scaly with tiny brownish scales. Leaves are alternate, leathery, oblanceolate to oblong or elliptic, 0.7-5 cm long (or 1.5-5 cm long) and 0.3-1.5 cm wide, rounded to blunt at the tip, pointed at the base, finely sharp-toothed, flat or with margins rolled under, scaly-hairy below, and becoming smaller and positioned to the upper side of the stem towards the branch tips. Flowers are white, urn-shaped, 6-7 mm long, hanging, solitary in the axils of small leaves, and arise from one side of the terminal inflorescence. Fruits are depressed-globose, woody, gray-brown capsules persisting through the winter.

Perennial herb from widespread rhizome-like root; stems erect, 1-3 m tall, usually simple, glabrous except for fine minute hairs in the inflorescence and on the ovaries. Evening primrose family (Onagraceae). Native, herbaceous perennial growing from spreading rootstocks. Plants are strongly rhizomatous with roots typically growing within the top few inches of the ground surface (Henderson et al. 1979). Fireweed plants are protandrous (male reproductive organs mature before the female reproductive organs) and self-compatible (capable of self-fertilization) (Mosquin 1966). Flower anthers open, and disperse pollen, within 24 hours of the flower opening while the stigmas remain closed and the style strongly reflexed away from the anthers for 2 to 3 days, a process that promotes cross-pollination (Mosquin 1966).

Edible shoots, leaves, buds, blossoms. Many sought out fireweed plants in the spring-time before they bloomed, to eat the sweet and succulent raw pith of the stems. In England and Russia the leaves were used as a substitute for, or an additive to, tea.

The beverage is called “Kaporie tea”.It may have a laxative effect. Fireweed was used by Interior Peoples (Canadian First Nations People) externally as a medicine against eczema, and they sometimes mixed it with other plants.

Stems and seed fluff used for fiber. Fluff used as filler, bedding, woven into cedar clothing or combined with mountain goat wool. Some boiled or steamed the stems and served them like asparagus, some used the leafy stems as flavoring or as matting in root-cooking pits or earth ovens.

Evening primrose family (Onagraceae). Native, herbaceous perennial growing from spreading rootstocks. Plants are strongly rhizomatous with roots typically growing within the top few inches of the ground surface (Henderson et al. 1979). Fireweed has 0.3–1.8 m., occasionally 2.7 m., tall stout erect stems that are often reddish, usually unbranched and usually glabrous below and pubescent above with small white hairs. Fireweed plants are protandrous (male reproductive organs mature before the female reproductive organs) and self-compatible (capable of self-fertilization) (Mosquin 1966). Flower anthers open, and disperse pollen, within 24 hours of the flower opening while the stigmas remain closed and the style strongly reflexed away from the anthers for 2 to 3 days, a process that promotes cross-pollination (Mosquin 1966).

Fireweed can be found in a wide variety of environments but is most frequently associated with species colonizing recently disturbed ground (Dyrness 1973). Habitats in which fireweed grows include burned or logged forests, woodland borders, forest meadows, alpine meadows, mixed forests, boreal forests, roadsides, and moist areas along streams, lakes and bogs (Dennis 1980). In some well-established plant communities, widely spaced fireweed colonies with low stem densities may persist for long periods (Moss 1936).

In some areas, shoots of fireweed are a preferred food of deer and cattle and are also eaten by moose, caribou, muskrat, and hares (Willms et al. 1980).
After most of the pollen of a flower is shed, the stigma comes forward while the anthers become deflexed.

Fireweed seeds are very small and difficult to plant when the pappus is still attached. In a greenhouse study, seeds had a higher germination rate when sown on the soil surface than when sown at a depth of 2 mm or more (Myerscough and Whitehead 1966). The highest rates of germination were obtained when seeds were sown on the surface under warm well lighted humid conditions (Myerscough and Whitehead 1966).
Rapidly colonizes burned and disturbed sites via wind-dispersed fluffy seeds and aggressive creeping rhizomes. No known cultivars or selected materials.

Many sought out fireweed plants in the spring-time before they bloomed, to eat the sweet and succulent raw pith of the stems. Prepared and applied to fill internal cavity of freshly caught game as seasoning to preserve and improve flavor. Greens used raw or cooked, young shoots taste like asparagus.
Treats prostate problems, asthma, whooping cough. Teas treat asthma and whooping cough. Root mash or peeled root applied to burns, swellings, boils, sores, and rashes.

Some boiled or steamed the stems and served them like asparagus, some used the leafy stems as flavoring or as matting in root-cooking pits or earth ovens. Fluff used as filler, bedding, woven into cedar clothing, or combined with mountain goat wool. Cordage/twine from stem fiber, fluffy seed fiber harvesting.

Fireweed (Chamerion angustifolium), Fireweed is alternate host of the rust Pucciniastrum Abieti-chamenerii (Pucciniastrum epilobii) that causes needle rust in Abies balsamea. The rust fungus Puccinia gigantean parasitizes C. angustifolium. Major infestations are reported to cause reduction in flowering, premature senescence of the shoot and even death of the entire plant.

Inhabiting dry open slopes, grasslands, shrublands, and open forest in the steppe and lower montane zones; frequent in extreme south-central British Columbia; ranging south to North Dakota, New Mexico, and California. Yellow rabbitbrush occurs in desert to semi-desert habitats in western rangelands, commonly associated with other rabbitbrush species (Chrysothamnus and Ericameria spp.) and sagebrush species (Artemisia spp.)

A perennial shrub of the sunflower family (Asteraceae), yellow rabbitbrush is a low- to moderate-growing plant featuring much-branched, brittle stems that are minutely to densely appressed-hairy, reaching mature heights of 20 to 100 cm tall (stem height 10-35 cm). Stems are covered with pale green to white-gray bark and can be glabrous or pubescent depending on variety. Leaves are linear to linear-lanceolate, 2-5 cm long, 2-7 mm wide (or narrow and linear to oblong, 1 to 6 cm [0.4 to 2.4 in] long and 0.5 to 8 mm [0.02 to 0.3 in] wide), 3-5-nerved, glabrous or densely appressed-hairy and sticky, and often appear twisted. Flower heads are borne in numerous compact to open terminal cymes, measuring 5 to 7.5 mm long and 2 to 4 mm wide with glandular or pubescent bracts.

Inhabiting dry open slopes, grasslands, shrublands, and open forest in the steppe and lower montane zones; frequent in extreme south-central British Columbia; ranging south to North Dakota, New Mexico, and California. Yellow rabbitbrush occurs in desert to semi-desert habitats in western rangelands, commonly associated with other rabbitbrush species (Chrysothamnus and Ericameria spp.) and sagebrush species (Artemisia spp.). Additional associates include broom snakeweed (Gutierrezia sarothrae), shadscale (Atriplex confertifolia), and winterfat (Krascheninnikovia lanata), and it can also be found growing in pinyon-juniper woodlands (Pinus-Juniperus). Yellow rabbitbrush and other rabbitbrush species are frequently subdominant in sagebrush communities, with rabbitbrush densities rapidly increasing following heavy disturbance and subsequently declining over time as sagebrush densities increase (Young and Evans, 1974).

Seed can be collected by hand with racquets and hoppers, or mechanically with vacuum type harvesters, flail vacs and other seed strippers. Yellow rabbitbrush seed is difficult to clean and low purity levels are common in seed lots. Jorgensen and Stevens (1994) list acceptable purities of 10 to 15 percent.

Yellow rabbitbrush does not exhibit dormancy and do not persist in the soil seed bank. Field establishment of yellow rabbitbrush is typically achieved with nursery grown plants or with fall dormant seedings. Seed should be broadcast or shallow drilled to no more than 3 mm depth.
There are currently no commercial releases of yellow rabbitbrush.

Yellow rabbitbrush increases with overgrazing and is difficult to completely control. It is susceptible to 2,4-D during periods of active growth and available moisture when herbicides will be translocated through the tissues to the dormant buds in the crown.
Wildland collected seed is available from commercial sources.

Buttercup Family (Ranunculaceae). Western clematis is a deciduous, perennial woody vine arising from a rhizome and anchored effectively to the soil by a taproot. Stems are clambering or climbing, generally reaching up to 6 m long, and vary from nearly smooth to densely short stiff-hairy or long soft-hairy; numerous stems emerge from the crown in hospitable environments, typically dying back each winter while the basal 1-5 m persist for several years, occasionally attaining lengths of 20 m (Hitchcock et al 1964). Plants are dioecious.

Erosion control/reclamation/landscape: Western clematis has great potential to improve roadsides and other dryland critical areas even though it typically occurs in riparian and run-on areas. It is very drought tolerant and transplants have performed very well in trials conducted on sites that receive as little as 17.8 cm of annual precipitation (Pullman PMC 1993). Placing plants along the top of a cut will allow the canopy to drape over the bare soil and effectively protect the soil. If allowed to climb fences, it will slow soil and catch tumbleweeds. Western clematis can provide excellent stabilization of intermittent streambanks because it does not require as much moisture as many other riparian plants. The stems develop a thick mat that effectively protect streambank soils and may deter livestock movement. The landscape value of western clematis is apparent in xeriscaping projects. It remains green late throughout the growing season and the leaves drop in late-fall. The dense leaf canopy can effectively shield background objects that the landscaper wishes to remain unseen. The flowers are smaller then hybrid floral varieties but the plumed seedheads are very attractive.

Rocky Mountain beeplant is recommended for use at sites receiving >300 mm mean annual precipitation in the intermountain West (Ogle et al., 2019). This species can be broadcast, or drill seeded into a firm, weed-free seed bed to depth of 0 to 3 mm (0 to 1/8 in). The full stand seeding rate is 17 lb/ac.

Rocky Mountain beeplant is broadly available on the commercial market, but no improved or released material is available. Seed should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use. It is easy to establish by direct seeding, and potted plants grow and mature quickly and often go to flower and fruit in the greenhouse before outplanting.

Canadian horseweed is a native winter or summer annual forb in the sunflower family. The plants are erect with one to several stems reaching 30 to 150 cm tall. Stems are typically unbranched at the base unless damage has occurred to the apical growing points. Foliage is linear to oblanceolate, 2 to 8 cm long and 2 to 8 mm wide.

Canadian horseweed has been described as both a summer annual and a winter annual with seed germinating at any time with sufficient moisture and warmth (Waggoner et al., 2011). In winter annual forms the seed germinates in the fall and the plant overwinters as a rosette.

Flowering dogwood root bark was used by Native Americans as a fever reducer, skin astringent, an antidiarrheal agent, and as a pain reliever for headaches, sores, and muscle inflammations. It was also used to counteract the effects of many poisons and as a general tonic for unspecified ailments. The bark was used for headache and backache relief, as a throat aid for hoarseness, and as an infusion for childhood diseases like worms and measles. Compound infusions of several plant parts were used as blood purifiers and as medicine for blood diseases like malaria.
It is occasionally used to make specialty items like golf club heads, roller skate wheels, knitting needles, and spools.

Edible fruit. The fruits were eaten by the Indians of the Missouri region. The berries are known to be tart and bitter, but were nonetheless eaten by all of the southern Interior peoples of British Columbia, including the Nlaka’pamux, St'át'imc (Lillooet), Syilx (Okanagan) / Colville, Secwépemc (Shuswap), Ktunaxa (Kootenay), Blackfeet, and the Flathead of Alberta and Montana The fruits were gathered from August to October and eaten fresh, a few at a time, or, more commonly, were pounded and mixed with other fruits, such as chokecherries (Prunus virginiana) or Saskatoons (Amelanchier almifolia).

The leaves and/or inner bark of redosier dogwood are also used as a smoking mixture by the Syilx (Okanagan) / Colville, the Flathead, the Ktunaxa (Kootenay), and the Blackfeet peoples in the western United States and Canada (Hellson 1974; Turner et al. 1980), The Navaho-Kayentaf and Navaho-Ramah used the plant ceremonially as a Mountain-top-way emetic. An infusion of redosier dogwood bark was used as an anti-diarrheal by the Chippewa and the Potawatomi, an antidote for weak kidneys by the Secwépemc (Shuswap), and a pediatric aid for children who wet the bed by the Secwépemc (Shuswap). The Chippewa used an infusion of the bark for eruptions caused by poison ivy.

The Ojibwa and the Chippewa used redosier dogwood bark as a dye. Some tribes ate the white, sour berries, while others used the branches for arrow-making, stakes, or other tools. In California, peeled twigs were used as toothbrushes for their whitening effect on teeth.

Occurring in moist to mesic, open rocky slopes, bluffs, streambanks, lakeshores, gullies, thickets, and forest edges across the lowland to montane zones; frequent in southern British Columbia north to 56° N; extending north to southern Alaska, east to Ontario, and south to South Dakota, Wyoming, and California.

A medium to tall shrub 1-7 m tall, with stout, straight thorns 1-2 (3) cm long and grey or brownish, rough and scaly bark. Deciduous small tree or broad shrub to 3-10 m with copious 1-2 cm thorns on reddish twigs; ovate serrated leaves; small white spring flowers; clustered dark purple/black apple-like berries. Inflorescences presented as short, terminal or axillary clusters; flowers several to many, stalked, 1-1.5 cm across; corollas white, the petals 5, nearly circular, 4-7 mm long; calyces 5-lobed, the lobes triangular, somewhat long-hairy toward the tip; ovaries inferior, smooth to short-curly-hairy, the styles usually 5; stamens 10 to 20.

To increase percent germination, seeds require acid scarification for 0.5 to 3 hours, followed by 84 to 112 days of cold treatment. Seedlings must not be kept in the nursery longer than a year.

Black hawthorn generally occurs on deep, moist, fine-textured soils, at lower elevations ranging from 671–1646 m. Although it will succeed in partial shade and different soil types, it grows best in full sunlight with sufficient moisture levels.

The Forage and Range Research Laboratory in Logan, UT, has determined Dalea ornata has 283 – 340 seeds per gram (128,367 – 154,227 seeds per pound) depending on environmental factors and genotype. The plants continue to flower while seed produced earlier in the season matures, complicating the harvest process.

To establish a planting, the seed must first be scarified using sandpaper or a laboratory scarifying device. When growing western prairie clover for seed production, the seed should be planted at a rate of 25 – 30 PLS per lineal foot (Cornforth, et al 2009).

This species can be established by seed; however availability of seed for this species is extremely limited. With releases planned in the near future by the ARS Forage and Range Research Laboratory in Logan, UT, and the Pullman Plant Materials Center in Pullman, WA, more seed may become available.

In all native forb plantings, weeds must be managed for several years to ensure successful establishment. One of the most common options for weed management is application of herbicide. In Nebraska, Masters et al. (1996) found stands of purple prairie clover (D. purpurea) had greater foliar cover when treated with imidazolinonone herbicides (imazapyr and imazethapyr) compared to untreated stands. Numerous pre-and post-emergent herbicides are labeled for rangeland use and can be applied to cover an entire area or spot-sprayed.

Barner (2009) processed small seed collections using a Westrup Model LA-H laboratory brush machine, with a #40 mantel, at a speed of 3, to remove seed from stems and de-awn. Seeds were finished by air-screening, to remove chaff and inert material, using an office Clipper, with a top screen: 5 1/2 round and a bottom screen: blank, medium speed, and low to medium air. Tilley (2023) followed a similar procedure using a multi-deck airscreen cleaner with 3.55 mm top screen and 6x38 bottom screen followed by a second run with 2.35 mm top and blank bottom screen.

Annual hairgrass germinates readily and is easy to establish on open, moist ground. There is no seed dormancy and therefore no requirement for physical conditioning or over wintering outdoors. The seed should be run through a debearder or brush machine to remove pubescence (hairs).
This plant is generally not available elsewhere within its range, requiring wild harvest or contract seed growing to provide material.

As an annual, this species requires regular disturbance or moist to wet open ground in fall and winter in order to proliferate. It is not competitive and is easily replaced by other species. Annual hairgrass should be well suited to moist soil management techniques (slow de-watering, disking, etc.) in shallow water impoundments and other controlled wetlands. Such methods are used to improve habitat for waterfowl, shorebirds, and other wildlife by maximizing seed production of annuals.

Plants and seeds are sometimes available in California and Oregon. This species is generally not available elsewhere within its range, requiring wild harvest or contract seed growing to provide material.

Restoration/reclamation: Hoary tansyaster is an early colonizer of rangelands and disturbed sites. It is commonly found on roadsides and gravel pits competing with invasive plants such as cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) and knapweed species (Centaurea spp). It can be planted to enhance species diversity in rangeland seedings throughout the western United States.
Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Taproot); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.

Clasping coneflower is a native, warm-season annual forb in the Asteraceae family (Missouri Botanical Garden, 2019) growing 30.5–71.1 cm (30 to 71 cm) tall. It arises from a solitary stem that branches out about halfway up the plant. The alternately arranged, oblong, glaucous leaves are 4.4–10.2 cm (4 to 10 cm) long and wrap around the stems at their base—a distinctive characteristic reflected in the species name from the Latin amplexus ('encircling') and caulis ('stem'). Blooming in late spring and early summer, it produces yellow ray flowers that resemble the black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia hirta) and droop as they mature.

Clasping coneflower prefers sites with full sun and moist soils but not poorly drained soils (Missouri Botanical Garden, 2019). This forb tolerates various soil types including acid or calcareous based sandy or clay loams (Ladybird Johnson Wildflower Center, 2019).

Broadcast seeding is the preferred method for planting clasping coneflower. Prepare a weed free seedbed using light tillage, herbicide applications, or close mowing. Lightly disk or harrow to loosen the soil surface then roll or cultipack prior to seeding. Prepare a weed free seedbed using tillage and/or herbicide application. Prior to planting, the seedbed must be firmed and accumulated moisture for improved establishment success. Broadcast seed at a rate of 4 PLS/acre during August or September.
Purchase seed based on local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

Clip or mow spent flowers to control self-seeding and/or encourage additional blooming (Missouri Botanical Garden, 2019). Clasping coneflower is a prolific reseeder, but eventually declines without soil disturbance. Disk the site every two to three years to control perennial weeds and promote clasping coneflower germination.
Clasping coneflower seed is commercially available.

Japanese millet (Echinochloa esculenta) is an introduced, annual, warm-season grass that is grown primarily as forage and wildlife habitat in the United States. It is a domesticated species derived from wild millet barnyardgrass (E. crus-galli). It is robust with coarse, hairless leaves 4–20 in (10–50 cm) long (Mitchell, 1989) has a thicker stem than most millets, grows 0.6–1.2 m tall, with a brown to purple inflorescence.

Deciduous shrub from a strong rhizome; stems silvery- to brownish-scaled, branched, old branches dark greyish-red, young twigs brown or green, 1-4 m tall. Leaves are alternate, short-stalked, lanceolate to oblanceolate, or ovate to oblong and ovate-lanceolate, 2-7 cm long (overall 2-10 cm long), wedge-shaped at the base, wavy-margined, and silvery-scaly on both surfaces with occasional scattered brown scales beneath. Flowers are bisexual or unisexual, sweet-scented, short-stalked in lateral clusters of 1-3 on twigs of the current year; petals absent, the sepals forming a 4-lobed tube from the top of the developing fruit (the ovary inferior), yellowish inside, silvery outside, 12-15 mm long.

Inhabiting wet meadows, tidal flats, ditches, and shorelines across lowland, steppe, and montane zones; common throughout British Columbia; circumpolar, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and the Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, California, and Mexico; also found in Greenland and Eurasia. It ranges from the West Coast of the United States east to the Upper Peninsula of Michigan and south to Louisiana.

A perennial herb of the Cyperaceae family (creeping spikerush) arising from freely branching rhizomes, found from low to mid elevations with a dense root mass extending deeper than 40 cm in the soil profile. Stems are scattered or in small clusters, ranging from slender to very stout, circular in cross-section, tapered or somewhat flattened, and 10-100 cm tall (reaching up to 1.2 m depending on water depth). Leaves are reduced to firm, reddish-brown sheaths clustered at the base, which are distinctly oblique, purplish or reddish below, and somewhat flaring upwards; leaf blades are lacking. Flowers are borne in a terminal spikelet from June through September, with 1 flower per scale and 2 stigmas.

Spikes are solitary, terminal, and lanceolate or narrowly egg-shaped, measuring 5-23 mm long, light to dark brown or chestnut in color, and several-flowered.

Basal scales number 1 or 2 (3), empty, with the lowest ones nearly encircling the top of the stem; fertile scales are mostly 2-4.5 mm long, egg-shaped, nearly sharp-pointed or blunt, reddish-brown, purplish-brown, or purplish-black with translucent margins and lighter-coloured midribs; perianth bristles number 4, sometimes 5 or 6, shortly surpassing the achenes, rarely reduced or lacking, with fine backward-directed barbs; stigmas 2; achenes are lens-shaped, yellow to medium brown, finely cellular roughened, spongy, minutely wrinkled, 1.5-2.5 mm long including the well-differentiated tubercles, which are separated from the achenes by constrictions, pyramidal, bulbous, longer than broad, and 0.4-0.7 mm long.
Establishes uniform stand cover within one growing season from plug plantings.
Non-allelopathic moderate clonal spreader (Rhizomatous); weaves steadily through mixed groundcover matrices without harsh chemical inhibition.
Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.

It grows in wet meadows, irrigation ditches, springs, seepage areas, freshwater marshes, rivers, and along lakeshores. It is a pioneering species that populates mud flats very quickly as the water draws down. It can grow in areas that are flooded in the spring and saturated in the fall.
Typically Non-Mycorrhizal or facultatively weakly AM (specialized root hairs or wetland nutrient uptake)
Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.

This species has utility for erosion control, constructed wetland system applications, wildlife food and cover, wetland creation and restoration, and for increasing plant diversity in wetland and riparian communities. Its dense root mass makes this species an excellent choice for soil stabilization in riparian and wetland sites. The rhizomes also form a matrix for many beneficial bacteria making this plant an excellent choice for wastewater treatment.

Wildlife and Livestock: Creeping spikerush has a moderately high protein content in the spring and good digestibility.

Collection and cleaning: Seeds may be collected by hand striping the seed from the plant or clipping it using a pair of hand shears. A power seed harvester may also be used. The hammer mill is used to break up the large debris and knock the seed loose from the stem.
The soil should be kept saturated. Allow no more than 8 cm of standing water at any time during the first growing season.
Planting plugs (either from the greenhouse or wild transplants) is the surest way to establish a new stand of this species. Plug spacing of 30-45 cm will fill in within one growing season.

Standing water should be no deeper than 1 m and should fluctuate throughout the growing season. If deeper water levels are desirable, increase the depth slowly over the course of the growing season. This species can tolerate periods of drought and total inundation. Water levels can be managed to enhance or reduce spread as well as control terrestrial weeds.

Forage/ Squirreltail is considered to be fair to desirable forage for cattle, horses and sheep in spring before seed head development and late summer to fall after seed shatter.
Seed can be planted in early spring, but late dormant fall seeding is recommended for best annual weed suppression.
For best results, seed should be planted to a depth of ¼ to ½ inches into a firm weed-free seedbed. For pure stands the recommended drill seeding rate is 7 lb pure live seed (PLS) per acre.

Because of the broad array of subspecies of squirreltail and the genetic variation between species and subspecies, careful identification of the species and subspecies native to the planting site is recommended. Care should be taken to match the appropriate phenotype and genotype of the plant materials with those of the local plant communities to improve the chance of stand success and to prevent genetic contamination of existing populations.

Seeds germinate in the fall or spring. Plants green up early and remain green through the fall and into winter. Stands should be protected from heavy grazing, especially during flowering to ensure sufficient seed production to maintain the stand. New plantings should also be protected from grazing for at least two growing seasons.

Second generation seed is maintained by the USDA-ARS Forage and Range Research Laboratory, Logan UT. G3 to G5 seed is available through the Utah Crop Improvement Association. G3 seed is maintained by the USDA-ARS Forage and Range Research Laboratory, Logan UT. Seed through G6 is available through the Utah Crop Improvement Association. G2 seed is maintained by the USDA-ARS Forage and Range Research Laboratory, Logan UT. Seed from G3 and G4 generations are available for seed certification through the Utah Crop Improvement Association. From the initial 131 collections, eight were selected for vigor, late flowering and higher seed yield. An equal number of seedlings from each accession were taken to form the composite, Tusas. Breeder and G2 seed are maintained by the NRCS NM Plant Materials Center. Seed is available through the New Mexico Crop Improvement Association. Eight bottlebrush squirreltail accessions were evaluated by the Upper Colorado Environmental Plant Center (UCEPC) from 1983 to 1987 and compared for forage production, seed production percent stand, leaf height, vigor, leaf abundance and stem height. The UCEPC will maintain G1 and G2 seed. G2 seed will be available to growers. Seed used for certified seed production must be obtained from UCEPC.

Erosion control/reclamation: Streambank wheatgrass (E. lanceolatus ssp. lanceolatus) and (E. lanceolatus ssp. psammophilus) are well adapted to the stabilization of disturbed soils. They do not compete well with aggressive introduced grasses during the establishment period, but are very compatible with slower developing natives, such as Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), Western wheatgrass (Pascopyrum smithii), and needlegrass (Stipa spp.) species. Their drought tolerance combined with rhizomes, fibrous root systems, and good seedling vigor make these species ideal for reclamation in areas receiving 20.3–50.8 cm annual precipitation. They are commonly used for reclamation in the Red Desert of Wyoming, where annual rainfall is 12.7–22.9 cm (50 - 70 percent growing season precipitation). Streambank wheatgrass’ low growth form, vigorous sod, and low maintenance requirements make it ideal for stabilization and ground cover purposes. These grasses can be used in urban areas where irrigation water is limited to provide ground cover and to stabilize ditchbanks, dikes, and roadsides.

Forage/ Squirreltail is considered to be fair to desirable forage for cattle, horses and sheep in spring before seed head development and late summer to fall after seed shatter. The long, sharp awns of the florets and glumes can be injurious to grazing animals during mid to late spring into summer.
Seed can be planted in early spring, but late dormant fall seeding is recommended for best annual weed suppression.
For best results, seed should be planted to a depth of ¼ to ½ inches into a firm weed-free seedbed. For pure stands the recommended drill seeding rate is 7 lb pure live seed (PLS) per acre.

Because of the broad array of subspecies of squirreltail and the genetic variation between species and subspecies, careful identification of the species and subspecies native to the planting site is recommended. Care should be taken to match the appropriate phenotype and genotype of the plant materials with those of the local plant communities to improve the chance of stand success and to prevent genetic contamination of existing populations.

Seeds germinate in the fall or spring. Plants green up early and remain green through the fall and into winter. Stands should be protected from heavy grazing, especially during flowering to ensure sufficient seed production to maintain the stand. New plantings should also be protected from grazing for at least two growing seasons.

Breeder seed is maintained by the Agriculture Canada, Saskatoon Research Station and the Agriculture Canada Experiment Farm, Indian Head. This variety has excellent germination, high seedling vigor, drought tolerance, early spring growth and an aggressive root system. It is primarily intended for range and pasture seedings in the dark soil zones of the prairies as well as for revegetation of roadsides and industrial disturbances. Breeder seed is available through Agriculture Canada Research Station, Lethbridge, Alberta. Hillcrest seeds also tend to ripen two weeks earlier than Revenue, an important quality in the shortened growing season of Alberta. Breeder seed is maintained by the Alberta Environmental Centre, Vegreville, Alberta. Foundation and Certified seed is maintained by Peace Valley Seeds, Rycroft, Alberta. Pullman Plant Materials Center maintains Breeder seed and Washington Crop Improvement Association maintain Foundation seed. It also matures earlier and has a larger mean seed size (213,000 seeds/kg compared to 320,000 seeds/kg). Virginia wildrye is a native, cool season, perennial, bunch grass. It is similar to Canada wildrye (Elymus canadensis) in appearance, but is typically shorter in height with shorter awns on the seed head. The seed heads are more erect than those of Canada wildrye which typically bow or droop (Philips Petroleum Company, 1963). There is evidence of variation in E. virginicus and E. canadensis due to hybridization of the two species (Grelen and Hughes, 1984).

Virginia wildrye will tolerate a wide range of soil textures, from coarse sands to heavy clay. It prefers heavier soils with moderate fertility and a pH between 5 and 7.

Virginia wildrye is shade tolerant and is equally at home in open grasslands and prairies as it is in wooded sites. It is more shade tolerant than Canada wildrye, and prefers soils with more moisture and fertility (Philips Petroleum Company, 1963). It is commonly found in moist sites such as wet prairies, margins of wetlands, ditches, and riparian areas. It is also commonly found in woodlands, especially those in association with flood plains.

The natural distribution of Snake River wheatgrass is limited to eastern Oregon, eastern Washington, and west central to northern Idaho, but it is widely used as a surrogate for bluebunch wheatgrass for restoration, reclamation, and rehabilitation of rangelands in the Columbia Plateau, Northern Basin and Range, Central Basin and Range, and Snake River Plain, which encompass large portions of eastern Washington, eastern Oregon, southern Idaho, Nevada, and western Utah. Snake River wheatgrass is a long-lived, perennial, cool-season native bunchgrass with an extensive root system with strong tillers. Snake River (left) vs. Awned (center) and awnless( right) bluebunch wheatgrasses Snake River wheatgrass has a seed of considerably smaller mass than bluebunch wheatgrass. Snake River wheatgrass can be morphologically distinguished from bluebunch wheatgrass by characters such as the ratio of spikelet length to internode length, glume shape, seedling pubescence, and seedling leaf marginal barbs (Jones et al., 1991).

Erosion control/reclamation: Snake River wheatgrass is very drought tolerant, stands are persistent once established, and it is adapted to stabilization of disturbed soils. It is very compatible with slower developing natives such as streambank wheatgrass, thickspike wheatgrass, basin wildrye, western wheatgrass, bluegrass species, and needlegrass species. It does not compete well with aggressive introduced grasses. Its drought tolerance, combined with an extensive root system and fair to good seedling vigor, make this species ideal for reclamation in areas receiving 25.4–50.8 cm annual precipitation. The cultivars ‘Discovery’ and 'Secar' compete well in areas as low as 20.3 cm annual rainfall. This grass can be used in urban areas where irrigation water is limited to stabilize ditch banks, dikes, and roadsides as a component of a native mix.

Grazing/rangeland: Snake River wheatgrass is palatable to all classes of livestock and wildlife.

This species should be seeded with a drill at a depth of 13 mm or less on medium-textured soils, 6 mm on fine-textured soils and 1.9 cm or less on coarse-textured soils. The single species seeding rate recommended for this grass is 8 pounds Pure Live Seed (PLS) or about 24 PLS per square foot.

Stands of Snake River wheatgrass should not be grazed until they have firmly established (usually two to three growing seasons) and started to flower. Six inches of new growth should be attained in spring before grazing is allowed in established stands. The growing point of Snake River wheatgrass is fairly high and stands can be easily overgrazed. Spring grazing should occur no more than one out of three years and no more than 40 percent utilization should occur during rapid growth.

Rubber rabbitbrush is fast growing, reaching maturity in 2 to 4 years, and has a lifespan of 5 to 20 years. Plants begin producing seeds when they are 2 or more years old. Seeds can be harvested in fall or early winter by shaking or stripping the heads from the branches.
Rubber rabbitbrush should be seeded in a mixture with forbs and grasses at a rate of 0.025 pound Pure Live Seed (PLS) per acre.
Rubber rabbitbrush can be established by transplanting seedlings, or drilling or broadcasting seed. Planting can be done in spring or fall, on prepared or unprepared seedbeds.

Rubber rabbitbrush is often associated with non-native invasive plants which establish at the same time following a disturbance. The presence of rubber rabbitbrush may actually reduce the severity of weed invasion. Where land managers intend to control invasive weeds while minimizing damage to rubber rabbitbrush, application of chlorsulfuron may be an effective strategy. A number of land managers consider rubber rabbitbrush to be undesirable due to its low forage value.

Native Americans also used rubber rabbitbrush for chewing gum, tea, cough syrup, and to treat chest pains (Stubbendeick et al 2003).

Bark used for green dye. The Navajo used the flowers to make yellow dye (Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center 2009). The Hopi stripped the bark from the branches of rubber rabbitbrush and used the branches for basket weaving.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Some ecotypes of rubber rabbitbrush are infected by stem galls, which are caused by two species of tephritid flies (Aciurina species). There are no reports of negative effects caused by the galls. Although rubber rabbitbrush may appear to dominate a plant community soon after disturbance, it is not overly competitive and is eventually replaced with other vegetation as the community matures.

Erosion control/reclamation/landscape: Snow buckwheat is a very successful pioneer species (Tiedemann, et al 1997). It tolerates extremely droughty soils and is a common occupant of dry, rocky southern exposures. It is an excellent candidate for stabilizing skeletal soils exposed in road cuts, and mine spoils that lack soil development. Snow buckwheat grows to 0.5 m in height in most areas but may be as much as 1m tall and 1m wide on better sites. The canopy, while quite short, can effectively protect the soil from erosive winds. Snow buckwheat is a very useful xeriscaping plant, because it requires very little moisture and does not become weedy. It can be shaped by careful pruning to produce a more formal looking round-full plant. The bloom period is very long and the white flowers take on a pink blush in late fall.

Snow buckwheat should be seeded in late fall. Standard reclamation drills and broadcast seeders are capable of handling snow buckwheat seed, however, ensure the seed is kept shallow (max. 6mm deep). Germination in the wild occurs during cool-wet conditions thus allowing the seedlings to develop while moisture is readily available and evaporative rates are low.
Umatilla' snow buckwheat was selected by the Pullman Plant Materials Center and released in 1991. It was developed from a native collection made in Umatilla County, Oregon.

Snow buckwheat is a low maintenance plant once established. Cheatgrass and other winter annuals should be controlled the first year to allow good establishment. Observations have shown that snow buckwheat withstands severe defoliation if the woody stems and crowns are not damaged. Digging up plants is not advised because it is difficult to extract a large enough portion of the root to support the plant.

A tea brewed from the roots of snow buckwheat and a related species, Indian tobacco (E. heracleoides) were used by Native Americans as a diarrhea remedy. Decocted roots and stems were used to treat a variety of ailments including cuts, colds, and blood poisoning.
It has been suggested that the Columbia Basin buckwheats were also used to develop dyes by the Native Americans.

Snow buckwheat is long-lived, spreading via seed in the wild. It is not considered to be a "weedy" or invasive species, but can spread into adjoining vegetative communities under ideal climatic and environmental conditions.

Naked buckwheat grows in abundant stands in dry open meadows, on rocky outcrops, and along trails and roadsides (Dayton, 1960). The native distribution of naked buckwheat is highly variable and extends from low to subalpine elevations (up to 3780 m) from southern Washington south to California and western Nevada, and into northwestern Mexico (Jepson Flora Project, 2012).
