Sulfur flower buckwheat inhabits dry, open, and frequently rocky habitats across a distribution stretching from California to western Canada, Colorado, and New Mexico, encompassing approximately thirty distinct subspecies distributed throughout the western United States.

Sulfur flower buckwheat (Polygonaceae) is a native, low-growing woody perennial herb arising from a strong taproot and freely branched crown, forming loose flat mats up to 60 cm wide (reaching one foot high to two feet across). Stems are prostrate to ascending, simple, several, 10-30 cm tall/long (or 7.6–40.6 cm tall), and usually white-woolly. Basal leaves are elliptic to spoon-shaped, grey- to white woolly-hairy on the lower surface and greenish on the upper, with blades 1-3 (4) cm long (or one inch long) that narrow gradually to the stalks; stem leaves are lacking. Commonly found on hot, dry, sunny exposures on rocky slopes and ridges throughout western mountainous regions at elevations of 762–3048 m, requiring well-drained sandy or gravelly soils with low fertility.

California poppy establishes well on marginal disturbed sites, but populations can be expected to decline in areas where competition for light and water becomes intense (Ratcliff et al., 1972), yet, what the species lacks in competitive ability, it regains in adaptive ability (Leger and Rice, 2003). In general, the species is capable of recovering from freeze events, as well as tolerating high temperatures, drought, variable precipitation regimes, and a wide range of soil textures, chemistries, and levels of fertility (Hickman, 1993).

Seed size for the species will vary; for large seeded types, there are approximately 270,000 seeds per pound. One pound of large-sized seed spread over one acre will result in approximately 6 seeds per square foot. For seed production, California poppy is typically grown as an annual, regardless of actual (variant-dependent) life history, though there are exceptions where production fields may be held over for additional years.

Seed Source Considerations: Selection of varieties for urban and garden plantings should be made with consideration to the local climate, soil or potting media, and whether the planting will receive supplemental irrigation. For urban areas, planting objective, floral qualities, and the price of seed are often the main factors in selecting a seed source. Successful natural area plantings depend on proper site preparation and the selection of adapted plant materials, i.e. seed from local populations or from populations with similar climate, soil texture and chemistry.
Cultivars should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

Once established, many adapted populations become self-perpetuating, both in terms of reseeding and plant density. Persistence within a site is dictated by the level of competition for soil and light resources. In a Madera California field mowed or grazed to unspecified stubble height, Ratcliff et al. (1972) attributed an increase in the density of poppy to a reduction in competition for light from an accumulated mulch layer and a reduction in the naturalized annual species ripgut brome (Bromus diandrus) and broadleaf filaree (Erodium botrys).

Inhabits moist to mesic river banks and lake shores in steppe and montane zones; infrequent in southern British Columbia; extending east to Newfoundland and south to Virginia and New Mexico. Euthamia graminifolia additionally occupies moist, open ground, meadows, prairies, roadsides, ditches, inter-dunal flats, exposed lakes, conifer swamps, lowland forests, calcareous seeps, and sandy moist shorelines.

A perennial herb arising from a creeping rhizome, featuring erect stems that are branched in the inflorescence, essentially glabrous, and 0.3-1.0 m tall; basal leaves are lacking, while alternate, numerous, unstalked stem leaves are lance-linear, 7-11 times as long as wide, up to 13 cm long and 12 mm wide, 3- to 5-nerved, glabrous or hairy, never glaucous, with the lower ones soon deciduous. E. graminifolia is an upright, native perennial of the Asteraceae family whose species name translates to "grass-leaf," growing 0.9–1.8 m in height with a 0.3–0.6 m spread. The upper half of the plant appears bushy due to branched stems and grass-like, narrow to linear, alternate leaves emerging from a long, slender rhizome. The stalkless, 5.1–10.2 cm long leaves taper to a long point and narrow towards the stem, exhibiting 3–5 nerves underneath, minute rough-pubescence along nerves and margins, and a few resinous dots on the underside, emitting a scent when crushed.

Adding nitrogen will increase plant size, including an increase of stem height, number of leaves, and stem diameter. Adding N has been shown to increase the density of stems in the second year after fertilization, thereby eliminating other plant species and reducing community diversity. Management of flat-top goldentop should consider the negative effect fertilization may have on existing community structure.

Found along moist river banks and lakeshores in the steppe zone; frequent in south-central British Columbia; extending east to Alberta and south to Nebraska, Arizona, New Mexico, and California. Western goldentop commonly occurs in riparian areas, coastal salt marshes, freshwater wetlands, and wet meadow habitats, frequently associating with cattails, rushes, and sedges, across western North America from Nebraska west to California, north to British Columbia, and south to Arizona and New Mexico.

A perennial herb from a creeping rhizome, presenting erect stems that are glabrous throughout except for the rough-hairy margins of the leaves, measuring 0.5-2.0 m tall; basal leaves are lacking, and alternate, unstalked stem leaves are lance-linear, 3-nerved, gland-dotted, up to 10 cm long and 1 cm wide, glabrous and sometimes glaucous, with lower stem leaves soon deciduous. Belonging to the Composite family (Asteraceae), western goldentop is a rhizomatous perennial forb with erect stems reaching up to 2 m in height. The erect stems bear numerous sessile, cauline, linear leaves 2 to 10 cm long and 1 to 10 mm wide. The inflorescence forms a large, flat-topped corymb composed of multiple small yellow flower heads.

Annual herb from a taproot; stems erect or sprawling, simple, several, 20-60 cm tall, smooth to hairy, hollow, reddish at maturity. Buckwheat family (Polygonaceae). Buckwheat is a warm-season, broadleaf annual with superficial surface roots, a weak tap root and erect, reddish stems. The plant produces multiple branches along the stems, heart-shaped leaves, and clusters of small white flowers at the end of the branches.
Stems erect or sprawling, simple, several, 20-60 cm tall, smooth to hairy, hollow, reddish at maturity.
Basal leaves egg- to arrowhead-shaped, the blades 3-10 cm long, the stalks up to 1/2 as long as the blades; stem leaves similar, reduced, the upper ones unstalked.
Inflorescence of dense axillary and terminal, several- to many-flowered racemes; perianths white to pinkish, the 5 smooth segments 2-3 mm long; stamens 8.
Achenes, 3-angled, 5-7 mm long, smooth, extending well beyond the persistent perianths.

Buckwheat grows best in soils with light to medium texture and good drainage (Clark, 2007) and will tolerate moderately acidic soils (to a pH of 5) (Myers and Meinke, 1994). It will not grow well in compacted, saturated, or coarse soils and is not tolerant of frost, flooding, soil crusting or extreme drought (Clark, 2007; Bjorkman and Shail, 2010).

Buckwheat plants begin to flower within 3 to 6 weeks after planting and flower continuously for several weeks. Seeds mature 10 days after flowering and shatter (fall off the plant) soon after maturing, which reduces yields and causes potential volunteer problems the following year.

Buckwheat should be planted after the risk of frost has passed, and at the appropriate time for its intended purpose. Buckwheat grown for grain harvest should be planted when vegetative growth can occur in warm weather and seed development can occur in cool weather (Berglund, 2003). Recommended planting dates vary from late May to mid-June in North Dakota (Berglund, 2003), mid-June to mid-July in New York (Bjorkman, 2009), and mid-July in central Washington (under irrigation).
The most popular buckwheat varieties in the U.S. differ by region. The variety is usually specified by a processor if the crop is contracted.

Buckwheat has the potential to fit into many rotations in regions around the country. It can be grown as a cover crop or commercial crop following early-harvested vegetables or grains, and planted for emergency cover if a spring crop fails to establish or if a fall crop planting is delayed. It can also be used as a companion crop or nurse crop of late-fall plantings and for transitioning idle or nutrient-poor fields into production.

Buckwheat grown as a cover crop is often planted with common seed (no specified variety). ‘Horizon’ is a large seeded variety that has produced high yields in trials in North Dakota and Canada. ‘Koma’ is a large seeded variety that often yields higher than ‘Mancan’. ‘Mancan’ is a large seeded variety that is commonly grown throughout the U.S. It has a large seed which is required by processors. ‘Springfield’ is a large-seeded variety that has yielded high in North Dakota trials.

Buckwheat was one of the first crops domesticated in Asia and was likely used as a food crop in China 5,000 to 6,000 years ago.

Few insect or disease pests affect buckwheat. Some of the worst pests in the Northeast are deer and turkeys that forage on young buckwheat plants. Buckwheat has the potential to attract tarnished plant bugs, lygus bugs and aphids; however, these may serve as a food source for the beneficial insects buckwheat also attracts.

Rough fescue is highly palatable to livestock. It is excellent forage for cattle and horses and good for sheep and wildlife during all growth stages.

Rough fescue reproduces primarily by seed (USDA Plants Database) and rarely produces rhizomes. On average there are 205,300 rough fescue seeds per pound. It produces seed erratically and several years may pass without appreciable seed set.

Rough fescue typically initiates growth immediately following snowmelt, completes growth before the onset of summer drought, and is dormant by October. Onset of growth in the spring appears to be controlled by soil temperature rather than soil water content or air temperature. In Alberta Johnston and MacDonald observed that growth began in early May when soil temperatures were 35.6°F (2°C) at 20.3 cm. Cultivated seed production has resulted in average production of 112.1 kg/ha or less (MSU EB 69).

Grazing – Rough fescue is tolerant of winter grazing; approximately 80% utilization can occur during dormancy without appreciable loss in summer vigor, whereas summer grazing above 1.2–2.4 AUM/ha causes stands to decline (Willms et al.; King & Hill).

The range of Idaho fescue extends through California, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming. It is recognized as one of the most common and widely distributed grasses in the Western States, though it remains either rare or absent in the southern portions of its western range.

Idaho fescue is a native, perennial, cool-season bunchgrass with erect culms measuring 0.3 to 1.0 m tall, which are glabrous, glaucous, and sparsely leaved with predominantly basal foliage in shades of fine bluish-green to green. Leaf sheaths are flattened, keeled, and glabrous to scabrous, with short, open basal sheaths wider than the blade; collars are indistinct and auricles are small or absent. Leaf blades are involute, 5 to 25 cm long, filiform, firm, elongate, scabrous, often glaucous, glabrous abaxially and pubescent adaxially. The truncate ligule is a ciliate membrane measuring less than 2 mm long.

It does not compete well with aggressive introduced grasses. Its drought tolerance, combined with extensive root systems and good seedling vigor, make this species ideal for reclamation in areas receiving 35.6–50.8 cm annual precipitation.

Grazing/rangeland: Idaho fescue is a fair to good forage for all types of domestic livestock (Stubbendieck, J. et al., 1992).

Natural establishment: Idaho fescue produces a fair amount of seed of comparatively high viability and maintains itself well on the range if given a reasonable opportunity (USDA, Forest Service, 1988).

One PLS pound of Idaho fescue seed contains approximately 425,000 to 460,000 seeds and a broadcast planting of one pound of Idaho fescue seed results in a seeding distribution of approximately 10.1 seeds per square foot (USDA, NRCS, 1996). The recommended pure stand seeding rate is 3 to 4 (PLS) pounds per acre for range seedings.
Idaho fescue characteristically has poor seed production and weak seedling vigor (Hafenrichter et al. 1968).

Idaho fescue is susceptible to overgrazing. Idaho fescue should be left un-grazed by livestock through the growing season every 3 to 4 years. This will promote vigor and seed production and encourage the development of a strong root system, which is beneficial in reducing soil erosion and weed competition. Also, deferred grazing during the growing season supplies dry forage for autumn and winter use.

Foundation and registered seed is available through the appropriate state Crop Improvement Association or commercial sources to grow certified seed. Idaho fescue characteristically has poor seed production and weak seedling vigor (Hafenrichter et al., 1968). The base population used for recurrent selection consisted of seed derived from inter-crossing 89 native ecotypes collected from northwestern states of the U.S. Joseph exhibited 18% better seed set, 37% larger seeds, 14% better germination compared to the original native ecotype collection. Seed production of Joseph is 30% more than Covar, but 40% less than Durar (Ensing, 1984). ‘Nezpurs’ exhibited 30% more seed set, 29% larger seed size, and 11% better germination than the original collections. Inhabiting wet to mesic beaches, tidal marshes, streambanks, meadows, gravelly sites, dry disturbed areas, roadsides, and fields across lowland to alpine zones, this species is common in coastal and southern British Columbia and infrequent in northern British Columbia. It exhibits a circumpolar distribution extending north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to Tennessee, North Carolina, Texas, New Mexico, and California, with additional ranges in Greenland, Iceland, and Eurasia, and xeric coastal meadows in the San Juan and Gulf Islands (14). Red fescue occupies a wide range of ecological sites and soils, from coastal sands, gravels, and pebble beaches to moist meadows and disturbed soils from sea level to 3353 m elevation. There are over 200 varieties of red fescue released. Many of them are proprietary varieties developed by private companies and have been developed specifically for lawn/turf applications and are not discussed here. Red fescue plugs are easy to propagate in a greenhouse. Seed is surface-sown into containers containing standard potting mix and seeds germinate within 15 days after planting.

Red fescue starts growth early in the spring, generally slows in mid-summer, and grows vigorously from late summer until freezing. Growth during the summer is dependent on precipitation or irrigation. Red fescue is tolerant of close grazing but the stand and forage yield will decrease with overgrazing. If grazed according to a grazing management plan and allowed adequate time to recover, it can maintain or even increase yield over time.

Basal leaves are borne in rosettes, palmately compound on stalks 4-20 cm long, with 3 thick, leathery, short-stalked, egg-shaped leaflets 1.5-4 cm long; the lower surface is strongly net-veined, pale, and somewhat hairy, while the upper surface is green, smooth, and wrinkled with coarsely toothed margins where the terminal tooth is shorter than its neighbours. Spreading by seed, short rhizomes, and leafless stolons, the leathery leaves are basal with a petiole generally 2-20 cm, occurring in leaflets of 3 that are glabrous above.

Inhabiting swamps and estuaries in the lowland zone; rare on western Vancouver Island; ranging south to California. Oregon ash occurs in mild climates characterized by wet, mild winters and very little precipitation in July and August.

A deciduous tree growing up to 25 m tall (or reaching 23 m in forest settings with narrow crowns, while riparian specimens are shorter and broader with round-topped crowns and large limbs). Forest trees feature straight trunks with diameters of 40.6–76.2 cm, whereas broader trees reach diameters up to 137.2 cm; the bark is rough, grey-brown, and furrowed with deep cracks at maturity. Young twigs of new growth and leaves are hairy to woolly, or may be smooth. The opposite, pinnately compound leaves measure 15.2–30.5 cm long, consisting of 5 to 7 yellow-green leaflets measuring 5.1–12.7 cm long and 2.5–7.6 cm wide, with the terminal leaflet being the largest.

Blanketflower is a herbaceous perennial forb in the Asteraceae family arising from a slender taproot with a minimum depth of 40.6 cm. Blanketflower lends itself to agronomic seeding methods when planted at the appropriate time and rate. Seeds should be planted in the spring after frost risk.

Blanketflower may be grown from seed or by dividing vegetative parts. Seed does not require cold stratification treatment to break dormancy. For range plantings, plant seed into a firm, weed free seedbed, preferably with a mechanical drill that will ensure uniform seed placement depth of ¼ to ½ inch (Winslow, 2002). Establish seed production fields in rows with 26 PLS per linear foot (USDA-NRCS, 2013).

Meriwether Germplasm Selected Class blanketflower was released in 2011 by the Bridger Plant Materials Center in cooperation with the agricultural experiment stations of Montana State University and the University of Wyoming. Meriwether Germplasm is a composite from 14 Montana collections and one collection in Wyoming (Winslow, 2011).

Blanketflower is drought tolerant and requires supplemental moisture only during extended hot, dry conditions. Periodic mowing during the establishment year is an option for weed suppression. If using chemical weed control, preemergence herbicides are most effective. Blanketflower had mixed responses to herbicides, such as bloom delays and less flower growth; caution should be used if applying herbicide on a mix of wildflowers with blanketflower.

The Havasupai people, who live in the Grand Canyon in Northwest Arizona, use blanketflower as food. The seeds are parched, ground, and kneaded into seed butter. Flower heads were eaten and are used in soups and broths by the Niitsitapi.

Blanketflower is used by many indigenous people for food and medicine. Nlaka'pamux, whose traditional territory spans what is now known as the Canadian province of British Columbia, use blanketflower as a tuberculosis remedy, treatment for cancer, pain reliever, and miscellaneous disease remedy. Among the Niitsitapi (Blackfeet Nation) whose traditional territory spans much of Alberta, from the north Saskatchewan River, down along the Eastern Rocky Mountains, and Só'taétaneo'o and Tsétsêhéstâhese (Cheyenne) of the Great Plains, blanketflower roots were used for gastroenteritis, saddle sore treatment, eyewash for horses, skin disorders, and more.
The Kiowa or Ka’igwu of the Great Plains, pick the flowers for good luck.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Inhabits mesic to dry grasslands, meadows, and open forests across the steppe and montane zones. Frequent in southern British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, becoming rare northward and on Vancouver Island, and ranging east to Saskatchewan and south to South Dakota, Colorado, Utah, and California.

A perennial herb of the Rose Family (Rosaceae) arising from a thick stem-base, growing 25-90 cm tall (also described as 40 to 90 cm tall), with ascending to erect, branched stems that are spreading short-hairy below, long hairy and often glandular-hairy above, and densely covered with sticky glandular hairs. The basal leaves are long-stalked, stiff-hairy, and more or less glandular, with blades 5 to 12 cm wide (stem leaves 4-12 cm wide, opposite, and more or less rounded in outline), deeply palmately divided 3/4 their length into 5 to 7 sharply toothed segments or divisions. The flowers measure 2.5 cm wide in open terminal clusters, possessing 5 petals that range from pinkish-lavender to deep purple-magenta with purple veins and soft pubescence on the lower half. The elongated, glandular-hairy seed capsules terminate in a beak shaped like a stork's or crane's bill, alluding to the generic name Geranium (derived from the Greek 'geranos', crane).

Sticky purple geranium occurs in foothills, canyons, and open woodlands to montane environments, frequently associating with subalpine, coniferous forest, aspen forest, meadow, mountain brush, and shrub steppe plant communities (Mee et al 2003). Seed pods mature indeterminately and shatter easily. The pods should be collected in mid-August before the capsules split, placed into paper bags, transferred to mesh bags and allowed to dry. Luna and Seeds are grey to brown when mature and can be cleaned with a hammer mill and office clipper There are about 121,000 seeds per kilogram (55,000 seeds per pound).
Robson and Kingery (2006) recommend scarifying seed with fine-grit sand paper prior to soaking in cold water for 24 hours.

Germination of sticky purple geranium is improved with a combination of seed treatments. Luna and Lapp (2008) achieved 50 – 84% germination by scarifying seed with a hot water bath for 5 – 10 seconds and immediately transferring to a cold water bath, where they left the seeds soak for 24 hours.

Sticky purple geranium requires low to moderate fertility. Many new plants can result from seed shatter in subsequent years. To prevent unwanted plants, remove the seedpods before they are fully ripe. Plants become woody with age and should be separated.

Ground ivy was used as a flavoring and clearing agent in brewing beer before it was replaced by hops. In the U.S., it is a potential food source for introduced boars in the Smokey Mountains. Old English recipes recommended adding ground ivy to jams, soups, oatmeal and vegetable dishes, as cited by Mitich, 1994.

European herbalists used it to treat disorders of the bladder, kidneys, digestive tract and skin. Gout, coughs, colds, and ringing in the ears. During the 19th century in the U.S., ground ivy was used for treating lung and kidney diseases, asthma, jaundice, hypochondria, “monomania” (a condition of “partial insanity”), and it was snuffed to treat persistent headache (Lestrange, 1971 as cited by Mitich, 1994).
It is toxic to horses when consumed in large quantities.

A perennial herb of the Legume family (Fabaceae), known as American Licorice, arising from extensive, deep, woody, aromatic, sweetish rhizomes, with reproduction occurring by seed and underground stems called rhizomes. Plants grow 0.3-1 m (0.5–1.1 m, 0.5 to 1.0-m) tall, bearing erect, branched, smooth stems that are sticky with unstalked glands. Leaves are alternate and odd-pinnately compound, with 7 to 19 oblong-lanceolate, glandular-dotted leaflets measuring 2-5 cm long that are narrowed to an abruptly pointed tip; stipules are lanceolate, membranous, deciduous, and 3-10 mm long. American Licorice is a native perennial legume common to disturbed areas, draws, woods, and depressions over much of temperate North America (Duke, 1981).

Whitman (1979) found the germinability of field collected G. lepidota seeds to be among the highest of 30 native forb species from North Dakota, but he also cautioned that germination varied considerably between years of collection. Boe and Wynia (1985) found that considerable variation was found among licorice populations for greenhouse and field emergence.
Percent emergence in the greenhouse ranged from 0 to 97%, while field emergence ranged from 0 to 73% with an overall mean of 41%.

The process of scarification of the seed produced a higher rate of germination and more uniform stands in the field. Since it is a legume licorice should be inoculated with rhizobium Glycyrrhiza Spec. 1 inoculant.

At the present time there are no cultivar releases or any type of plant materials release of American licorice. Seed used by Boe and Wynia (1985) in their greenhouse and field experiments were all scarified for 5 seconds in a Forsberg laboratory scarifier prior to planting.

The management of American licorice is determined by the intended use of the species. If used for forage then management would be to incorporate the plant into a warm-season grass mix for foliage and nitrogen production.

Young shoots eaten raw. Roots used for food. Kindscher (1987) also detailed the Native Americans use of licorice as food.

American licorice was widely used as medicine by Indians of the Great Plains. The Cheyenne’s drank medicinal tea made from the peeled, dry roots of the plant for diarrhea and upset stomach. The Lakota’s used the root as a medicine for flu.
The loss of seeds as a result of insect predation is a potential threat to the maintenance and expansion of plant populations.

Native Americans regarded Great Valley gumweed as a useful medicinal plant for a variety of treatments, including respiratory and dermatological afflictions. The Costanoan Indians boiled leaves and flower heads of gumweed for healing dermatitis caused by poison oak, and for wounds, burns, boils, and sores. The Kawaiisu people used a similar decoction as a general analgesic and orthopedic aid, applying the plant material to their sore muscles (Zigmond, 1981); Miwok Indians used fresh, resinous buds as a treatment for blood disorders.

Small scale production fields and wildland collections can be made by beating the seeds off the plant into a bin or bag, or by clipping the flower heads. Seed is cleaned by running the collected material through a hammer mill followed by sieving and air-screening. Seed often contains small grubs.

Tests conducted at Aberdeen Plant Materials Center indicate there are approximately 400,000 seeds/lb and 39 lbs/bushel. Based on a seeding rate of 50 pure live seeds (PLS) per foot, the full stand seeding rate is 5 lbs/ac. Seeding rate should be adjusted to match the desired percentage within a seed mixture.
There are currently no commercial releases of curlycup gumweed; however multiple accessions are currently under investigation at Aberdeen Plant Materials Center for potential release.

Due to its low moisture requirements and limited palatability, curlycup gumweed increases under drought conditions in irrigated pasture as well as under poor grazing management practices, and is often associated with pastures and range that have been over grazed. Curlycup gumweed should be used as a minor component of pollinator and restoration seed mixtures. Management strategies should be based on the key species in the established plant community. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment.
Limited quantities of wildland collected seed may be available from commercial sources. Seed sources should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

The resin of curlycup gumweed contains many medicinally beneficial compounds. Indigenous peoples traditionally used this species for a variety of ailments. A decoction of root was used for liver trouble, and a paste made from flowering tops was applied to skin diseases, scabs and sores.

Curlycup gumweed has been shown to have the capacity to serve as a host plant of the Colorado red node virus of bean (Thomas, 1949). It may also have the ability to accumulate selenium from the soil and become toxic to livestock (SDSU, 2016); Curlycup gumweed is native to western North America. It will spread under favorable conditions.

Perennial herb of the Pea Family (Fabaceae), known as Utah sweetvetch; this native, cool-season, herbaceous legume develops from a branched, woody stem-base or crown, deep taproots, and several lateral roots, sometimes being rhizomatous, with the deep taproot system extracting deep soil moisture and nutrients to confer significant drought resistance and winter hardiness. Stems are decumbent to ascending, 10-60 cm long/tall (or main stems growing 0.3–0.6 m tall), sometimes branched above, and greyish stiff-hairy. Leaves are alternate, compound (odd-pinnate with two or more leaflets), 3-12 cm long on short stalks, hairy on both sides to glabrous on the upper surface (or hairless), and minutely gland-dotted above; leaflets number 9 to 15, are oblong to lance-elliptic, thick and firm with lateral veins usually not evident, 10-40 mm long by 3-14 mm wide, and abruptly sharp-pointed at the tip; stipules are straw-coloured, leathery, distinct or shortly joined below, and 5-10 mm long. Flowers can be pink, purple, or white arranged in a loose raceme; seeds develop in a long constricted pod with several sections, each containing one brown kidney-shaped seed.

Grazing/Rangeland/ Utah sweetvetch can be used as a complimentary species in rangeland seedings. It is considered succulent and its foliage is highly nutritional and palatable to livestock and big game, including bison, deer, elk, and moose.

Utah sweetvetch can be grown from seed. Planting should be done in early spring or late fall. Fall planting is preferable to take advantage of natural weather conditions during winter to get proper germination.

‘Timp’ Utah Sweetvetch (Hedysarum boreale Nutt.) Is a seed-propagated cultivar. The genetic material originated from two sources: (1) a site at the base of the Wasatch Mountains and east of Orem County in Utah, and (2) a single-plant selection made by Dr. Robin Cuany. ‘Timp’ was selected based on its seedling vigor, site adaptability, persistence, seed production, dinitrogen fixation, and stability. It was released in 1994 by Upper Colorado Environmental Plant Center, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Colorado State University Agricultural Experiment Station, Utah State University Agricultural Experiment Station, and USDA-Soil Conservation Service. ‘Timp’ Utah sweetvetch is adapted to a wide range of soil types, however, performs better in well-drained loamy soils.
Reduce or withhold stocking during establishment and avoid overuse after establishment to maintain a healthy stand. Utah sweetvetch is moderately to fairly tolerant of grazing.
‘Timp’ certified seed is available commercially and breeder seed is maintained at Upper Colorado Environmental Plant Center.

Inhabiting mesic to dry gravel bars, river terraces, rocky slopes, and roadsides from the montane to lower alpine zones. Perennial herb supported by a branched, woody stem-base and a thick, fibrous taproot, with decumbent to ascending, greyish stiff-hairy stems 10-60 cm long/tall that are sometimes branched above. Leaves are alternate, odd-pinnate, 3-12 cm long on short stalks, hairy on both sides to glabrous on the upper surface, and minutely gland-dotted above; leaflets number 9 to 15, are oblong to lance-elliptic, thick, firm, 10-40 mm long by 3-14 mm wide, abruptly sharp-pointed at the tip, and with lateral veins usually not evident; stipules are straw-coloured, leathery, distinct or shortly joined below, and measure 5-10 mm long. Pea Family (Fabaceae). Utah sweetvetch is a native perennial, cool season, herbaceous legume with deep taproots and several lateral roots, sometimes rhizomatous.

‘Timp’ Utah Sweetvetch (Hedysarum boreale Nutt.) Is a seed-propagated cultivar. The genetic material originated from two sources: (1) a site at the base of the Wasatch Mountains and east of Orem County in Utah, and (2) a single-plant selection made by Dr. Robin Cuany. ‘Timp’ was selected based on its seedling vigor, site adaptability, persistence, seed production, dinitrogen fixation, and stability. It was released in 1994 by Upper Colorado Environmental Plant Center, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Colorado State University Agricultural Experiment Station, Utah State University Agricultural Experiment Station, and USDA-Soil Conservation Service. ‘Timp’ Utah sweetvetch is adapted to a wide range of soil types, however, performs better in well-drained loamy soils.

Wildland seed is harvested by hand or with racquets into paper sacks or hoppers. The seed can be removed from the flower heads by light threshing or with a hammer mill. Air screens can be used to separate seed from chaff.

Oneflower helianthella can be drilled or broadcast into rangeland seedings. For optimum establishment, seed should be seeded dormant in late fall to a depth of 0.3 to 0.6 cm (1/8 to 6 mm) in a firm, weed-free seed bed. The recommended full stand seeding rate for oneflower helianthella is 29.1 kg/ha; for a seed mixture adjust the seed rate accordingly (Ogle et al 2011).
There are no released varieties or cultivars of oneflower helianthella.

Oneflower helianthella should be used as a minor component of seed mixtures. Management strategies should be based on the key species in the established plant community. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment (Ogle and others, 2011; Stevens and Monsen, 2004).
Seed is available in limited quantities from commercial sources. Seed is also available through contract harvesting (Walker and Shaw 2005).

Burning also added nutrients to the soil.

Originally cultivated by North American Indians, it has a long and interesting history as a food. Sunflower seeds were and still are eaten raw, roasted, cooked, dried, and ground, and used as a source of oil. The roasted seeds have been used as a coffee substitute. Seeds historically cultivated and used for food in Indigenous gardens.

Had reputed medicinal value in soothing chest pains. Lange, an anthropologist at the University of Texas, wrote that “among the Cochiti, a reliable ‘home remedy’ for cuts and other wounds is the juice of freshly crushed sunflower stems. The juice is smeared liberally over the wounds, bandaged, and invariably results in a speedy recovery, with never a case of infection.”
Edible seed, shells used for dye. Purple and black dyes extracted from wild sunflowers were used to dye basketry materials. A yellow dye was also derived from the ray flowers.

The Navaho-Kayenta used the plant for the sun sand painting ceremony and as a disinfectant to prevent prenatal infections caused by the solar eclipse. The Zuni used a poultice of sunflower root to treat snakebite, along with much ritual and ceremony.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Maximilian sunflower occurs on rocky upland and loess hill prairies, rocky ledges, and along railways, roadsides, fences, and other disturbed areas. In drier regions, it is found along streams and near wetter areas. In mixed-grass prairies, it is associated with bluestem, switchgrass, Russian thistle, silverberry, milkweed, and snowberry species. In tallgrass prairies, it is associated with big bluestem, switchgrass, Indian grass, heath aster, ironweed, and Canada goldenrod.

Maximilian sunflower exhibits fire tolerance in its dormant stage. Seedlings will emerge on open, post-burned sites from the underground seedbank and rhizomes.

Erosion control: Maximilian sunflower has a perennial root crown and rhizomatous root system. Annual stems are produced from underground stems. This growth pattern allows Maximilian sunflower to spread and form dense plant clusters, reinforcing soil and preventing erosion.
Not suited for heavy foot traffic; best planted in restoration beds, meadows, or borders.

Heracleum maximum, commonly known as cow parsnip or hogweed, is a member of the carrot family (Apiaceae). Cow parsnip is a large, biennial or short-lived perennial, herbaceous plant native to North America. During the first year of growth, large palmate trifoliate basal leaves form a low-growing rosette from a fleshy taproot or thick cluster of fibrous roots (Whitson & Burrill, 2000). The 20.3–50.8 cm clasping basal leaves are as wide as they are long. Leaves are alternately arranged around a light green, deeply ridged, hollow stem.

Dried seed is estimated to be viable for up to three years when stored at 1–3°C (Luna et al., 2008).

Erosion Control: The fleshy roots of cow parsnip can be used for erosion control in areas that are gently sloped (Dittberner & Olson, 1983). It establishes quickly by seed and readily reseeds, making it a good choice for short and long-term revegetation projects (Esser, 1995).

The inflorescence is a spike ¾ to 10.2 cm long bearing flower clusters in groups of three long bristles (awns) that reach up to 15.2 cm in length, though awns may be absent in some varieties.

Inhabiting dry roadsides and waste areas across lowland and montane zones, this species is rare in southwestern and south-central British Columbia. Introduced from Europe, barley is an ancient cereal crop with no known wild populations, its precise global origins remaining obscure (Harlan, 1979). It may have evolved from Hordeum spontaneum, a weedy plant widespread throughout the Fertile Crescent of the Near East, though evidence suggests Hordeum agriocrithon, discovered in Tibet in 1938, may be a closer ancestor to modern cultivars. Not native to the United States, barley persists exclusively in cultivation, occasionally volunteering in fields and disturbed areas without establishing permanent populations (Hitchcock and Chase, 1971), and can be found in grainfields and along roadsides from Connecticut to New Jersey, South Dakota, Montana, Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, and California.

Barley, like other small grain crops, can be grazed by livestock before seedheads are produced. Barley can be planted sooner than wheat, and provides early season grazing.

Barley seed/grain production occurs in cool, dry areas of the United States. North Dakota is the nation’s leading producer of barley seed. Barley is generally planted in North Dakota as a spring crop in April.

Prepare a clean, weed-free seedbed prior to planting. Deep, fibrous roots will absorb residual nutrients from the soil, so fertilization is not typically needed when planted as a cover crop. If barley is planted in an arid climate, a minimum of one irrigation event is needed for establishment (Munda et al., 1998).
Malting varieties must meet rigorous standards for germination quality, kernel size and weight, kernel plumpness, and moisture content.

Management differs according to crop use. In arid areas, irrigation should be applied at boot stage (when seedheads begin to form) and after grazing. The most important management consideration when planting barley as a cover crop is ensuring that it is terminated at the proper time. Allowing barley to reach full maturity or failing to terminate growth at the proper time may inhibit germination and growth of the primary crop.
There are two types of barley seed stock commonly available: malting and feed varieties.

Common St. Johnswort is an early-flowing forb (June or July) that requires full sun or part shade. It can be propagated by seed, division, or by softwood cuttings.

Common St. Johnswort does not exhibit invasive tendencies in undisturbed areas, but in disturbed areas it is much more dominant. St. Johnswort can be potentially invasive in prairie, mountain grassland, western hardwoods, maple-beech-birch, oak-hickory, and oak-pine complexes. Repeated cultivation has been found to destroy the weed. Colonies can also be controlled by mowing several times before maturation.

It is a well-investigated medicinal herb.

Externally iris rhizomes are successfully used on infected wounds, ulcers, fistulas and to take away freckles. This is a useful medicinal plant but in general should be used with care and preferably in combinations where less energetic plants forming the bulk of a medicinal formula.

Iris makes some of the finest cordage. Iris cordage was used for fishing nets, string, rope, snares, hairnets, and regalia. Rope was made from fibers, which occur, on the outer margins of iris leaves.

Coiled basketry prevails in southern California, with the mottled yellowish brown of rush providing a natural colored and variegated background Rush stems are used in the coiled baskets of southern California and Mexican Indian basketweavers, such as the Cahuilla, Luiseño, Chumash, Diegueño, Agua Caliente, Gabrieliño, Juaneño, Death Valley Shoshone, and Fernandeno. Chumash baskets, from southern California, are made with rush stems for the tan color and roots for the black color. The foundation material is made of mountain rush and the sewing material is made of basket rush (J. textilis). The Cahuilla, Diegueño, Luiseño, and Chumash dye the mature rushes black by steeping them for several hours in an infusion of either horned sea-blite (Suaeda calceoliformis) or bush seepweed (Suaeda moquinii). Juncus species are also dyed yellow in an infusion of indigo bush (Psorothamnus emoryi).
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Occurs along lakeshores and sandy river bars in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; frequent throughout British Columbia. Baltic rush is a perennial, rhizomatous wetland plant of the Rush Family (Juncaceae) featuring perennial habit from long, creeping rhizomes. Perennial herb from long, creeping rhizomes; stems arising singly, not densely clustered, round, usually straight, smooth, wiry, erect, 40-60 cm tall. The lowest bract of the inflorescence is round and 2-20 cm long, appearing as a continuation of the stem.

Coiled basketry prevails in southern California, with the mottled yellowish brown of rush providing a natural colored and variegated background Rush stems are used in the coiled baskets of southern California and Mexican Indian basketweavers, such as the Cahuilla, Luiseño, Chumash, Diegueño, Agua Caliente, Gabrieliño, Juaneño, Death Valley Shoshone, and Fernandeno. Chumash baskets, from southern California, are made with Juncus stems for the tan color and roots for the black color. This dye is very penetrating and the color is durable, but it has a fetid, disagreeable smell. The Cahuilla, Diegueño, Luiseño, and Chumash dye the mature rushes black by steeping them for several hours in an infusion of either horned sea-blite (Suaeda calceoliformis) or bush seepweed (Suaeda moquinii). Juncus species are also dyed yellow in an infusion of indigo bush (Psorothamnus emoryi).
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Soft rush is a rhizomatous perennial with a large, cespitose growth form; stems are stout yet soft, smooth or finely lined with 30 to 60 longitudinal ridges, 30-120 cm tall (or 5-15 dm tall and 1.5-3 mm wide). Basal sheaths are reduced to short sheaths, bladeless or the inner ones tipped with a short awn, with edges usually overlapping nearly to the subtruncate or emarginate tip, and veins converging at the apex. Leaves are dull chocolate brown or chestnut-colored at the base, with inner sheaths dark toward the summit.

Juncus species can tolerate periods of drought and total inundation.

Plugs are grown in a greenhouse over winter, and are transplanted out into fields covered with weed fabric on a 0.3 m by 0.3 m spacing in the spring.

Typically a small, erect evergreen tree to 10 m tall with a conical form, though occasionally a sprawling shrub less than 1 m, possessing reddish-brown, scaly or fibrous and stringy bark. Leaves are mostly scalelike, opposite, and non-prickly, while young leaves are needle-like, 5-7 mm long, and arranged in whorls of three on the stem. Seed cones are fleshy, berrylike, 5-6 mm long, glaucous, and bluish-purple when mature; pollen and seed cones occur on separate plants within the Cypress Family (Cupressaceae). The Rocky Mountain cedar (Juniperus scopulorum) is a medium-sized dioecious or rarely monoecious tree ranging from 10-20 m (33-66') tall (McGregor et al. 1986), This evergreen tree has a scraggly habit with a rounded to pyramidal crown.

The following information on the Traditional Resource Management (TRM) for Rocky Mountain juniper was provided by Lynn Youngbuck, who is Cherokee, Chiracahua, and Fox. TRM includes the following: Take what you need, leaving the best to reproduce. Speak to the plant, leave an offering of tobacco or sage before harvesting. The plant will grow back two stems for every one cut.
Juniperus scopulorum is readily available from nurseries throughout its range.

The Blackfeet made a tea from the berries of the Rocky Mountain juniper to stop vomiting. Mixed with Populus leaves this root tea became a liniment for stiff back or backaches, The Cheyennes steeped the leaves of the Rocky Mountain juniper and drank the resulting tea to relieve persistent coughing or a tickling in the throat. The Cheyenne, along with the Flathead, Nez Perce, Ktunaxa (Kootenay), and Sioux, made a tea from juniper boughs, branches, and fleshy cones.

A Blackfeet remedy for arthritis and rheumatism was to boil juniper leaves in water, add one-half teaspoon of turpentine, and when cooled, rub the mixture on affected parts. The Blackfeet also drank a tea made from Juniperus scopulorum root as a general tonic. Cheyenne women drank juniper tea to speed delivery during childbirth.
Wood for bows and combs. Cleansing wash for clothing, walls, bedding.

Bog Labrador tea inhabits bogs, fens, muskegs, open tundra, and dwarf shrub communities. It covers significant areas in bogs with black and white spruce (Picea mariana and Picea glauca), and tamarack (Larix laricina) in the boreal forests of Canada and high-elevation northeastern United States; eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis), pitch pine (Pinus rigida), eastern white pine (Pinus strobus), sugar maple (Acer saccharum), white ash (Fraxinus americana), and paper birch (Betula papyrifera) in the Northeast and Great Lakes region; as an understory shrub in open or closed moist forests in association with lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta var. contorta), Sitka spruce (Picea sitchensis) and western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla) in the Pacific coastal forests of Oregon, Washington, Canada, and Alaska; and shrub birch (Betula glandulosa) in the Yukon (Cronquist 1991).

Heath family (Ericaceae). An erect, aromatic shrub growing up to one meter in height with twigs densely covered in long, soft hairs (villous). Leaves are narrow, leathery, 2-5 cm long, alternate, and evergreen, featuring a dark green upper surface with margins that curl under, and a dense mat of orange-brown hairs on the underside. Numerous white flowers in tight clusters bloom from May to July, each possessing a small five-toothed sepal tube, five separate petals, and 5-7 stamens.

Indians in different regions burned these wetlands periodically (Anderson 2009; Patterson 2003). The primary role of fire was to maintain open habitats such as prairies, bogs, and forest clearings. Many of the fens and bogs that provide important habitat for bog Labrador tea in North America were created by glaciation. These wetlands have been disappearing over thousands of years, due to a decrease in native ungulates that graze the bogs, and encroachment by conifers and hardwoods.

Medicinal Use: The sophistication and complexity of bog Labrador tea’s medicinal use is demonstrated by the wide variety of ailments that were treated with this plant. Hudson Bay Company writer Edward Umfrewille (1954) wrote in 1790 about the Indians and Europeans of Canada and how they used the tea medicinally: “Its virtues are many.” Tribes used the leaves to treat inflammatory pathologies such as asthma, rheumatism, and burns. The Makah, for example used a strong infusion for a blood purifier.

Lentils are cultivated across 53 countries globally, with Canada, India, Turkey, Australia, and the United States serving as major producers. In the United States, Montana, North Dakota, Washington and Idaho lead production (USDA-National Agricultural Statistics Service, 2012).

Legume family (Fabaceae). Lentils are 30.5–76.2 cm tall, slender, semi-erect annuals that can exhibit a single stem or a branched, bushy form. Leaves are pinnate with up to 14 sessile, ovate to lanceolate leaflets, each approximately 1.3–3.8 cm long, bearing two small stipules at the base and occasionally terminating in a tendril. Flowers are typically double, or occasionally one to four on racemes, small (less than 13 mm long), and range from white to pale or dark purple, blooming sequentially from the lower branches upward (Cash et al., 2001).

Leaves and twigs browsed by caribou and moose. Livestock feed: Lentils that do not meet food grade standards (#3 or below) are used for livestock feed (Oplinger et al., 1990).

Lentil seed size varies with seed type and cultivar. Large-seeded cultivars ‘Laird’ and ‘Merrit’ have approximately 6,500 seeds per pound, and small-seeded varieties ‘Eston’ and ‘Pardina’ have about 12,600 to 19,700 seeds per pound.

Spring varieties of lentils should be planted when the soil has warmed to 4°C. Timely spring planting results in taller plants, which may improve ease of harvest and yield (Oplinger et al., 1990). Lentil seedlings can generally withstand frost and temperatures as low as -6°C (Cash et al., 2001).
Numerous lentil cultivars are available for commercial production. A few of the most common cultivars for each market class are listed below.

Weed management prior to lentil establishment is critical since lentils do not compete well with weeds and plants are easily damaged by post-planting cultivation. Applications of pre-emergent herbicides such as linuron and metribuzin (applied post-planting) are common. A few post-emergence herbicides are labeled for lentils, however they are not typically used since they may cause damage to the crop. These include sethoxydim and triallate for grass weeds, and imazethapyr and metribuzin for broadleaf weeds.

Popular lentil dishes are dhal in India, mujaddara in Arab countries, kik wot in Ethiopia, and kushari in Egypt. The lentil is celebrated every year in Pullman, Washington, at The National Lentil Festival with a parade and the “world’s largest bowl” of lentil chili.

Lentils are an important food in Jewish mourning ceremonies because their round shape symbolizes the cycle of life, and in Italy and Hungary, people consume lentils on New Year’s Eve to bring about wealth and prosperity since lentils are shaped like coins (USA Dry Pea and Lentil Council, 2015).

Lentils are attacked by insects at all stages of plant growth. Seeds and seedlings are eaten by seedcorn maggots (Delia platura), wireworms (Limonius spp. and Ctenicera spp.), cutworms (Agrotis spp.), and weevil larvae (Sitona spp.)

Basin wildrye (Poaceae) is a large, coarse, robust, perennial bunchgrass forming a coarsely tufted habit from short, smooth to strongly short-hairy rhizomes that create large clumps up to 1 m wide, supported by an extensive, deep, coarse fibrous root system. Stems are solitary or in groups, usually finely short-hairy or smooth especially near the nodes, standing 70-220 cm tall with growing points 25.4–30.5 cm above the crown. Sheaths are open; leaf blades are tough, rough to sometimes finely hairy, mostly flat, measuring (5) 8-20 mm wide and 38.1–63.5 cm long, featuring well-developed ear-shaped lobes (long pointed auricles) at some leaf-bases; ligules are usually short-hairy, membranous, and (2) 3-7 mm long. Reproductive stems are dense, stout, and strongly erect, bearing seed heads 15.2–25.4 cm long.

Erosion control/reclamation: Basin wildrye is well adapted to stabilizing disturbed soils. It does not compete well with aggressive introduced grasses during the establishment period, but it is very compatible with slower developing natives such as Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), thickspike wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus ssp. lanceolatus), streambank wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus ssp. psammophilus), western wheatgrass (Pascopyrum smithii), and needlegrass species (Stipa spp., Nasella spp., & Ptilagrostis spp.) Basin wildrye’s drought tolerance, combined with fibrous root system and fair seedling vigor, make it desirable for reclamation in areas receiving 20.3–50.8 cm annual precipitation. It is commonly used as a grass barrier for wind erosion or blowing snow control. It has also been planted on hilly cropland as a vegetative terrace for water erosion control.

Dotted gayfeather is a native, long-lived herbaceous forb belonging to the composite or sunflower family (Asteraceae). Dotted gayfeather is a native long lived herbaceous forb that is 20 to 80 cm tall, with stems single or in clusters from a woody rootstock. The taproot system is remarkably extensive, featuring lateral branches that spread 1.0 to 1.5 meters; the generalized root system more or less thoroughly occupies the first 2.5 meters of soil, absorbing little in the first 30 cm, but sometimes reaching a depth of 5 meters. Leaves are alternately arranged on the stem, closely spaced, and linear, measuring up to 15 cm long and 1.5 to 5 mm wide.

A robust perennial herb up to 1.3 m tall with thick, hollow, finely ribbed stem, deeply finely-divided fern-like leaves, purplish to yellow umbel flowers, and corky winged fruits 1-1.5 cm long. Inhabits dry grasslands, shrublands, talus, and rocky slopes in the steppe and montane zones, with var. dissectum rare in southern British Columbia and var. multifidum frequent in south-central and southeastern British Columbia, ranging east to Saskatchewan and south to Colorado, Arizona, and California.

A robust perennial herb up to 1.3 m tall (mature plants up to 1.3 m or 129.5 cm) belonging to the carrot family (Apiaceae), featuring a thick, hollow, finely ribbed stem, a large sometimes branching taproot reaching approximately 30 cm long and 5 cm thick, and deeply finely-divided fern-like leaves. Stems number several, 0.5-1.5 (2) m tall. Leaves are mostly basal, ternate and pinnately compound, 1-3 times divided; blades of the larger mature leaves are 15 to 30 cm long, with larger ultimate segments 2 to 3 mm wide (generally narrow and scarcely leaflike, usually less than 5 mm wide). Flowering occurs from April through May with yellow to purple, purplish to yellow umbel flowers borne in umbels with 10 to 30 rays, each ray 4 to 10 cm long.

Fernleaf biscuitroot is adapted to coarse-to fine-textured soils with pH of 6.5 to 7.5. Dry grasslands, rocky slopes, grassy bluffs, and open montane habitats at low/middle elevations; shade intolerant and adapted to dry, well-drained soils.

It is also found in grasslands, open slopes, and meadows across Secwepemcúl̓ecw, including Neskonlith Meadows, as well as dry, open, rocky slopes and vernal meadows at low to mid elevations from British Columbia to Saskatchewan and south to California, New Mexico, Wyoming, and Colorado. This plant grows as common in mountain and Wyoming big sagebrush, pinyon-juniper, and mountain shrub communities from 150 to 3,000 m throughout its range (Welsh et al., 2003). Fernleaf biscuitroot naturally occurs from British Columbia and Saskatchewan south to California and New Mexico, extending eastward to Wyoming and Colorado.

Small scale production Seed matures in July into August. Wildland seed disarticulates readily and is easily hand collected. Very clean collections can be made by shaking ripened inflorescences over a bag or tarp.

Seed can be broadcast or drilled to 0.3 to 0.6 cm (1/8 to 6 mm) into a well prepared, weed-free seedbed. This species should be seeded in late fall as a dormant planting to allow for natural stratification of the seed over winter.
There are currently no commercial releases of fernleaf biscuitroot.
Once established, fernleaf biscuitroot is very competitive against weeds due to its long taproot; however additional measures to control weeds are necessary for seed production.

Lomatium triternatum; Nineleaf Biscuitroot; Triternate Biscuit-root

Inhabiting dry open slopes and grasslands in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; frequent in south-central and southeastern British Columbia (subsp. triternatum), and rare on southern Vancouver Island (subsp. platycarpum); extending east to southwestern Alberta and south to Colorado, Utah, and California. This plant grows as common on sunny valley bottoms, open ridges, and slopes of foothills and lower mountains, occasionally reaching higher elevations.

Nineleaf biscuitroot is an herbaceous perennial forb of the carrot family (Apiaceae) arising from an elongated, seldom thickened taproot surmounted by a simple branched crown or stem-base, capable of extending several feet into the soil and conferring high tolerance to grazing, trampling, drought, and fire. Stems or scapes are solitary or few, erect, glabrous, and 10-80 cm tall, allowing mature plants to reach 70 cm tall. Leaves are mostly basal, ternate-pinnately compound, divided 1-3 times or 2-3 times at the base, with 9 to 21 leaflets or segments, and bear petioles up to 20 cm long featuring a dilated base that forms a sheath around the stem.

Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
It is reported to grow in soils with a pH of 6.5 to 8.8 and minimum of 120 frost free days.
Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.

Perennial herb arising from a stout, woody stem-base belonging to the bean family (Fabaceae); stems are few to several, erect or ascending, up to 1 m tall but barely 10 cm in exposed areas, often cylindric-hollow, and soft-shaggy (especially when young) to short-stiff-hairy. Leaves are alternate, palmately compound, borne on stalks rarely twice as long as the longest leaflet, with leaflets numbering 5 to 8, broadly oblanceolate, blunt to rounded at the tip, 1-7 cm long, shaggy-soft-hairy below, and generally glabrous above. Nootka lupine is a native perennial that dies back annually to a thick rhizome (MacKinnon, 1994), featuring palmately compound leaves up to six centimeters long. Blossoms are blue, occasionally tinged pink or white, pea-like, up to two centimeters long, and arranged in dense clusters measuring as much as thirty centimeters long.

Nootka lupine seeds should be pre-soaked for twenty-four hours, to break down the tough seed coats, and then sow in the early spring in a greenhouse. The seedlings should be thinned out as soon as the first true leaf appears. Division should be done in the spring, just before new growth commences.

Lupines are most valuable because of the masses of nitrogen fixing bacteria, which live in nodules on their roots and convert the free nitrogen of the atmosphere into compounds that are essential to plant and animal growth.

Although bigleaf lupine prefers cool, subalpine climates and damp to wet soils, it can also tolerate full sun and seasonally drier soils (Robson et al., 2008). Observations indicate it can even prefer acidic, nutrient-poor mineral soils, giving it a competitive advantage over other plants in the community (Fremstad, 2010).

Moist to mesic meadows, riverbars, streambanks, seashores, clearings, roadsides, glades and open forests in the lowland, steppe and montane zones; frequent in SW, SC and WC BC, less frequent northward. This species prefers moist habitats and seasonally wet soils, but will tolerate seasonal dryness (Robson et al., 2008). It is commonly found in a variety of habitat types including seasonally dry to marshy meadows, wetlands and damp forests, along stream banks and ditches, and in disturbed areas (Turner and Gustafson, 2006). Bigleaf lupine is native to western North America, from British Columbia and Alberta south to California and east to Montana, Idaho and Nevada.

Bigleaf lupine can be hard-seeded, so physical or chemical scarification can improve uniformity of germination.

Prior to planting, reduction of the weed seed bank on site and proper field preparation is important. Bigleaf lupine, like many legumes, has hard - coated seeds, so will germinate unevenly if not scarified prior to sowing.

The preferred planting method for seed production fields of this species is to plant plugs on wide row spacing (61–91.4 cm) to accommodate plant size and weed management strategies. Direct seeding is not recommended because weeds can out-compete seedlings in the spring.

Planting in late fall, near a water source, or with irrigation is ideal for emerging L. polyphyllus seedlings. As they mature, however, the established plants are often very prolific and hearty and will not necessarily require irrigation throughout the dry season.
Container plants or seed of native varieties are generally available from commercial native plant growers in the West.

Tribes throughout the range of bigleaf lupine reportedly used different parts of the plant for medicinal or tonic purposes. Although the Nlaka'pamux (Thompson) tribes of British Columbia considered it poisonous, they used it medicinally for themselves and their horses. The Salishan used it to make tonics and the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) ate the roots, fresh or steamed.
Seeds may be toxic to ruminant livestock or wildlife if consumed in large quantities.

Seeds and foliage contain quinolizidine alkaloids potentially toxic to livestock and pets if ingested raw in quantity. Aphids and powdery mildew are known to be problematic for this species. Bigleaf lupine can be hard - seeded, so physical or chemical scarification can improve uniformity of germination.

Prior to planting, reduction of the weed seed bank on site and proper field preparation is important. Bigleaf lupine, like many legumes, has hard - coated seeds, so will germinate unevenly if not scarified prior to sowing.

The preferred planting method for seed production fields of this species is to plant plugs on wide row spacing (61–91.4 cm) to accommodate plant size and weed management strategies. Direct seeding is not recommended because weeds can out - compete seedlings in the spring.

There are a number of horticultural cultivars available commercially that are sometimes called bigleaf lupines but are actually crosses of L. polyphyllus with L. arboreus and possibly L. nootkatensis. These Russell Hybrids (named for British horticulturist George Russell) are sold under hybrid names such as Rainbow Lupins, Lupin Tutti Fruitti, and Band of Nobles (mixed), Chandelier (yellow), My Castle (red), Noble Maiden (white), The Chatelaine (pink), and The Governor (blue).

The Salishan used it to make tonics and the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) ate the roots, fresh or steamed.

Seeds are collected by hand when seeds are tan to gray colored at maturity. Because seeds dehisce forcefully at maturity, pods are cut from field plants just as they begin to dry and placed into paper bags for transport. Pods are then spread out to dry and covered with a fine mesh cloth.
In western Montana plant growth begins in early May and flowering occurs in June and July. Seeds disseminate in August. The seed coat of silky lupine is hard, causing a physical dormancy.
There are no cultivars, improved, or selected materials of silky lupine.
Keep pregnant cattle away from silky lupine during the 40th to 100th days of gestation to prevent congenital deformities.
Common wildland collected seed is available from commercial sources (Native Seed Network).

The Syilx (Okanagan) / Colville tribe of British Columbia used a mixture of strained, pounded seeds mixed with water as an eye medicine. The Nlaka'pamux (Thompson) Indians of British Columbia considered the plant poisonous but thought that horses consumed the plant as a medicine (Native American Ethnobotany Database).
They also used the plant for bedding and floor covering in sweathouses.

Cattle grazing lupine between the 40th and 100th days of gestation often give birth to calves with crooked legs and other congenital deformities. Consumed hay containing lupine has also caused death of sheep and cattle. The amount of lupine that will kill an animal varies with the stage of plant growth. Keeping cows away from lupine during the 40th to 100th days of gestation will prevent most deformities.

Seeds and foliage contain quinolizidine alkaloids potentially toxic to livestock and pets if ingested raw in quantity. Because of its toxic qualities to domestic livestock, stock growers may consider silky lupine to be a weed where it is prevalent and interferes with livestock grazing. Dense stands can spread aggressively and crowd out surrounding vegetation if unmanaged. Greenhouse grown plants are susceptible to root rot and fungus attack (Hosokawa and others, 2004). The authors have observed natural stands of silky lupine that have been consumed by Mormon crickets. | Host insect damage: Glaucopsyche lygdamus: on flowers/fruits/leaves; Plebejus icarioides: on flowers/fruits/leaves

Immigrants might have deliberately introduced L. salicaria for its value as a medicinal herb in treating diarrhea, dysentery, bleeding wounds, ulcers, and sores, for ornamental purposes, or as a source of nectar and pollen for beekeepers. Decoction used to treat diarrhea, dysentery, and skin sores.

An important consideration in controlling purple loosestrife is its prolific seed production, the ease with which seeds are dispersed, and their ability to remain viable for several years. Also, this plant can spread vegetatively by resprouting from stem and rootstock cuttings. Overruns native wetland food plants (cattail, bulrush). The loss of native species and habitat diversity is a significant threat to wildlife, including birds, amphibians, and butterflies, that depend on wetlands for food and shelter. Forage/Livestock/Ley-farming: Bur clover is a nutritious, highly palatable and N2 fixing forage plant for slightly neutral to alkaline soils in Mediterranean climate regions (Del Pozo, 2002).

Seeds are produced in round, coiled burs surrounded by spiny hooks, which can cling to animal coats, assisting seed distribution. There can be 3-11 seeds per bur and are separated by partitions. The seeds are 2-4 mm long and oval.
Inoculate seed with Group AM Rhizobium; drill ¼–¾ in deep at 6.7–11.2 kg/ha (or 16.8–24.7 kg/ha monoculture) in October–November.
Bur clover requires about 25.4–63.5 cm of rainfall per year, where ample moisture is available early in the fall. It will produce plants in low-rainfall years if winters are not too cold.

Normal tillage and mowing equipment are appropriate for managing stands, but pure stands may lie close to the ground and be difficult to mow. To maintain bur clover stands, the area should be mowed leaving about 7.6–12.7 cm on the surface. Use phosphorus, and sulfur to encourage bur clover in mixed grass/clover stands. Those nutrients are often needed in establishing and maintaining bur clover seedings, as are potassium and nitrogen on poorer soils.

It was initially selected for its high seed yield and spineless pods. High seed yields have resulted in high plant densities in regeneration pastures, meaning higher dry matter production, especially in winter and spring. The seeds are yellowish brown, kidney shaped, and weigh 4 mg. Scimitar demonstrates excellent salt tolerance during critical growth periods and its adapted to short-lived waterlogged conditions (See Cavalier for seeding, management, and other properties) (Department of Agriculture Farmnote 83, 2004). The seeds are slightly larger, are yellow brown, kidney-shaped and weigh about 4.5mg. Cavalier produces high seed and herbage yield. Its hard seed will soften more readily, which allows for better pasture regeneration. Cavalier needs good weed control prior to seeding. It can be successfully established when seeded with other medics and clovers. It is adapted for south Texas with seed being available through Pogue Seed Company. It may re-seed itself for many years with proper grazing. It has shown some hardiness when seeded with warm season grasses. If broadcasted, increase the seeding rate to 9–13.5 kg/ha, and even higher rates up to 17.9 kg/ha if broadcasting into sod of warm season pastures.

Bur clover is used for medicinal purposes for skin plagues and dysentery. In the Bolivian Andes, bur clover has been used since the 16th century, for medicinal purposes, environmental uses, and animal feed. In Italy, bur clover leaf has been used for many centuries, such as medicinal purposes for treating rheumatic pains and wounds and is still used today.

Alfalfa weevil damage can be very widespread and cause extensive damage. Tarnished plant bugs and small loppers have also been found on bur clover plants at extremely high densities. Nematodes associated with bur clover include Ditylenchus dipsaci, Heterodera glycines, H. trifolii, Meloidogyne incognita, and Pratylenchus. | Host insect damage: Mirificarma eburnella: on spun leaves; Colias lesbia: on leaves

Inhabiting wet to dry meadows and open forests in the montane and subalpine zones, this species is rare in west-central and southern British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, extending east to southwestern Alberta and south to Colorado, Utah, Nevada, and northern California. Purple oniongrass occurs scattered throughout foothill and lower elevation mountain shrub-covered slopes and along forest margins from 1189–2591 m elevation and in 16-20+ inch (406-508+ mm) annual precipitation zones, ranging from Alberta and British Columbia in Canada south to Montana, Wyoming, and Colorado, and westward to the Pacific Coast states of California, Washington, and Oregon.

There is very little published information available regarding seed or plant production of purple oniongrass.
The seed matures in July/August and the seed needs cold stratification for 80 days at 0°C prior to planting.
Information in the scientific literature on establishment of purple oniongrass is very limited. Link (1993) reports there are approximately 556,000 seeds per pound.
There are no improved, selected materials or cultivars of purple oniongrass.
Purple oniongrass appears to decrease when subjected to overgrazing by large animals.
There may be unnamed selections or ecotypes of this species available from commercial sources.

Purple oniongrass is susceptible to stripe smut fungus (Ustilago striiformis) but is not susceptible to flag smut fungus (Urocystis agropyri) (University of Illinois, Online). It may be susceptible to other unknown pests or other problems. Purple oniongrass is a species native to the western United States and is not considered a weedy or invasive species.

Biennial or short-lived perennial herb belonging to the Loasa family (Loasaceae), featuring a deep taproot and several ascending to erect, branched, angular stems that are harshly barbed-hairy throughout but nearly glabrous near the bases, measuring 0.3-1 m tall. Leaves are alternate, brittle, 3-15 cm long (with basal leaves linear to shallowly lobed at 10-15 cm long, and stem leaves unstalked, oblong to egg-shaped, and less deeply lobed), bearing barbed pubescence that causes them to readily attach to touched foreign objects. Blooming from June through September, the star-like, yellow flowers possess 5 linear, sharp-pointed petals 2.5 to 8 cm long and approximately 50 filaments measuring 2 to 4 cm long, where five outer filaments may lack anthers and appear petal-like though narrower than true petals. Flowers open fully either strictly in bright sun or exclusively during nighttime hours, featuring a single style extending above the cup-shaped nectary atop the inferior ovary.

There are 660,000 seeds per kilogram (300,000 seeds per pound). Skinner (2007) found 10% seed emergence without stratification, 48% emergence with 30 days stratification, and 65% emergence with more than 90 days stratification.

Seed should be planted in a late dormant winter planting (November or December) with a drill into a weed-free seed bed at a rate of 6 kg PLS/ha (7 lbs PLS/ac) and at a depth of 1.3 – 0.6 cm. If included in a mix the seed rate should be adjusted according to the proportion of the mix, and if the seed is broadcast the rate should be doubled.

Mentzelia laevicaulis can be established by seed or transplanted seedlings. Seed should be planted in a late dormant winter planting (November or December) with a drill into a weed-free seed bed at a rate of 6 kg PLS/ha (7 lbs PLS/ac) and at a depth of 1.3 – 0.6 cm. The seed requires a cold-moist stratification period for optimal germination.

Managing weeds with hand hoes and wheel hoes can be detrimental to Mentzelia laevicaulis plants. Plants barely touched with equipment can dislodge from the ground. For this reason, it may be impossible to mechanically harvest seed of Mentzelia laevicaulis, unless the plant is treated like an annual and reseeded every year.

Oregon saxifrage is found along stream banks and in bogs, marshes, wet prairies, vernal pools and moist meadows with seasonally wet soils (Hitchcock and Cronquist, 1961).

Oregon saxifrage is a strong perennial that comes back from a simple or branched persistent and sometimes woody base, or caudex (Hitchcock and Cronquist, 1961). The glandular, densely hairy leaves are 7.6–25.4 cm long and are linear to widely egg shaped, tapering to a petiole (leaf stem) of 0–5.1 cm in length (Hitchcock and Cronquist, 1961; Turner and Gustafson, 2006). Leaf margins may be entire (smooth) or toothed.

In germination trials at the Corvallis Plant Materials Center, highest germination occurred after exposure to warm temperatures (18°C or above) for two weeks followed by cool temperatures (10°C) for 4 weeks.
Oregon saxifrage can be planted on restoration sites that contain wet areas such as stream banks, seasonal wetlands, or vernal pools.
Persistent fruit, hips, cones, or dried seedheads add late-season visual interest and winter wildlife forage.
Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Oregon saxifrage is adapted to grow in most soil types with adequate winter and spring moisture. The plants flower in the spring and go dormant by mid-summer to cope with dry conditions.

Inhabiting mesic to dry slopes and open forests in the steppe and montane zones, this grass is infrequent in northeastern, south-central, and southeastern British Columbia, ranging north to Yukon Territory and southwestern Northwest Territories, east to Manitoba, and south to New York, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. Serving as an important native grass of the Northern Great Plains and extending as far south as Arizona, green needlegrass grows on medium- to fine-textured soils in both the True Prairie and Mixed Prairie.

A perennial, tufted grass originating from fibrous roots, with stems that are smooth or sometimes more or less hairy, standing 50-110 cm tall. Sheaths range from smooth to short-hairy, with margins typically long-hairy and fringed with fine hairs near the tips, and collars that are usually long-hairy. Blades are strongly in-rolled and 3-6 mm wide. Ligules range from smooth to hairy on the outside and are rounded, with the lower ones measuring 0.5-1.5 mm long and the upper sometimes reaching up to 3 mm long.

Inhabiting mesic to dry slopes and open forests in the steppe and montane zones, this grass is infrequent in northeastern, south-central, and southeastern British Columbia, ranging north to Yukon Territory and southwestern Northwest Territories, east to Manitoba, and south to New York, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. Serving as an important native grass of the Northern Great Plains and extending as far south as Arizona, green needlegrass grows on medium- to fine-textured soils in both the True Prairie and Mixed Prairie. On medium-textured soils, it associates with western wheatgrass, needleandthread, and blue grama; on fine-textured soils, needleandthread drops out, and on even finer soils, blue grama decreases, leaving green needlegrass and western wheatgrass as dominants. This species naturally occurs on bottomlands, flat benches, and overflow areas along streams.

Rangeland/hayland: Green needlegrass is well suited for use in mixtures for range seeding, critical area establishment, mineland revegetation, wildlife habitat, and other plantings where the establishment of native vegetation is the objective. This plant grows as nutritious, palatable, but decreases under grazing use.

Seed production: Seed yields from green needlegrass fields vary from about 125 lb/ac on dry land to more than 250 lb/ac for irrigated fields. Older references indicate that this species can be grown in either rows or in a solid seeding.
Studies have shown that seed dormancy in this species is inversely related to maturity.
This plant is recommended for seeding mixes in the 30.5–45.7 cm precipitation zone. High dormancy is a characteristic of the seed of this species.

Many older references mention a variety of green needlegrass named ‘Green Stipa.’ This variety is no longer available, and was replaced by ‘Lodorm,’ which was released by the Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota Experiment Stations, along with the Plant Science Research Division of the Agricultural Research Service, Mandan, North Dakota. Lodorm originates from a bulk collection made in a native stand north of Bismarck, North Dakota, in 1935.

Due to its early spring green-up, green needlegrass is an important component of natural plant communities. This plant is harvested for hay in native grass mixtures. In some areas, it makes up an appreciable portion of the yields of native hay from upland areas or from flats, on loamy to heavy clay soils. The hay is of good quality and is readily eaten by livestock.

It was selected for low seed dormancy after harvest. Seed is commercially available, and the USDA, NRCS Plant Materials Center, Bismarck, North Dakota, maintains Foundation seed. Seed is available from Proven Seed/Agricore United. Seed is available from the Utah Crop Improvement Association.

The Cherokee, Iroquois, Ojibwas, and Potawatomi were among several Native American tribes that used common evening-primrose for both food and for medicinal purposes. A tea was made from the plant and used as a dietary aid or stimulant to treat laziness and “overfatness.” A hot poultice made from the pounded roots was applied externally to treat piles and boils. A poultice made from the entire plant was used to treat bruises.
