The first seed crop can be harvested the second year after establishment.
Seed yields can be as high as 1120.8 kg/ha under irrigated conditions. Under dryland conditions, seed yields are rarely more than 224.2 kg/ha.
Sainfoin can be planted in the spring or fall. Seeding depth should be between 0.25 and 1.9 cm.

Do not graze for two seasons after planting. Stands should be allowed to naturally reseed every 2 to 3 years for reestablishment. Stands will persist 3 to 6 years under irrigation but will last longer if root and crown rot diseases are controlled. Some plantings in Montana have survived for over 60 years and are still used for pasture.

Eski was selected from seed from Eskisehire, Turkey that survived severe winters at Sidney, Montana. The seed increased from these hardy plants was designated as breeder seed. Melrose showed higher forage yields, seed yields and greater winter hardiness than Eski (Cooke et al 1971). Breeder seed is maintained by the Canada Department of Agriculture Research Stations at Melfort and Saskatoon, Saskatchewan and Lethbridge, Alberta, Canada. Certified seed is maintained by SeCan Association, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada. Foundation seed is maintained by the University of Wyoming, Seed Certification Service in Powell, Wyoming. Foundation seed will be maintained by the Foundation Seed Programs of Montana and Wyoming.

Proso millet matures 60–90 days after planting. Seeds mature from the top of the inflorescence to the bottom, and may shatter before harvesting. Proso millet is self-pollinating, but some cross-pollination may occur by the wind.

Proso millet will germinate between 10–45°C (Baltensperger, 1996). The optimum soil temperature for planting is 13–18°C (McDonald et al., 2003). It is typically drilled at 30–40 lb/ac for forage or feed, ½ – ¾ inches deep, on 7, 10, or 30.5 cm rows (McDonald, 2003).

‘Dove’ proso millet is a cultivar developed by the USDA-NRCS Plant Materials Center in Americus, GA in 1972. ‘Sunrise’ and ‘Huntsman’ are white-seeded varieties co-released by the University of Nebraska and the USDA. ‘Earlybird’ and ‘Horizon’ are shorter season varieties.

Proso millet does not seem to benefit from high-input additions of nutrients or water. Like foxtail millet (Setaria italica), there will be little regrowth after being cut. Proso millet has been used in a winter wheat/sunflower/proso/fallow rotation in the Great Plains. In September it is cut and gathered into windrows to dry and cure.
White-seeded varieties are most often grown in the major production areas.

Fields, roadsides, shorelines and waste areas; infrequent in S BC; introduced from Eurasia. Proso millet grows best in full sun, moist to dry conditions, and can perform well in many soil types. This species naturally establishes across croplands, fallow fields, roadsides, waste sites, and disturbed soils. Erosion control/reclamation: Western wheatgrass is well adapted to stabilization of disturbed soils because of its strong spreading rhizomes. It does not compete well with aggressive introduced grasses during the establishment period, but is very compatible with slower developing natives such as bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), thickspike wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus ssp. lanceolatus), streambank wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus ssp. psammophilus), and needlegrass species (Nasella spp., Stipa spp., and Ptilagrostis spp.) Stands are generally slow to develop and may be non-existent the establishment year. However, over 50 percent stands are typically achieved by the end of the fourth growing season. Poor germination accounts for the poor initial establishment and strong rhizome spread accounts for stand development in later years. Its relative drought tolerance combined with strong rhizomatous root systems and adaptation to a variety of soils make this species ideal for reclamation in areas receiving 30.5–50.8 cm annual precipitation. Its low growth form, vigorous sod, and low maintenance requirements make it ideal for ground cover purposes. This grass can be used in urban areas where irrigation water is limited to provide ground cover and to stabilize ditchbanks, dikes, and roadsides.

Leaves are predominantly basal and stalked, lanceolate, 4-7 cm long, pinnately lobed to deeply cleft, with toothed or cleft lobes whose ultimate divisions are further toothed, all set along a broad leaf axis; stem leaves number 0 to 2 or 3, are alternate, and reduced.

Penstemon attenuatus grows in dry meadows and moist, open to wooded slopes in the mountains and foothills (Burke Museum of History and Culture 2012). The range of Penstemon attenuatus extends from eastern Washington and Oregon to western Montana, southern Idaho and north-central Wyoming (Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture 2012). The species is currently divided into four varieties (ecotypes): var. attenuatus (found in Washington, Oregon, Idaho and Montana), var. militaris (found in Idaho and Montana), var. palustris (found in Oregon and Idaho), and var. pseudoprocerus (found in Idaho, Montana and Wyoming).

Experiments with seed of P. attenuatus var. attenuatus at the Pullman Plant Materials Center demonstrated an extended cold moist stratification period is needed to break seed dormancy.

Plants can be established by seed or seedlings. Seed should be planted in a firm, weed-free seed bed in the fall at a rate of 1.65 kg PLS/ha (1.5 lb PLS/ac). Skinner (2007) had 0% emergence with no seed treatment, 10% emergence with 45 days of cold, moist stratification, and 72% emergence with 90 days of cold, moist stratification.

Penstemon attenuatus is able to withstand infrequent mowing. This method may be used for weed control in newly-established forb plantings, however mowing should be delayed until after seed maturity. Fields for seed production can be established by transplanting greenhouse grown containerized stock or from direct seeding. Direct seeding should take place in the fall to allow for natural stratification of the seed.

There are currently no releases of hotrock penstemon. Greenhouse materials can be established by seeding into cones or flats in winter for natural stratification or by stratifying the seed for 8 - 12 weeks in cold/moist conditions.

When planted in a native reclamation mix, hotrock penstemon should be a minor component of the establishing plant community; therefore management should be based on other key species in the mixture. Grazing on seeded lands should be deferred for at least two growing seasons to allow for establishment.
Wildland harvested seed is available through commercial sources.

Impact from insect pests on penstemon seed production can be significant. Penstemon borer larva can infect the crown and upper root area of all penstemon species resulting in the loss of individual plants to entire fields. Presently, penstemon borers are known only from extreme southwestern Colorado.

Inhabiting dry open slopes and terraces in steppe and montane zones, fuzzytongue penstemon is infrequent in southeastern British Columbia, extending east to Alberta and south to Nebraska, Colorado, Idaho, and Washington. It is commonly found on dry open slopes among meadows, mixed grass prairies, and mountain areas from 259–2499 m in elevation, growing in shallow, gravelly, sandy to sandy-clay soils and soils derived from limestone.

A perennial herb arising from a taproot surmounted by a frequently branched, largely underground stem-base, with usually several ascending to erect stems 10-40 cm tall that are minutely grey-hairy, sometimes additionally long-soft-hairy above and glandular-hairy in the inflorescence. Leaves are opposite with entire to remotely toothed margins; basal and lower leaves are lanceolate to egg-shaped, stalked, and reach up to 13 cm long, while upper leaves are lanceolate to oblong, nearly unstalked, and measure 3-7 cm long. Fuzzytongue penstemon is a perennial forb with a short taproot and one or more stems that grow 10.2–40.6 cm tall and are occasionally decumbent at the base. Basal leaves are spatula-shaped, tend to be poorly developed, but can grow to 7.6 cm long.

Drill seeding, broadcast seeding, or container planting are effective methods for establishing fuzzytongue penstemon. Drill or broadcast seed at a depth of 6 mm or less into a firm, weed-free seedbed. Adjust per acre seeding rates based on between-row spacing, percentage in the mix, and method of seeding. Seed production at the USDA-NRCS Plant Materials Center in Bridger, Montana, involves dormant fall sowing of 25 to 35 PLS seeds per linear foot at approximately 1/8 - to 1/4 -inch depth with a plot seeder. Row spacing is 76.2 cm between rows, a spacing largely dictated by available equipment and supplies.

Old Works Germplasm fuzzytongue penstemon was released in 2002 by the Bridger, MT Plant Materials Center, USDA-NRCS and is intended for conservation uses including revegetation of sites with moderate heavy metal soil concentrations and soil with acidic pH.

For optimal fuzzytongue penstemon establishment, manage weeds and other herbaceous competition with mowing before the flowering stage. Fuzzytongue penstemon is responsive to herbicide application on undesired species; establishment was negatively affected by trifluralin/pendimethalin and trifluralin/imazapic herbicide combinations in a 2006 native plant seed mix study in Bozeman and Bridger, MT. These herbicide combinations are not recommended for herbaceous competitor control when fuzzytongue penstemon growth is desired.
These plant materials are somewhat available from commercial sources.

Alpine penstemon (P. venustus) is a selected release from seed originally collected in the Clearwater River drainage, Idaho. 'The Clearwater Selection' of alpine penstemon was selected by Aberdeen Plant Materials Center and was released in 1994.

Growth of penstemons begins in early spring and flowers appear in May through July depending on species. Weed control and removal of very competitive species may improve chance of establishment. Damage from wildlife and rodents may occur and they may need to be controlled. Disease problems are minimal except under irrigation.

Foundation and registered seed is available for each variety through the appropriate state Crop Improvement Association or commercial sources to grow certified seed. Venustus is a selected release from seed originally collected in the Clearwater River drainage, Idaho. Certified seed is not readily available at this date and Aberdeen PMC maintains breeder seed. Strictus Rocky Mountain penstemon was developed from seed originally collected in Torrance County, New Mexico. Certified seed is available and Los Lunas PMC maintains breeder seed. Palmeri Palmer penstemon was developed from seed originally collected near Cedar City in Iron County, Utah. Certified seed is available and the Forest Service maintains breeder seed. Eatonii is a selected release from seed originally collected near Richfield, Utah. A number of other penstemons are seeded primarily for soil stabilization on depleted, disturbed and erosive areas for erosion control and as ornamentals. Please check the PLANTS database for the names of native penstemons in your state, then check with your area native plant nurseries for their availability.

Fields for seed production can be established by transplanting greenhouse grown containerized stock or from direct seeding. Direct seeding should take place in the fall to allow for natural stratification of the seed.

There are currently no selected releases of royal penstemon. Greenhouse materials can be established by seeding into cones or flats in winter for natural stratification or by stratifying the seed for 8 to 12 weeks in cold/moist conditions.

When planted in a native reclamation mix, royal penstemon will be a minor component of the establishing plant community; therefore management should be based on other key species in the mixture. Grazing on seeded lands should be deferred for at least two growing seasons to allow for establishment.
Wildland harvested seed is available through commercial sources.

Penstemons are considered desirable forages for deer, antelope, either as herbage or seed.
'The Clearwater Selection' of alpine penstemon was selected by Aberdeen Plant Materials Center and was released in 1994.

Growth of penstemons begins in early spring and flowers appear in May through July depending on species. Weed control and removal of very competitive species may improve chance of establishment. Damage from wildlife and rodents may occur and they may need to be controlled. Disease problems are minimal except under irrigation.

Foundation and registered seed is available for each variety through the appropriate state Crop Improvement Association or commercial sources to grow certified seed. Alpine penstemon (Penstemon venustus) is a selected release from seed originally collected in the Clearwater River drainage, Idaho. Certified seed is not readily available at this date and Aberdeen PMC maintains breeder seed. Other penstemons available commercially include the following: 'Bandera' (Penstemon strictus) Rocky Mountain penstemon was developed from seed originally collected in Torrance County, New Mexico. 'Cedar' (Penstemon palmeri) Palmer penstemon was developed from seed originally collected near Cedar City in Iron County, Utah. Firecracker penstemon (Penstemon eatonii) is a selected release from seed originally collected near Richfield, Utah. A number of other penstemons are seeded primarily for soil stabilization on depleted, disturbed, and erosive areas for erosion control and as ornamentals. Please check the PLANTS database for the names of native penstemons in your state, then check with your area native plant nurseries for their availability.

Rocky Mountain beeplant is recommended for use at sites receiving >300 mm mean annual precipitation in the intermountain West (Ogle et al., 2019). This species can be broadcast, or drill seeded into a firm, weed-free seed bed to depth of 0 to 3 mm (0 to 1/8 in). The full stand seeding rate is 17 lb/ac.

Rocky Mountain beeplant is broadly available on the commercial market, but no improved or released material is available. Seed should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use. It is easy to establish by direct seeding, and potted plants grow and mature quickly and often go to flower and fruit in the greenhouse before outplanting.

Seeds are planted with a drill at a depth of a ¼ inch in late fall or early winter in order to obtain the cold stratification period required to overcome seed dormancy.

Field Control competing vegetation by spraying and/or cultivating the planting site well in advance of seeding. Control of existing broadleaved weeds after stand emergence is difficult and consists primarily of spot spraying, mechanical cultivation, and hand-pulling. Seeds should be planted ¼-inch deep into a firm seedbed with a row spacing of 30.5–35.6 cm. Silverleaf phacelia seed production has been successful when planted at the rate of 2.8 PLS lb./acre or approximately 24 PLS seeds per linear foot on a 76.2 cm row spacing. Increasing the seeding rate to 40 PLS seeds per linear foot or 4.5 PLS lb./acre increases stand density.

Silverleaf phacelia is rarely planted as a monoculture, and should be used as one component of a multi-species restoration mixture. Once established, silverleaf phacelia is relatively low maintenance. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for establishment. The species is not aggressive and unlikely to dominate and become weedy, especially in conservation plantings.

In its native range Phacelia tanacetifolia is found in communities of Chaparral, Creosote Bush Scrub, Coastal Sage Scrub, Pinyon-Juniper Woodland, Southern Oak Woodland and Central Oak Woodland (Walden et al., 2016). The genus Phacelia consists of approximately 200 species in North and South America. The center of diversity is in California where 93 taxa occur, of which 39 are endemic (Gilbert et al., 2005).

Lacy phacelia is a native annual forb in the Hydrophyllaceae family. The stems are erect or semi-erect and succulent, glandular with short stiff hairs. The height varies from 0.3–0.9 m. Leaves have a petiole and blade, are oblong to ovate and generally compound subdivided into smaller leaflets and toothed lobes, length is variable up to 20.3 cm in length.

In its native range Phacelia tanacetifolia is found in communities of Chaparral, Creosote Bush Scrub, Coastal Sage Scrub, Pinyon-Juniper Woodland, Southern Oak Woodland and Central Oak Woodland (Walden et al., 2016). The genus Phacelia consists of approximately 200 species in North and South America. The center of diversity is in California where 93 taxa occur, of which 39 are endemic (Gilbert et al., 2005). In California, lacy phacelia is widely distributed and found in the Northern and Southern Coastal Ranges, the Sierra Foothills and High Sierra, the Sacramento and San Joaquin Valleys, the mountain ranges of southern California and into the Mojave Desert (Calflora, 1997). Native populations are also found in found in Southern Nevada and Arizona (Walden et al., 2016).

Lacy phacelia seeds germinate in 15 to 30 days without treatment. Germination is inhibited by light and high and low temperatures, seeds grow when soil temperatures are between 40 and 68o F (Tiraki and Keles. 2012). Late spring, summer and fall plantings may all be successful depending upon the location.
Cultivars have been developed for use in Europe, but these are not currently available in the US. Cultivars should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

The management of lacy phacelia will depend upon the desired use for the plantings. For pollinator plantings termination should occur post bloom. If a self-regenerating stand is the goal, the plants should be left to senesce and die for maximum seed production. For forage and hay production, plants should be cut prior to bloom to obtain maximum biomass and nutritional value.

Reed canarygrass seed is quite small, very dense, and resembles timothy seed because both are small, heavy, and naked. Fully sodded stands produce only 30-50 pounds seed/acre. Old stands tend to have a higher proportion of vegetative culms than reproductive culms.

Seeds require several days at cool temperatures for a high percentage of the seeds to germinate. The rate and amount of germination is typical for most cool season pasture grasses, but pales in comparison to many annual weeds. For comparison, yellow starthistle and cheatgrass can achieve 75% germination within 2 days. Seedling development of reed canarygrass is similar to other cool season pasture grasses.
Rhizomes grow outwardly from a mother plant until the terminal bud develops a shoot. This is unlike quackgrass, which develops shoots all along the rhizome axis.
Rhizomes account for much of the localized spread of reed canarygrass.
These plant materials are readily available from commercial sources.

A perennial, tufted grass arising from fibrous roots, possessing stems that are usually enlarged and more or less bulbous at the base (with one or occasionally two basal internodes swelling into a haplacorm), growing up to 100 cm tall (50 to 100 cm, or 50.8–101.6 cm). Sheaths are smooth, split, and hairless with overlapping margins; blades are flat, 4-8 mm wide (about 0.6 cm or 6 mm wide), narrowing gently toward the tip, with rough margins and lengths varying from a few inches to more than a foot. Inhabiting wet to mesic bogs, fens, swamps, and lower slopes in the montane zone; common in the interior of central and northern British Columbia; ranging north to Alaska, east to Newfoundland, and south to Minnesota and Pennsylvania. Black spruce occurs across the northern range of North America, from Alaska, Yukon, and British Columbia eastward to Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, New Brunswick, and Québec.

Small tree up to 20 (-25) m tall, often shrub-like near tree-line, with short, drooping branches that frequently layer, and a narrowly conic, spire-like, or irregularly subcylindric crown. Bark is gray to blackish, thin, and scaly; young twigs are densely hairy and glandular, slender, and yellow-brown. Evergreen needles are short, 0.6-1.5 (-2) cm long, 4-angled, stiff and blunt-tipped, waxy and pale blue-green with a whitish bloom, standing out in all directions or mostly pointing upwards. Seed cones 1.5-2.5(-3.5) cm long, fusiform, purple-brown at maturity; cone scales fan-shaped, broadest near apex, 8-12 mm long, rigid, margin at apex irregularly toothed.

Persistent fruit, hips, cones, or dried seedheads add late-season visual interest and winter wildlife forage.

An early successional keystone/foundation tree species (Pinaceae) occurring as upright, multi-stemmed clusters, krummholz, or as a medium to tall tree with a rounded or irregularly spreading canopy, reaching 4.5–5.5 m height and 11.3–19.2 cm dbh in open stands. Mature trees reach 5 to 20 m tall (also noted as 5-10 m tall, or a shrubby sprawling timberline tree, but straight and up to 20 m). Very long-lived (1000+ years, with specimens over 1,200 years old). In open areas trees tend to be multi-stemmed and spreading, single-stemmed and upright in dense growth, and krummholz above timberline.

Found on mesic to dry slopes in subalpine to alpine zones; frequent in southern British Columbia in and east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, rare northward to central and northeastern British Columbia; extending east to southwestern Alberta and south to California, Nevada, and Wyoming. Inhabiting high-elevation, cold, windy, snowy subalpine areas including the southern Coast Mountains of British Columbia (Blowdown Pass, Downton Creek, Texas Creek, Seton Ridge), Coast Ranges, Cascades, Sierra Nevada, and Rockies. Whitebark pine is adapted to steep slopes and windy exposures in subalpine and alpine habitats, frequently acting as an early to mid-seral species growing alongside other cold- and wind-tolerant alpine trees such as lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta), Engelmann spruce (Picea engelmannii), and subalpine fir (Abies lasiocarpa). Whitebark pine trees inhabit cold, windswept ridges and peaks in western North America with many geographically isolated stands, occurring from the coastal mountain ranges of British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon south to the Sierra Range of California and east to the Rocky Mountains of Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, and Alberta, with scattered populations in the Great Basin.

Widespread throughout Northwestern Ontario, jack pine typically occurs on sandy soils of the Spodosol and Entisol soil orders. It also grows on loamy soils, thin soils over granites and metamorphosed rocks of the Canadian Shield, over limestone, on peat, and on soils over permafrost.

Jack pine is a small to medium-sized, native, evergreen tree averaging 17-20 m high with a straight to crooked trunk. The crown is small, irregularly rounded or spreading and flattened irregular, with descending to spreading-ascending branches that are poorly self-pruning. Twigs are slender, orange-red to red-brown, aging gray-brown, and rough; branchlets are yellow to greenish-brown when young, turning gray-brown with age, featuring very resinous buds. Bark is initially dark and scaly, later developing scaly ridges.

With medium thick bark, mature individuals have only moderate fire tolerance, but populations survive because of delayed seed release from serotinous cones, early reproductive maturity, fast growth in full sun, and preference for mineral soil seedbeds. Jack pine invades areas where mineral soil has been exposed by major disturbance such as fire. Usually grows in dry, acidic sandy soils with a lower pH limit of 4.0, but also loamy soil, thin soil over bedrock, peat, and soil over permafrost. Does not usually grow in moderately alkaline soil, but can grow in calcareous soils up to pH 8.2 if normal mycorrhizal fungi are present.

Ponderosa pine is propagated by seed. Cones are ready for collection in October and November when they turn reddish brown. Mature seed is firm and brown in color.
The seed is sown for an initial density of 237 seedlings/m2 (22 seedlings/ft2).

Ponderosa pine can be over-irrigated in poorly drained soils, or drowned out on high water table sites. It responds well to thinning, which should be done as stands become older to develop larger crowns, resulting in heavier seed crops for wildlife. More forage for deer and elk become available from associated plants by opening the canopy. The use of repellents or other control measures may be necessary to prevent overuse of the trees by rodents.

Pisum sativum is currently grown in temperate regions, at high elevations, or during cool seasons in warm regions throughout the world (Elzebroek and Wind, 2008). Major pea-producing countries include China, India, Canada, Russia, France, and the United States, with primary domestic production centered in Washington, Montana, and North Dakota.

A cool-season annual vine belonging to the legume family (Fabaceae), smooth in texture with a bluish-green waxy appearance, and vines reaching up to 2.7 m long, though modern cultivars average about 0.6 m long. Stems are hollow, requiring support for taller cultivars. Leaves are alternate, pinnately compound, and consist of two large leaflike stipules, one to several pairs of oval leaflets, and terminal tendrils (McGee, 2012). Inflorescences occur in leaf axils as racemes of one to four flowers, which possess five green fused sepals and five white, purple, or pink petals differentiated into a top 'standard' petal, two fused middle 'keel' petals, and two base-tapering 'wings'.

Forage crop: Peas are grown alone or with cereals for silage and green fodder (Elzebroek and Wind, 2008). Peas can also be grazed while in the field.
Depending on the cultivar, there can be 1,000 to 3,000 pea seeds per pound.

Peas are established by seed in the spring or fall. Seed should be inoculated with Rhizobium leguminosarum prior to planting in fields where peas have not been previously grown to ensure root nodule formation and the fixation of atmospheric nitrogen. Seeding rates vary with cultivar, soil type, seed size, climate, disease pressure and seeding method.

Peas grown as commercial crop: Peas grow well on soils with moderate fertility levels, but on soils with low fertility, application of 45 lb/ac nitrogen and 90 lb/ac phosphorus and potassium can be advantageous. Nutrients applied in excess or at the wrong time may promote vegetative growth and be detrimental to pod development. Fresh and dry peas are mechanically harvested by cutting the plants and threshing them to remove the seeds from the pods and vines.

Breeders have selected for height, vegetative growth form, season of maturity, disease resistance, pod shape and length, seed color, tenderness, sweetness, seed shape, number of seeds per pod, and pod production per node (Hartmann et al., 1988).

Common foliar pea diseases (and their causal organism) include bacterial blight (Pseudomonas syringae pv. Pisi), ascochyta blight (Ascochyta pisi, Mycosphaerella pinodes and Phoma medicaginis var. pinodella), powdery mildew (Eryisphe pisi), downy mildew (Peronospora viciae f. sp. pisi), septoria blight (Septoria pisi), and white mold (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum). Rhizoctonia (Rhizoctonia solani) and Pythium (Pythium spp.) are common seed rot and seedling damping-off diseases. Seeds germinate at temperatures between 20 and 30°C.

Seed should be planted into a clean, firm seedbed to a depth of ¼ inch. Drilling is preferred to ensure uniform seeding depth but broadcast seeding followed by harrowing and packing can be utilized where soil moisture is not lacking. Canada bluegrass plugs are easy to propagate in a greenhouse. Seed is surface-grown into containers containing standard potting mix.

Canada bluegrass greens up early in the spring and if fall rains are adequate will make fall growth. Growth during summer is dependent on precipitation or irrigation. It stays green into late fall and early winter and is tolerant of close grazing and heavy trampling. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment.

Breeder seed is maintained by Ontario Agricultural College. Certified seed is apparently not available (USDA, 1994). It was selected for seedling vigor, rate of spread, forage production, seed production, and uniform ripening. It was tested with comparison to ‘Reubens’ and found to have superior seedling vigor, rate of spread, and seed production. Bridger Plant Materials Center maintains Generation 1 (G1) seed which is made available to seed growers for production of Certified G2 and G3 seed (Majerus and Holzworth, 2003). Breeder Seed is maintained by the Jacklin Seed Company and Certified seed is available (USDA, 1994). ‘Talon’ was developed by Cascade International Seed Company at its breeding facility located in Aumsville, Oregon. The first Breeder seed was produced in 1995. Breeder and Certified Seed are maintained by L&H Seeds, Connell, Washington (AOSCA, 2010).

Found in dry grasslands and ridges within steppe and lower montane zones, this species includes ssp. fendleriana (rare in SC BC, and extending east to MB and south to TX, NM, AZ, and CA) and ssp. longiligula (infrequent in BC, and ranging south to SD, TX, NM, AZ, and CA). A perennial tufted grass from fibrous roots and rhizomes, with rhizomes that are often short and inconspicuous, and stems that are erect or decumbent, measuring 15-70 cm tall/long. The sheath margins are open about 2/3 of their length, and sterile shoots mainly emerge inside sheaths featuring well-developed two-keeled buds protecting the scales. Blades measure (0.5) 1-2 (4) mm wide, are in-rolled, thick, with a smooth outer surface; upper blades are often absent or very reduced, with the uppermost one often vestigial, rigid, and always less than 1/5 the sheath length, while the inner surface of blades of sterile shoots is usually distinctly rough or minutely soft-hairy. The ligules measure 0.2-1.8 mm long with smooth or rough backs.

Native species restoration: Muttongrass has been used sparingly to improve diversity in sagebrush and piñon-juniper communities. It can be used to restore areas where juniper encroachment has depleted the herbaceous understory following juniper removal. The species is drought tolerant and has potential for use in restoration and native diversification projects throughout the West.

Muttongrass is a good source of forage and has been rated as excellent forage for cattle and horses, and good for sheep, elk and deer (USDA 1937). During the winter, seedheads are eaten by pronghorn antelope.
Plants require 30 lb/ac available nitrogen during the establishment year and 45 lb/ac available nitrogen on established fields. Apply phosphorus according to soil test recommendations.

Plant in late fall (dormant) with a pure seeding rate of 2 lb PLS/acre. If seeding as part of a mix, adjust seeding rate to the desired percentage of the mixture. Seed should be planted with a drill ¼ inch deep, into a firm, weed-free seedbed or seed can be broadcast followed with a cultipacker or harrow operation to provide a shallow covering of soil. Plant in early spring into a firm, weed-free seedbed at 24 to 36 spacing.

Weed control in seed production fields can be achieved by between-row cultivation but may require some hand weeding during the first growing season because seedlings are very small. After plants reach the 3 to 5 leaf stage, broadleaf herbicides can be applied at low rates.
There are no releases currently available. Wildland collected seed can be obtained through commercial vendors.

A perennial, densely to loosely tufted grass originating from fibrous roots and rhizomes or occasionally isolated shoots, characterized by erect or decumbent stems 30-70 (100) cm tall/long with lowermost nodes usually not exserted. Sheaths are hairless or infrequently sparsely to moderately hairy, featuring margins open 1/2-3/4 their length; sterile shoots break through sheath bases and emerge inside sheaths. Basal bladeless leaves are present; blades are 0.4-4.5 mm wide, flat or folded, infrequently in-rolled, lax to moderately firm, and the upper surface sometimes bears sparse soft straight hairs. Ligules are 1-2 (3) mm long, having blunt to rounded tips, margins slightly rough or smooth towards the tips, and smooth or slightly rough backs.

A perennial, densely to loosely tufted grass originating from fibrous roots and rhizomes or occasionally isolated shoots, characterized by erect or decumbent stems 30-70 (100) cm tall/long with lowermost nodes usually not exserted. Fast-growing deciduous tree reaching up to 50 m in height, characterized by sweet-smelling resinous buds and white seed fluff, possessing a soft, heavy outer bark without slivers; dioecious, not colonial; first-year branches brown, turning grey subsequently; twigs smooth or sparsely hairy; leaves alternate, deciduous, simple, narrowly to broadly egg-shaped or lanceolate, 5-20 cm long, 3-12 cm wide, with tapered to heart-shaped or squared-off, smooth bases, and finely toothed, hairy margins bearing teeth often tipped with a callous gland, lower surface whitish or pale green and brownish; leaf stalks 2-10 cm long, frequently bearing a pair of glands near the blade; buds finely hairy with fringed scales. Ssp. balsamifera - common in N and E BC; ssp. trichocarpa - common throughout BC except rare on Queen Charlotte Islands; ssp. balsamifera - N to YT, AK and NT, E to NF and S to NY, VA, IL, IA, CO, ID and OR; ssp. trichocarpa - N to S AK and YT, E to SW AB and S to ND, WY, UT, NV and CA. The range of black cottonwood extends from Alaska, including various islands, through coastal regions of western Canada (Yukon, British Columbia, and Alberta) into the northwestern US (Washington, Oregon, Montana, Idaho, and Nevada; rare in North Dakota, Wyoming, Utah, and California) and as far south as Baja California Norte.

Fast-growing deciduous tree reaching up to 50 m in height, characterized by sweet-smelling resinous buds and white seed fluff, possessing a soft, heavy outer bark without slivers; dioecious, not colonial; first-year branches brown, turning grey subsequently; twigs smooth or sparsely hairy; leaves alternate, deciduous, simple, narrowly to broadly egg-shaped or lanceolate, 5-20 cm long, 3-12 cm wide, with tapered to heart-shaped or squared-off, smooth bases, and finely toothed, hairy margins bearing teeth often tipped with a callous gland, lower surface whitish or pale green and brownish; leaf stalks 2-10 cm long, frequently bearing a pair of glands near the blade; buds finely hairy with fringed scales. Inhabiting moist uplands and floodplains in the montane zone, this species comprises two subspecies: ssp. balsamifera, which is common in northern and eastern British Columbia and ranges north to the Yukon Territory, Alaska, and the Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to New York, Virginia, Illinois, Iowa, Colorado, Idaho, and Oregon; and ssp. trichocarpa, which is common throughout British Columbia except for being rare on the Queen Charlotte Islands, and ranges north to southern Alaska and the Yukon Territory, east to southwestern Alberta, and south to North Dakota, Wyoming, Utah, Nevada, and California.

Quaking aspen is the most widely distributed tree species in North America. It grows from Alaska across the Northwest Territories to Quebec and Newfoundland, south to West Virginia and Virginia, and in all of the western North America US states (except Oklahoma and Kansas) -- in all Canadian provinces and all but 13 US states (absent from the Southeast).

Dioecious tree up to 25 m tall, colonial; branches and smooth twigs greenish-white; leaves alternate, deciduous, simple, broadly egg-shaped, kidney-shaped, or circular, 2.5-9 cm long, 2.5-8 cm wide, bases rounded to slightly heart-shaped, smooth, finely toothed and fringed with long white hairs, upper surface green, lower surface paler; leaf stalks 2-7.5 cm long; buds smooth. Within the Willow Family (Salicaceae), this native tree grows 5-30 m high, typically under 15 m, with a rounded crown; lateral roots may extend over 30 meters and vertical sinker roots from the laterals may extend downward for nearly 3 m; bark typically smooth, greenish-white to gray-white, often thin and peeling, becoming thicker and furrowed with age, especially toward the base. Leaves simple, deciduous, broadly ovate to nearly round, 4–6 cm long, with small, rounded teeth on the margins, on a slender, flattened petiole, dark green and shiny above, pale green below, turning bright yellow, yellow-orange, gold, or reddish after the first frosts. The male (staminate) and female (pistillate) flowers are on separate trees (the species dioecious – or ‘polygamodioecious,’ because bisexual flowers may be produced at low frequencies on staminate and pistillate trees), each type of flower borne in pendent catkins.

Conservation: Quaking aspen is valued for its white bark and brilliant fall color, especially when clustered. The species been widely used in landscaping but is best in sites away from structures that might be damaged by the aggressive roots. The trees provide good visual screening and noise abatement. Aspen stands are good firebreaks, often dropping crown fires in conifer stands to the ground when they reach aspens and even sometimes extinguishing the fire because of the small amount of flammable accumulation. They allow more ground water recharge than do conifer forests and they also play a significant role in protecting against soil erosion. They have been used in restoration of riparian habitats.

Indigenous peoples traditionally used Populus bark (including aspen) as a food source. They cut the inner bark into strips, dried and ground it into meal to be mixed with other starches for bread or mush. Catkins were eaten raw, and the cambium was eaten raw or in a soup.
Bark decoction used as a traditional tonic and fever reducer. Medicinal tea made from white bark.
Wood used for light firewood. Bark sometimes used as cordage.

The Nlaka'pamux (Thompson) tribe used a poultice of mashed leaves and roots on wounds to draw out the pain.

Inhabiting moist open forests, thickets, rocky slopes, and streambanks across lowland, steppe, and montane zones, bitter cherry is common in southwestern British Columbia, disjunct in west-central British Columbia, and infrequent in southern British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains. Its range extends south to California and east to Montana, Wyoming, and Arizona.

A shrub or small tree 2-15 m tall, sometimes thicket-forming, ranging from smooth to densely hairy throughout, with reddish-brown or grey bark marked by horizontal lenticels. Leaves are alternate, deciduous, elliptic to egg-shaped or lanceolate, 3-8 cm long, finely round-toothed, rounded or blunt to sometimes sharp-pointed at the tip, wedge-shaped to pointed at the base, and densely hairy (at least below) to smooth; leaf stalks are 5-12 mm long, usually lacking small glands at the apex. Bitter cherry (Prunus emarginata) is a native, deciduous shrub, four to twelve feet high, or sometimes a small tree up to thirty feet high (McMinn 1939). Leaves are oblong to oval, fine-toothed, and rounded at the tip, accompanied by fragrant flowers that bloom between April and May in clusters of five to twelve.

A perennial slender shrub or tree reaching 10 m in height with reddish-brown bark, alternate simple elliptical leaves, and white 5-petaled flowers arranged in racemes, producing glossy red-purple, astringent, spherical drupe fruits. Chokecherry occupies a large geographic area, growing abundantly in diverse habitat types and plant associations either in thin stands, dense thickets, or as isolated individuals in open forest clearings. Several cultivars have been released by government agencies and private nurseries for use in landscaping and/or fruit production. Chokecherry can be propagated by seed, rhizome cuttings, suckers, crown division, semi-hardwood cuttings and grafting.

Management of chokecherry will be dependent on whether it is looked upon as a desirable or undesirable plant. On range and pastures it is often considered a potential hazard to livestock. As a consequence either mechanical and/or herbicide treatments combined with good grassland management is needed to prevent animal loss. When it is used in windbreaks, as an ornamental plant or as a wildlife resource it is beneficial.

This species should be seeded with a drill at a depth of 13 mm or less on medium-textured soils, 6 mm on fine-textured soils and 1.9 cm or less on coarse-textured soils. Single-species seeding rate recommended for this grass is 7 pounds Pure Live Seed (PLS) per acre or 21 PLS per square foot. If used as a component of a mix, adjust to percent of mix desired. Row spacing of 61–91.4 cm are recommended under irrigation and 91.4 cm under dryland conditions. Seeding rates of 3 to 4 PLS per acre are recommended.
‘Anatone’ bluebunch wheatgrass (P. spicata ssp. spicata) was selected from seed originating near Anatone, Washington by the Forest Service Shrub Sciences Laboratory.

Bluebunch wheatgrass has good palatability to livestock and wildlife. Established stands do not tolerate heavy continuous grazing. Stands of bluebunch wheatgrass should not be grazed until they are firmly established (usually two growing seasons) and have headed out. Six inches of new growth should be attained in spring before grazing is allowed in established stands.

Deciduous perennial fern arising from a long, creeping, underground rhizome, attaining a height of 30 to 100 cm with thick starchy underground rhizomes; fronds large, triangular, 3-pinnate, 60-170 cm long, 30-100 cm wide, featuring long, thick stipes and numerous ultimate segments that are woolly to smooth on the lower surface. Inhabiting dry to wet forest margins, peat bogs, avalanche tracks, clearings, roadsides, burns, and dry openings in forests and meadows across lowland, steppe, and subalpine zones; common in British Columbia south of 55°N (ssp. lanuginosum) or rare in the southern British Columbia steppe zone (ssp. latiusculum); cosmopolitan, ranging east to west in Alberta, disjunct to Manitoba and Ontario, and south to Georgia, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California, as well as Eurasia, Africa, Australia, and South America.

The most significant use of blue oak was for its highly desirable acorns for food. Acorns were shelled, dried, pounded into flour, sifted for fineness, leached of bitter tannins, and mixed with other acorn types such as black oak (Quercus kelloggii) and prepared as mush, soup, paddies, or bread. Acorns leached and ground into flour for bread and porridge.
The inner bark of the blue oak was boiled and the brew drunk for relief of arthritis by the Kawaiisu.

These shoots were used for basketry and oak sprouts were reputed to have great strength. Types of baskets included Miwok, Pomo, and Maidu cradleboards with frameworks of oak shoots, and Kawaiisu twined work-baskets made with rims of blue oak branches. The Yana used an oak paddle in cooking and the Achomawi made spoons of oak.
Called "acorn" by contemporary gatherers, this food is still relished for ceremonies, festivals, dances, and family gatherings.

Inhabiting moist to mesic meadows, pastures, clearings, fields, and roadsides in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones, this species is frequent in British Columbia south of 56°N and was introduced from Eurasia. Within its native range, tall buttercup is common and abundant in damp meadows and pastures on calcareous or neutral substrata.

Perennial herb arising from a fibrous-rooted stem-base with occasional rhizomes, featuring single, erect or nearly so stems 20-110 cm tall that are stiff-hairy or smooth and hollow. Basal leaves are 5-sided in outline, deeply 3- to 5-parted, 2-5 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, with leaflets 1- to 2-times incised, ultimate segments narrowly elliptic or oblong to lanceolate, margins toothed or shallowly lobed, tips pointed to rounded, and stalks up to 20 cm long. Lower stem leaves are similar to basal leaves but shorter-stalked, transitioning to upper stem leaves and bracts that are reduced to 3 linear, entire or few-toothed segments unstalked on the sheath. Known commonly as tall buttercup, the plant grows from a stout, praemorse rootstock with a short, thick rhizome capable of forming daughter plants in clumps up to three feet (one meter) wide, bearing thick roots below and persistent vascular fibers from decayed petioles above.

Inhabiting moist to mesic meadows, pastures, clearings, fields, and roadsides in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones, this species is frequent in British Columbia south of 56°N and was introduced from Eurasia. Within its native range, tall buttercup is common and abundant in damp meadows and pastures on calcareous or neutral substrata. In the British Isles, it frequently occurs on rock ledges, in gullies, and occasionally on mountain top detritus at elevations of 1219 m. On Dutch river flood plains, the habitat preference of tall buttercup is the intermediate position on the elevational gradient in a zone with approximately 30 days of flooding per year. Survival increases under disturbance that removes neighboring vegetation.

A perennial forb and native member of the Ranunculaceae family, standing 15-50 cm tall (or stems measuring 15-40 (60) cm tall, extending from 15.2 cm to 0.8 m tall) with yellow flowers bearing 5 to 14 petals. Inhabiting moist to mesic meadows, grassy slopes, coastal bluffs, shores, clearings, and open forests from the lowland to subalpine zones; common in coastal and northern BC, infrequent elsewhere; ranging north to AK, YT, and NT, east to AB, and south to CA.

Basal leaves are broadly egg-shaped, semi-circular, or kidney-shaped, with blades 1.5-5.5 cm long and 2-8 cm wide, deeply 3-lobed or -parted, the segments 1- to 2-times incised, and ultimate segments oblong, elliptic, oblanceolate, or lanceolate, toothed, with pointed to rounded tips; leaf stalks are long, measuring 1 to several times the length of the blade. Stem leaves are alternate, more deeply dissected, shorter-stalked, and transition into 3- to 7-parted lower bracts and entire upper bracts. Perennial Forb, 15-50 cm height with yellow flowers.

This native taxon grows as a great choice for wetland prairie restoration throughout its range. Its versatility enables it to thrive in moist upland or lowland sites as a quickly establishing native (Stanley et al., 2010).

While western buttercup prefers vernal pools and wetland sites, it will also tolerate drier upland sites away from the coast that retain seasonally moist soils. It also does quite well in plant and seed production fields, tolerating all soil types and a range of pH values.

R. occidentalis prefers seasonally moist soils in a variety of habitats from coastal prairies and bluffs to disturbed areas, meadows, and forested areas (Turner and Gustafson, 2006). It is generally associated with wetland areas, although it will tolerate seasonal drought and is also found in non-wetland sites. This plant is found from sea level to 2134 m elevations in western North America, from California and western Nevada north through western Canada and into Alaska.

Radish seed production occurs in the northwestern US in Idaho, Washington, and Oregon. Locations where summer temperatures exceed 32°C produce poor seed set. Radish is a cross-pollinated species and seed set benefits from pollination; however, wild radish (Raphanus raphinastrum) can cross-pollinate with oilseed radish if within one mile of the crop.
Prepare a clean, firm, weed-free seedbed prior to planting oilseed radish. Planting times should allow at least 60 days of plant growth before winterkill.

Oilseed radish establishes quickly if soil moisture is adequate (soil moisture varies by soil texture). Plants will scavenge leftover nitrogen in the soil profile and do not typically need additional fertilization. The most important management consideration when planting oilseed radish is ensuring that plants do not to go to seed. As taproots decompose a foul rotten-egg or natural gas-like odor is emitted.

Seeds are available from select commercial sources, but can be more expensive than many other cover crop species. Commercially available ‘common’ varieties are also sold under ‘VNS’ for variety not stated.

Oilseed radish, also called Japanese radish or daikon, has been cultivated as a food staple in Japan for many centuries. Oilseed radishes with different colored taproots are used for specific purposes and food types. Leaves are edible and sometimes eaten as mustard greens.
It is an ingredient in traditional dishes, such as kayu (rice gruel with vegetables or red beans), and snegiri or kiriboshi (radish strips dried for winter storage).
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Avoid planting oilseed radish as a cover crop when the cash crop includes broccoli, cabbage, radish, or other members of the mustard family, it can encourage the establishment of pathogens and pests. Brassicas are susceptible to clubroot disease caused by the soil-borne fungus Plasmodiophora brassicae, cabbage root maggot (Delia radicum), and flea beetle (Phyllotreta spp.). Harlequin bugs (Murgantia histrionica) and flea beetles may attack oilseed radish if it survives the winter.

Inhabiting dry grasslands and shrublands in the steppe zone; locally frequent in southeastern British Columbia; ranging east to Manitoba and south to Minnesota, Missouri, Arkansas, Texas, and Washington. Prairie coneflower ranges from Alberta to Mexico, east to Manitoba, Minnesota, Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Texas, and New England (Steyermark 1963).

Biennial or perennial herb from a taproot and short woody stem-base, featuring several erect stems branched above, 0.3-1.2 m tall, with stiffly coarse-hairy indumentum. Basal leaves are lacking, while stem leaves are alternate, pinnately cut, 10-20 cm long and 2-7 cm wide, with linear or lanceolate, entire segments that are coarsely short stiff-hairy. Belonging to the Composite Family (Asteraceae), the prairie coneflower is a native perennial about a foot and a half tall with rays generally three to five centimeters long, greatly exceeding the solid central disk. The floral disk is somewhat globe-shaped, ovoid, or shortly ellipsoid, twelve to twenty millimeters high (Steyermark 1963).

Smooth sumac (Anacardiaceae) is a deciduous shrub or small tree up to 3 m tall, forming thickets from root suckers with smooth to hairless branches covered in a whitish waxy coating and exuding milky juice when cut. Leaves are alternate, pinnately compound, 3-5 dm long, comprising 7-31 (or 11-31) oblong-lanceolate to elliptic or lanceolate leaflets measuring 5-12 cm (or 7-9 cm) long, turning golden to scarlet in fall; leaflets taper to a point at the tip, are rounded at the base, and feature sharply serrated margins, with a dark green, lustrous upper surface and a whitish waxy-coated lower surface. The branched, racemose inflorescence measures 10-25 cm long, maturing from the bottom up with greenish flowers. Fruits are flattened-globe drupes 3.5-4.5 mm long covered with red, sticky hairs, containing smooth, yellowish seeds 3-3.5 mm long.

Found in mesic disturbed areas and forest edges; a rare horticultural escape in southwestern and south-central British Columbia; native to the eastern United States. Black locust is typically found in mountains and piedmont, usually on disturbed sites, growing best on deep, well-drained limestone-derived soils. Tolerating a pH range of 4.6 to 8.2, it is commonly found on south and west slopes in West Virginia (Kurtz, 2017). Black Locust is hardy to -38°C, and requires 40.6–165.1 cm of annual precipitation, a minimum of 140 frost free days and at least 91.4 cm rooting depth (Kurtz 2017).

Germination can be achieved by scarifying the seed mechanically. The seed should then be soaked in water overnight.
Black locust seeds have high dormancy due to an impermeable seed coat and light requirement for germination.

Black locust is considered a pioneer species colonizing areas before other forms of vegetation. Plant bare rooted seedlings or container material in full sun (preferably more than 6 hours/day) in the early spring (before leaves emerge) or late summer/early autumn. It does not tolerate wet or shady locations.

Cultivars should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use. Black locust should be used only in difficult urban areas (see Uses Ornamental Tree/Urban section).

During the first two years after planting, weed control and deer protection are the main priorities. Site preparation should include weed control (herbicides, mulch and/or mowing), with continued weed control after planting. In areas with high deer pressure tree tubes or other protection may be required. Since it’s a fast-growing tree, black locust doesn’t need active management for more than two years after planting unless straight trunks are desired for fence posts- (see Pests and Potential Problems section for information about controlling locust borers).

A medium to tall shrub standing 0.5-3 m tall, spreading via rhizomes to form thickets, featuring stout to spindly, erect to arching stems with blackish mature bark and a pair of large prickles at each node while typically lacking internodal prickles. The alternate, deciduous, odd-pinnately compound leaves have a glandular-hairy or short-hairy leaf-stalk and axis, bearing 5, 7, or (9) elliptic to egg-shaped leaflets measuring 1-7 cm long with coarsely single- or double-toothed margins and somewhat glandular-short-hairy undersides, accompanied by usually glandular-blunt-toothed stipules. Persistent fruit, hips, cones, or dried seedheads add late-season visual interest and winter wildlife forage.

Inhabiting mesic to moist thickets, forest edges, river terraces, shorelines, streambanks, clearings, and roadsides within lowland and montane zones; common throughout British Columbia south of 55°N except in the Chilcotin area, infrequent northward, and absent in northeastern British Columbia; ranging north to Alaska and south to California, Colorado, and Utah. Rosa nutkana is an understory plant in dry and moist forest communities, including Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa), mountain hemlock (Tsuga mertensiana), Sitka spruce (Picea sitchensis), lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta), redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) and western hardwoods (Reed, 1993). It also grows in sagebrush (Artemisia spp.), and in mountain and plains grasslands (Reed, 1993).

Rosa woodsii is a rhizomatous subshrub or shrub native to the Rosaceae family, growing 0.2-2(-3) m high with shallow, frequently branching fibrous roots and sometimes forming nearly impenetrable thickets. Its stems range from reddish-brown to gray with straight or slightly curved prickles (often featuring weak internodal prickles or bristles on young shoots), and become reddish- to greyish-brown at maturity. The alternate, deciduous, odd-pinnately compound leaves have a short-hairy and sometimes glandular leaf-stalk and axis, bearing 5, 7, or 9 elliptic to egg-shaped (or obovate to ovate) leaflets measuring 1.5-5 cm long (ca. 1.5-3(-4) cm long) with coarsely single-toothed margins (finely toothed toward the tip, the teeth not gland-tipped) that are short- or glandular-hairy to smooth beneath; stipules are entire or glandular-blunt-toothed and short-hairy on the back. Flowers are borne on lateral branches from old wood in 10-20 cm long clusters of few flowers or less commonly solitary, featuring 5 pink, lilac-pink, or lavender petals measuring (10-)15-25 mm long, lanceolate, erect, and usually persistent sepals 1-2 cm long that are tomentose on the margins and inner surface.

Found in moist to wet waste places, roadsides, ditches, and fencerows within the lowland zone; common in southwestern British Columbia; introduced from Eurasia. Vacant lots, railroad rights-of-way, degraded riparian areas, fence lines, and electricity power transmission lines serve as common habitats, where it flourishes despite degraded soils (Brinkman 1974).

Medium to tall, coarse, thicket-forming shrub, 2-5 m or more long; stems 5-15 mm in diameter, erect to ascending, then high-arching, sprawling and trailing along the ground, some rooting at the ends, five-angled, with stout, flattened, hooked prickles. Leaves alternate, evergreen, palmately compound, 5-20 cm long; leaflets 5 on first-year canes, mostly 3 on flowering canes, egg-shaped, 5-12 cm long, double-saw-toothed and abruptly sharp-pointed at the tip, green and smooth above, greyish-woolly beneath, with prickly leaf-stalks and midveins beneath; stipules linear. This arching woody shrub features persistent leaves, thorny biennial canes up to 10 meters long that may root upon touching the ground, and can form impenetrable thickets up to 2 meters tall or taller when supported. Flowers possess 5 petals, vary from white to light-pink in color, occur in loose clusters, and produce black aggregate fruits composed of multiple drupelets.

Sagittaria is an aquatic plant with tuberous roots that can be eaten like potatoes. The tubers of Sagittaria species were eaten by many different Indigenous groups in Canada, as well as many groups of Washington and Oregon. The tubers were widely traded from harvesting centers to neighboring areas.

Medicinally, the Maidu of California used an infusion of arrowhead roots to clean and treat wounds. The Navaho use these plants for headaches. The Ojibwa and the Chippewa used Sagittaria species as a remedy for indigestion. The Iroquois used wapato for rheumatism, a dermatological aid, a laxative, and as a ceremonial blessing when they began planting corn.

Indian women collected wapato in shallow water from a canoe, or waded into ponds or marshes in the late summer and loosened the roots with their toes. The roots would rise to the top of the water where they were gathered and tossed into floating baskets.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

A decoction of the branches was taken by women for several months after childbirth to increase the blood flow. A poultice of bark and sap was applied as a wad to bleeding wounds. A poultice of the damp inner bark was applied to the skin over a broken bone.

The diamond shaped wood is carved into canes, lampposts, furniture, and candleholders. The wood has also been used to make furniture, baskets, baseball bats, charcoal, and gunpowder. Snowshoe hares, deer, elk, and moose browse Bebb willow. Bark and stems used in basketry and as cordage. The depressions on these willows are caused by one or more fungi, which attack willows at the junction of a branch with the main trunk. The term “diamond willow” applies to species when the stems are carved resulting in a pattern of diamond-shaped cavities with a sharp contrast between the white or cream sapwood and the reddish-brown heartwood.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Drummond willow provides important streambank protection by effectively stabilizing soils. Heavy grazing in moist Drummond willow communities can lead to soil compaction, streambank sloughing and damage to willow plants. Dioecious shrubs or trees, 0.5-6 m tall, forming colonies by root shoots; branches erect, flexible at base; twigs yellow- to red-brown, smooth or sparsely to densely hairy. Leaves alternate, simple, linear to strap-shaped, 3-16 cm long, 0.2-1 cm wide; lower surface glaucous or not, silky or long-soft hairy to nearly smooth, hairs white, upper surface shiny, silky or long soft-hairy to nearly smooth, margins entire or remotely and minutely spiny-toothed, bases wedge-shaped, tips pointed to tapered; leaf stalks without glandular dots at apex; stipules leaflike, rudimentary, or absent. Representing the willow family (Salicaceae), Salix exigua is the most distinctive species with its long, thin leaves featuring very short petioles, mature blades 50-124 mm long, linear shape, acuminate tips, and serrate or entire edges. Coyote willow grows as a shrub under 7 m tall, spreading clonally by root-sprouting, with catkin inflorescences appearing with or after leaves in spring, measuring 22-70 mm long on leafy shoots 5-110 mm long, and bearing tawny yellow flower bracts.

Traditional Resource Management: Willow is nature’s healer. Poles of willow readily sprout, and help to stabilize stream banks and provide habitat. Sweat lodges constructed of willow have been known to sprout and grow, even though the willows were subjected to very high heat. Willows were traditionally tended by pruning, to produce long straight stems.

Containerized coyote willow saplings are available from most nurseries in the areas where adapted. Coyote willow poles, suitable for transplanting, are available from the NRCS Plant Materials Center at Los Lunas, New Mexico and Tucson, Arizona. The Plant Materials Centers vegetatively propagate these poles from parent stock.

Tea made from willow leaves will cure laryngitis. Young willow shoots can be stripped of their bark and eaten. The inner bark can be eaten raw, prepared like spaghetti, or made into a flour.

Aspirin is the pharmaceutical equivalent of willow bark tea, which is an effective remedy for headache, fever or sore throat. More than 2,400 years ago, the Greeks learned to use extracts of several native willow species to treat pain, gout, and other illnesses. When used as an analgesic, willow treats urethra and bladder irritation, infected wounds, and eczema.

Cordage (bark processed for rope-making). Willow branches are used as the warp for twined baskets and the foundation in coiled baskets. Willows are used to weave water jugs, cradles for newborn infants, hats, cooking vessels, serving bowls, trays, seed beaters, and storage baskets.

Other implements made from willow include fire sticks twirled as a spindle to generate enough heat to ignite a flame and what appear to be prayer sticks recovered from various archaeological sites. Willow is still used for making prayer sticks by the Zunis and doubtless by some of the Rio Grande pueblo.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Aspirin is the pharmaceutical equivalent of willow bark tea, which is an effective remedy for headache, fever or sore throat. More than 2,400 years ago, the Greeks learned to use extracts of several native willow species to treat pain, gout, and other illnesses. When used as an analgesic, willow treats urethra and bladder irritation, infected wounds, and eczema.

Cordage (bark processed for rope-making). Willow branches are used as the warp for twined baskets and the foundation in coiled baskets. Willows are used to weave water jugs, cradles for newborn infants, hats, cooking vessels, serving bowls, trays, seed beaters, and storage baskets.

Other implements made from willow include fire sticks twirled as a spindle to generate enough heat to ignite a flame and what appear to be prayer sticks recovered from various archaeological sites. Willow is still used for making prayer sticks by the Zunis and doubtless by some of the Rio Grande pueblo.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Tea made from willow leaves will cure laryngitis. Young willow shoots can be stripped of their bark and eaten. The inner bark can be eaten raw, prepared like spaghetti, or made into a flour.

Aspirin is the pharmaceutical equivalent of willow bark tea, which is an effective remedy for headache, fever or sore throat. More than 2,400 years ago, the Greeks learned to use extracts of several native willow species to treat pain, gout, and other illnesses. When used as an analgesic, willow treats urethra and bladder irritation, infected wounds, and eczema.

Stems used for basketry and cordage. Willow branches are used as the warp for twined baskets and the foundation in coiled baskets. Willows are used to weave water jugs, cradles for newborn infants, hats, cooking vessels, serving bowls, trays, seed beaters, and storage baskets.

Other implements made from willow include fire sticks twirled as a spindle to generate enough heat to ignite a flame and what appear to be prayer sticks recovered from various archaeological sites. Willow is still used for making prayer sticks by the Zunis and doubtless by some of the Rio Grande pueblo.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Mackenzie willow provides important streambank protection by effectively stabilizing soils. Heavy grazing in moist Mackenzie willow communities can lead to soil compaction, streambank sloughing, and damage to willow plants. Grazing is particularly detrimental to the establishment of willows. Plants recover rapidly when browsing is excluded.

Salvia dorrii has about 530,000 seeds per kilogram (240,000 seeds per pound) (Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, Seed Information Database 2008). Purple sage can be established by seed or transplanted seedlings.

Seeds should be planted in a late fall dormant planting (November or December) with a drill into a weed - free seedbed at a rate of 5.6 kilograms PLS (pure live seed) per hectare (5 pounds PLS per acre) and at a depth of 1.3 – 0.6 cm.

Salvia dorrii produces new branches each season throughout the spring, summer and early fall. Most of the new growth dies back in the winter, though some persists and becomes woody. For this reason pruning of Salvia dorrii is not necessary in order to increase the number of flowering branches. Pruning the lateral branches, however, may encourage a more upright form to facilitate machine harvesting.
However seedlings are commercially available from several nurseries in western states. Seed availability is extremely limited.

This plant was used for multiple medicinal and cultural purposes by tribes throughout its range. People of the Kawasiiu, Paiute, Shoshoni, Washoe and Syilx (Okanagan) / Colville tribes made infusions and decoctions of the leaves and stems of purple sage for a cold remedy. They also made poultices of the leaves to apply to the chest, smoked dried leaves and made steam baths with the leaves to ease congestion.

The Pullman Plant Materials Center has found a large portion (>50%) of harvested seed damaged by insect predation. Sassafras albidum; Sassafras; Common Sassafras; Ague Tree
A pioneer tree of disturbed sites within its native range, adapted to a variety of low-pH soils. It occurs in woodlands, fields, and along roadsides, and is native to the eastern United States.

Members of the Laurel Family (Lauraceae), Sassafras are native, perennial, deciduous shrubs or trees reaching 9 to 18 m tall with a spread of 6 to 8 m. Young trees exhibit greenish bark, while older trees develop reddish brown bark that is rough, thick, and deeply ridged. Leaves are alternate and variable in shape, bearing either no lobes or one to three lobes at the apex, with two-lobed leaves being mitten-shaped; they are light, bright green in summer, transitioning to bright yellow-orange and red-orange in autumn. The trees are dioecious with fragrant flowers; female flowers measure 1 cm across, are borne in small terminal clusters before the leaves emerge, lack petals, and possess six greenish-yellow sepals measuring 3 to 5 mm long, whereas male flowers are inconspicuous.

The roots, bark, leaves, new shoots, and pith from the branches of sassafras were used extensively for a wide variety of purposes by many Native American tribes including the Cherokee, Chippewa, Choctaw, Creek, Delaware, Oklahoma, Houma, Iroquois, Koasati, Mohegan, Nanticoke, and Rappahannock. Root bark and leaves used by Anishinaabe, Iroquois, and others for a beverage tea, to season cooking meat/foods, and later adopted by settlers to flavor root beer. The leaves were used fresh as a spice, much like bay leaves, for flavoring in meat soups.

The medicinal uses of sassafras by Native Americans were many. Infusions made from the bark of the roots were taken internally as a preventive to ward off fever, as well as a remedy to treat diarrhea, rheumatism, measles, and scarlet fever. Root infusions were also used to treat fevers that occurred in women after giving birth and as a wash for eyesores. An infusion of the roots was used as a blood purifier, and as a dietary aid to treat “overfattness.” Infusions of the plant were used as a cough medicine, mouthwash, and gargle for colds. An infusion of the plant was mixed with whiskey and used for rheumatism, tapeworms, and as a blood remedy to purify the blood.
It is used for purposes requiring lightwood, such as boat construction, because it is soft but durable.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

The trees can develop a variety of insect and disease problems that are generally not serious. Insects will eat the foliage, but rarely eat the entire leaves. American three-square is a medium to tall, erect native perennial herb belonging to the Sedge Family (Cyperaceae), rising from long, stout rhizomes to heights of 40-250 cm (fifteen to one hundred centimeters, or up to seven feet). Stems grow singly or in small groups, are sharply triangular in cross-section with concave sides, and remain stiff and emergent along most of their length when growing in water. Leaves are few, basal, measuring less than 1/2 the stem length, with sheath orifices that often split; blades number 1 to 3, are firm, long, strongly folded, V-shaped near the base and triangular to asymmetrically flattened on the sides near the tips, smooth or with rough angles near the tips, measuring 2-8 mm wide (sometimes flat and 2-4 mm wide) and 25-200 cm long. Fruits are dark-brown, seedlike, pointy-tipped achenes measuring two to three millimeters long.

Annual grass from fibrous roots; stems hollow, mostly 60-150 cm tall. Cereal rye is an upright, cool season, annual grass. It can grow 0.9–1.8 m tall, has flat leaf blades, and is topped with awned flower spikes called heads.
Sheaths open; blades flat, (3) 4-10 mm wide; ear-shaped lobes at the leaf-bases fairly prominent; ligules short membranous.

Inflorescence a terminal spike, 8-15 cm long, with spikelets 1 per node; spikelets unstalked, 2-flowered, the florets side by side, the rachilla prolonged between the two; glumes stiff, slender, awl-like, 1-nerved, shorter than the lemmas; lemmas curved, 5-nerved, strongly fringed with fine hairs on the keels and exposed margins, awns mostly 4-7 cm long.
Annual completing its full lifecycle from germination to seed within one growing season.
Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.

Cereal rye can be cut for hay when it is in the early heading stage of development (Oelke et al., 1990). It provides the best hay forage when it is grown with other species such as red or crimson clover, or annual ryegrass (Oelke et al., 1990).

For seed production, the seedbed should be smooth, firm, and weed free. Seeding rate will vary depending on climatic conditions and variety of rye that is being used. Seeds should be planted 2.5–3.8 cm deep (Government of Alberta, 2011).
Establishment methods and timing of planting depends on the management objective of the producer. Cereal rye is planted from late summer to midwinter depending on the geographic region.

Management of cereal rye can vary widely. It can be managed to produce a grain crop to mill for flour, where it can be harvested and threshed using a combine. In a cover crop or green manure system, a multitude of management options are available. It can be killed at different times for weed suppression, to prevent nitrogen uptake, or incorporated into soil for organic matter build up.

Flour made from cereal rye is gluten free, which makes it an ideal flour for people with celiac disease.

Cereal rye is susceptible to some diseases, although it is generally more resistant than other cereal species (Oelke et al., 1990). Ergot, stem or stalk smut, anthracnose, and various rusts of the leaves or stem are the most likely disease problems that will be encountered. In the spring, armyworm moths are attracted to cereal rye and may lay eggs on it.

A mat-forming perennial herb arising from a slender rhizome, developing several decumbent to ascending, glabrous stems branched above that measure 5-25 cm tall/long. The stem leaves are alternate, linear to linear-lanceolate, succulent, rounded in cross section, not strongly keeled, and strongly pointed, with surfaces varying from finely pimply to smooth. The upper leaves are deciduous by flowering time, while the lower leaves are crowded to form basal rosettes that are often reddish-green, sometimes covered with a white waxy powder, and turn golden in autumn.

Lambstongue ragwort is a perennial forb in the sunflower family (Asteraceae) featuring a short semi-rhizomatous caudex that gives rise to 1 or more upright stems growing 10 to 60 cm tall.

Wildland collections can be made by hand stripping or shaking ripe seed into collection bags. Seed can be collected shortly before maturity by harvesting the entire inflorescence and allowing the seed to continue ripening while drying. Mature seed can be removed from the floral heads using a laboratory brush machine with a number 7 mantle at a speed of 2.

The full stand seeding rate, based on 50 pure live seeds Pure Live Seed (PLS) per foot at 30.5 cm spacing, is 5 lbs PLS/acre. When planted in a mixture, the seeding rate should be adjusted according to the proportion of the mix.
There are currently no commercial releases of lambstongue ragwort.

Management strategies should be based on the key species in the established plant community. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment. Blaisdell and Mueggler (1956) reported light mortality of lambstongue ragwort from spraying 2,4-D in sagebrush rangelands.

Foxtail millet is self-pollinated and will produce seed in 75–90 days (Hancock Seed, 2014). There is a very quick transition period from vegetative growth to flower-development. Flowering occurs top-down on each of the stemmed branches.

Plant during late spring/early summer to ensure adequate yield. Soil temperatures should be at least 18°C before planting (Cash et al., 2002). It should be seeded ¼–½ in deep at 15–20 lb/ac drilled or 20–30 lb/ac broadcast in a well-prepared, firm seedbed (Hancock Seed, 2014).
‘Sno-Fox’ is a cultivar developed for use as a grain in the United States. Other varieties include ‘Butte’, ‘German’, ‘Golden German’, ‘Manta’, ‘White Wonder’, and ‘Common’ (Cash et al., 2002).

If controlling weeds through cultivation, plant foxtail millet in 30-in rows. If foxtail millet is terminated by roller-crimper without the use of herbicides, residue will be more persistent than soybean or buckwheat residue. There may be some disadvantage to leaving too much millet residue on the soil surface as it can impede subsequent cash crops or native vegetation recruitment in restoration projects. Like proso millet (Panicum miliaceum), there is little regrowth after cutting.

Rose checker-mallow is a member of the mallow family (Malvaceae). It is an herbaceous perennial that typically grows 20.3–101.6 cm tall (Hitchcock and Cronquist, 1961). Plants have a strong taproot and short to trailing rhizomes (horizontal underground stems). The aboveground stems are often trailing or reclining on the ground, freely root at the base, are generally not hollow, and are covered in soft, branched (stellate), fairly long hairs.

Rose checker-mallow occurs in prairie and meadow habitats that were historically maintained by fire, so fire may be an important tool in managing appropriate habitat for this species (WDNR, 2003).

If direct seeding, sow in the fall or spring at a depth of ¼ to ½ inch and a rate of 4 to 6 lb/ac on 24-to 91.4 cm row spacing (approximately 30 seeds per square foot).

For restoration plantings, proper weed control and site preparation (tilling to create a clean, firm seed bed) are critical for good establishment and long-term survival. Seeds are not dormant but appear to benefit from scarification prior to sowing based on observations at the Corvallis Plant Materials Center. Field Establishment & Maintenance: For seed production, this species is best established from transplanted plugs in the fall or spring. Transplanting plugs creates cleaner fields and results in an established productive field in the first growing season.
Conifer and non-native shrub encroachment can displace native prairie forbs from their historical distribution.
Nursery Plugs (2-inch / 50-cell); 4-inch to 1-gal Container; Restoration Seed (PLS); Rooted Divisions
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Seed weevil larvae (Macrorhoptus spp.) have decimated yields some years in seed production fields at the Corvallis Plant Materials Center. Vole, mouse, and rabbit predation and leaf rust can also be detrimental to seed production of this species. Silene spaldingii; Spalding's Silene; Spalding’s Catchfly; Spalding’s Campion

Inhabiting dry grasslands in the montane zone, this species is rare in southeastern British Columbia, known solely from Tobacco Plains, and ranges south to Montana, Idaho, and Oregon. The species occurs in dry to moist grasslands within bunchgrass and sagebrush-steppe habitats, where Idaho fescue and bluebunch wheatgrass are the dominant components; plants are occasionally found in open pine habitats (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2007).

A perennial herb arising from a simple or branched stem-base, featuring several erect stems that are branched above, long woolly-hairy and more or less glandular-hairy, and 20-60 cm tall. Basal leaves are few and soon deciduous. Stem leaves occur in 4-7 opposite pairs, ranging from oblanceolate below to lanceolate above, long woolly-hairy and more or less glandular-hairy, measuring 6-7 cm long and 0.5-1.5 cm wide, unstalked and slightly fused; stipules are lacking. Belonging to the carnation or pink family (Caryophyllaceae), Spalding's catchfly is a long-lived perennial forb emerging in spring from a woody root crown and dying back below ground level each fall.
