Inhabiting dry grasslands in the montane zone, this species is rare in southeastern British Columbia, known solely from Tobacco Plains, and ranges south to Montana, Idaho, and Oregon. The species occurs in dry to moist grasslands within bunchgrass and sagebrush-steppe habitats, where Idaho fescue and bluebunch wheatgrass are the dominant components; plants are occasionally found in open pine habitats (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2007). Spalding's catchfly is native to portions of Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia, Canada, occupying five physiographic regions: the Palouse Grasslands in west-central Idaho and southeastern Washington; the Channeled Scablands in eastern Washington; the Blue Mountain Basins in northeastern Oregon; the Canyon Grasslands of the Snake River and its tributaries in Idaho, Oregon, and Washington; and the intermountain valleys of northwestern Montana. There are currently 99 known populations of Spalding's catchfly, with 66 populations composed of fewer than 100 individuals each, 23 populations containing 100 or more individuals apiece, and the 10 largest populations each comprising more than 500 plants (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2007).

Restoration: Sisyrinchium idahoense is a prime candidate for wetland or riparian zone restoration sites, such as wetland and riparian restoration projects. It attracts multiple pollinators and beneficial insects, provides cover for small animals, and its clumpy root structure provides soil stability. It grows in full sun to shaded areas and is highly desirable because of its productive versatility.
Not suited for heavy foot traffic; best planted in restoration beds, meadows, or borders.

To overcome seed dormancy, sow seeds in containers and place in a warm location (18°C) for 2-4 weeks then move containers to a cold location (7°C or lower) for at least eight weeks.

S. idahoense seeds are dormant and need to experience warm, early fall temperatures followed by cold winter temperatures to initiate germination in early spring as soils warm. Seeds can be shallowly drill planted (surface to 3 mm) or broadcast at a single species rate of 6 to 7 pounds pure live seed (pls) per acre in the fall if there is good site preparation and weed control for at least the previous year.

Be sure to choose areas that are at least seasonally moist, if not swampy, or employ irrigation and the plants will grow well. Plug Propagation and Field Establishment: It is recommended to establish fields from plugs to avoid competition from weeds and the need for dry-season irrigation during the first years. Production work done at the Corvallis Plant Materials Center indicates that transplanting plugs into weed fabric creates cleaner fields and results in an established, productive field in the first growing season.

Once established in appropriate areas, there is little maintenance required to keep these plants growing. While Idaho blue-eyed grass will self-sow and be prolific, it is not aggressive and is unlikely to become dominant in most areas.

Inhabiting moist to mesic meadows, grasslands, shrublands, ditches, fields, roadsides, and forest openings across lowland, steppe, and montane zones, this introduced species is widespread in British Columbia, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon, and the Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to Florida, Texas, and California. It also occupies open woods, damp thickets, abandoned farmland, and tall-grass prairies at pH 4.8-7.5 across Canada and the USA. Canada goldenrod typically grows in moist soil with medium texture and moderate levels of organic matter (Werner et al. 1980). Canada goldenrod plants are indeterminate, and seed ripens about 6 weeks after flowers bloom. Seed is wind-disseminated and will blow away when ripe. Seed can be harvested with a combine, however the most efficient method is with a vacuum, which removes only mature seed and minimizes amount of undesired plant material.

Plants established by seedlings can be started by sowing seed in containers placed in a greenhouse in January. Seed should be planted into a firm, weed-free seed bed at a rate of 0.6 kg PLS/ha (0.5 lb PLS/ac) and at a depth of 0.3 to 0.6 cm. If planted in a mix, the seeding rate should be adjusted according to the proportion of the mix.

This plant spreads by rhizomes and by seed. Where plant spread is not desired, seedlings should be planted in a large pot or barrel submersed in the soil, or new growth should be cut and removed each year. To prevent seed dispersal, flower heads should be removed prior to seed ripening. Plants will withstand vigorous cutting, and will regrow if cut during the growing season.

The Navajo also smoked the root with other plants and used the plant as a charm for success in gambling.

Goldenrods have a reputation of being weedy due to their aggressive rhizomatous growth, which enables them to rapidly colonize disturbed sites and causes them to be difficult to control. Basal leaves are oblanceolate, stalked, 5-30 cm long, 0.5-3 cm wide, essentially glabrous, 3-nerved, and entire or remotely toothed; stem leaves are similar, alternate, becoming linear, entire, unstalked, and much reduced upwards. Belonging to the sunflower family (Asteraceae), Solidago missouriensis is a native, warm-season, short-lived perennial. Stems grow singularly or in groups from a creeping rhizome or woody caudex, being reddish-green, smooth, slender, erect, and 20 to 90 cm tall.

Plants grow well in sandy loam to clay loam soils, and poorly in gravel and dense clay (Walsh, 1993). Plants are tolerant of weakly acidic to moderately basic and weakly saline conditions (Wasser, 1982, as cited by Walsh, 1993) and not tolerant of extremely acidic and saline conditions (Dittberner and Olson, 1983, as cited by Walsh, 1993).
Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.

Occurs in dry grasslands, shrublands, and open forests in the steppe and lower montane zones; infrequent in south-central, southeastern, and northeastern British Columbia; extending east to Ontario and south to Tennessee, Texas, and Arizona. Missouri goldenrod grows on dry, open slopes in upland prairies, plains, meadows, deciduous and evergreen forests and deserts, and along roadsides, railroads, ditches and fences (Walsh, 1994). The species frequently establishes in open, disturbed sites while maintaining tolerance for partial shade, and functions as a mid-seral species in northwestern Iowa. Distributed across most Midwestern and western United States and south-central and southwestern Canadian provinces, it comprises four recognized varieties: var. fasciculata, occupying most of the species range; var. missouriensis, occurring primarily in the western portion; var. tenuissima, restricted to Colorado, New Mexico, and Arizona; and var. tolmieana, endemic to Washington and Oregon.

Stands of Missouri goldenrod produce seed crops for at least five years. Plants are indeterminate, and seed ripens about 6 weeks after flowers bloom. Seed is wind-disseminated and will blow away when ripe.

Plants established by seedlings can be started by sowing seed in containers in January and placed in a greenhouse. Seed should be planted into a firm, weed-free seed bed at a rate of 1.1 kg PLS/ha (1 lb PLS/ac) and at a depth of 0.3 to 0.6 cm. If planted in a mix, the seeding rate should be adjusted according to the proportion of the mix.

This plant spreads by rhizomes and by seed. Where plant spread is not desired, seedlings should be planted in a large pot or barrel submersed in the soil, or new growth should be cut and removed each year. To prevent seed dispersal, flower heads should be removed prior to seed ripening. Plants will withstand vigorous cutting, and will regrow if cut during the growing season.

Prairie cordgrass occurs in wet meadows, sloughs, potholes, and drainage ways, as well as floodplains and back dune areas (Bush, 2000), where it associates with various species including sedges and rushes; the species grows throughout the Northeast, Great Lakes, and Midwest States, alongside most other states across the country. Prairie cordgrass is a warm-season perennial grass native to the tallgrass prairies across most of the United States and Canada, reaching an average height of 0.9–2.4 m.

Prairie cordgrass is a warm-season perennial grass native to the tallgrass prairies across most of the United States and Canada, reaching an average height of 0.9–2.4 m. The leaf blades are coarse, very tough, thick, 3–13 mm wide, and up to 76.2 cm long, with serrated, sharp margins and stiff stems. It is strongly rhizomatous, possessing very tough, scaly rhizomes capable of growing 1.5–3 m per year, which distinguishes it from other desirable native warm-season grasses. The seedheads comprise 10 to 20 spikes attached to the main stem, with each spike bearing up to 40 spikelets growing in two rows on the side of the spike away from the stem.

Seed production fields: Seed fields established from rhizomes will produce some seed the first year. Seed fields established from seed usually take 2 to 3 years before producing a seed crop. The seed typically matures within a week or two of frost.

Vegetative propagation: The strong rhizomes can be used for propagation. The ideal piece of vegetative material is a “J” hook piece of rhizome with buds and 5.1–30.5 cm of dry stem. Other rhizome pieces can be used if there are roots and at least one bud.
Red River Germplasm prairie cordgrass is a selection named and released by the Bismarck, North Dakota Plant Materials Center. It is a composite of plant materials from Grant County, Minnesota.

Seedling vigor is moderate, and seed often germinates throughout the course of the summer. Seedlings develop slowly. Stands are established more quickly by planting vegetative material compared to seeding. Adequate water at planting time is critical for establishment of seed and vegetative material.

Plants in the Sphaeralcea genus are important forage sources for a number of rodents, rabbits and other lagomorphs, and ungulates such as deer and antelope Smith 1970.

Gathered seed can be cleaned by processing with a brush machine or hammer mill and air screening equipment. There are approximately 804,760 seeds per kilogram (365,800 seeds per pound). S. munroana and other members of the Sphaeralcea genus have an impermeable seed coat which causes challenges for plant production.

Munro’s globemallow can be established by seed or seedlings. Seed should be planted with a drill into a weed-free seed bed at a rate of 4 kg PLS per ha (3.5 lbs PLS per acre) and at a depth of 0.6 cm. When planted in a mix, the seeding rate should be adjusted according to the proportion of the mix.
‘ARS-2892’ is select-class germplasm released by the ARS in 1993.

For optimal production of Sphaeralcea munroana seed, the pollination services of bees are required. James Cane, ARS (2011) has found outcrossing of S. munroana increases seed production 4-fold. He also discovered in one study 37 out of 57 of the bees that visited S. munroana and related plant species were ground-nesting floral specialists, such as Diadasia diminuta, D. lutzi, and Colletes sphaeralcea. The other 20 species that visited were also ground-nesting but floral generalists.

Seed was collected from plants growing on the Hyrum Lake Dam in Cache County, UT and compared to 49 other accessions of Sphaeralcea species. It was selected for its large shoot size, succulence, leafy growth form and seed yield potential (Rumbaugh and Pendery 1993).

This species spreads naturally from seed once established and increases on depleted rangelands and wastelands. Sand dropseed plants are able to withstand heavy use due to their protected root crown, late maturity and because they are less preferred than other species. Plants can be killed by overgrazing as a result of continued close cropping. When grazed properly, sand dropseed increases on poor condition, low seral ecological sites.

Its primary intended use is for rangeland seeding for livestock and wildlife. Generation 0 seed is maintained by the Plant Materials Center and is available in limited quantities for seed increase (USDA-NRCS, 1999). It was selected for its vigor, forage production, and seed quality throughout the intended area of use.

A perennial, aquatic herb arising from fine, tufted roots, featuring branched stems up to 100 cm long. All leaves are submersed, linear, thin, green, 5-10 cm long, up to 1 mm wide, with 1 to 3 veins, sharp-pointed tips, and stipules 0.5-2 cm long where the blades arise close to the tips. Belonging to the Pondweed Family (Potomogetonaceae), sago pondweed is an aquatic herbaceous plant growing up to 1 m tall (Bare, 1979). It is generally completely submersed except for the reproductive spike that peaks above the water, flowering from June to September (Larson, 1993), and is nearly unbranched at the base, becoming freely branched towards the top (Larson, 1993).

Waterfowl extensively use and rely on sago pondweed as a food source; The whole plant can be consumed, and parts are utilized by diving, dabbling, whistling ducks, many types of geese, swans, coots and the long-billed dowitcher. Preeminent waterfowl food plant.

Druplets can be broadcast seeded into shallow water, less than 2 meters, however, the best establishments have been by imbedding druplets, turions, or plant tops in clay and dropping them from boats in the spring. A planting rate of 3,000 plant parts per hectare is recommended and stands are not likely to be very robust until the second season after root systems have developed. Sago pondweed does not compete well with other macrophyte competitors such as Myriophyllum, Ceratophyllum, Ruppia, and Chara.

Sago pondweed can be cultured in liquid media for experimental purposes from druplets, turions, rhizomes, leafy tops, or cuttings. This method eliminates uncontrolled variables that can be introduced from the substrate or soil in which sago pondweed would normally be grown. Druplets can be stored in wet or dry conditions.
There are no known cultivars, improved, or selected materials at this time.

Managers have tried to manipulate populations of sago pondweed for use by waterfowl and wildlife by adjusting the water levels. Results from these trials are variable and depend on water chemistry, water levels, geography, and other macrophyte competitors. In some cases, declines in populations have been achieved by partially dewatering of the pools. In other instances, an increase in sago pondweed was observed by partially or fully dewatering the pools.
These plant materials are somewhat readily available from commercial sources.

Occurring in mesic to dry meadows and forests in lowland and montane zones, smooth blue aster is common in southern British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains and south of 55°N, less frequent in northeastern British Columbia and southern Vancouver Island, and lacking from northwestern British Columbia. A perennial herb belonging to the aster family (Asteraceae). Smooth blue aster develops from a fibrous-rooted, usually short rhizome or woody stem-base with a stout underground stem (caudex), producing erect stems that are branched above, glabrous or nearly so, and 0.4-1.2 m (30 to 100 cm) tall, with typically six to seven aerial stems sprouting from the caudex. Basal leaves are stalked and soon deciduous, dropping early in the autumn. Stem leaves are lanceolate to broadly lanceolate or egg-shaped, unstalked and usually clasping, 8-18 cm long, 1-3.5 cm wide (thick and stout, 1 to 2.4 cm wide and less than 5 times as long as wide), entire or shallowly toothed, sometimes toothed along the margins, glabrous or nearly so, tending to be glaucous, and clasped to the stem by a lobed appendage (auricle).

The Hopi of Northern Arizona used a decoction of the leaf and root of spineless horsebrush as a gynecological aid to shrink the uterus and stop discharge after birth and as an herbal tonic. The Navajo used the plant to cause onset of menstruation, as a analgesic for various aches and pains, a cold remedy to treat coughs and fever, an herbal steam inhalant.
Traditionally utilized together with other flowers for dye.

The Navajo used the plant to cause onset of menstruation, as a analgesic for various aches and pains, a cold remedy to treat coughs and fever, an herbal steam in sweat bath medicine, to relieve stomach ache, as a yellow dye for wool and in various religious ceremonies (Native American Ethnobotany Database).

Spineless horsebrush is tolerant to fire and can invade recently burned rangeland. Resprouting and seedling establishment of spineless horsebrush after fire should be considered when planning prescribed fires on sagebrush dominated landscapes. Dense stands can spread aggressively and crowd out surrounding vegetation if unmanaged. Sheep that feed on spineless horsebrush following or in conjunction with consumption of black sagebrush (A. nova) and then exposed to bright sunlight may develop a characteristic swelling of the lips, ears, and face, commonly referred to as “bighead”. Sheep grazing spineless horsebrush in the absence of black sagebrush may still die without developing bighead but suffer from swollen, engorged liver with severe fatty changes and low grade nephritis (inflammation of nephrons) of the kidney along with hemorrhaging of the sub-skin and organ linings. Sheep may also experience abortions from consuming spineless horsebrush. Most sheep losses occur during stormy periods when sheep change their grazing habits as they are trailed through areas with heavy infestations of spineless horsebrush and desirable forage is lacking. | Host insect damage: Scrobipalpopsis tetradymiella: in stem galls

A native shrub or tree of the cypress family (Cupressaceae) growing to 15 (-38) meters tall, featuring a narrowly conic to broadly pyramidal crown with spreading, densely crowded branches and flattened, fan-sprayed branchlets. The gray to reddish-brown bark is 6-9 mm thick, fibrous, and separated into flat, connected ridges. Leaves are evergreen, scale-like, abruptly pointed, 2 mm long, arranged oppositely in alternating pairs (in 4 rows), bright green above and pale green below, sometimes turning yellow-brown in winter, and emit a spicy fragrance when crushed. This plant can be toxic. Meadow deathcamas may be considered weedy in some regions or habitats. Consumption of deathcamas has been linked to deaths of livestock and humans. Pollen and nectar of foothills death camas (V. paniculatus) was found to contain the same toxins as are found in the vegetative plant parts. Adults of the generalist solitary bee, Osmia lignaria (Megachilidae), were paralyzed and soon after died when fed biologically relevant doses of deathcamas toxins; larval progeny eating dosed provision masses likewise died. Contains toxic alkaloids; early-spring shoots can poison grazing livestock. The inedible bulb can be mistaken for edible Camassia. Toxic look-alike weed removed from edible camas beds during cultivation to increase productivity. Maintain proper grazing regimens so deathcamas does not increase on overgrazed rangelands, and keep livestock out of heavily infested areas in early spring.

Alsike clover is a true species in spite of its specific name which originally implied that it was a hybrid of red clover (T. pretense) and white clover (T. repens). It is an introduced, short-lived, non-creeping perennial with a growth habit similar to red clover. It can be distinguished from red clover by the absence of crescent-shaped marks on each leaflet and more conspicuously toothed leaves.

Alsike clover is usually planted with grasses for pasture and hay in areas where other higher yielding legumes are not adapted. Pure stands of alsike clover should be harvested for hay when in full bloom. There may be many heads with ripe seed when a field is in full bloom. Alsike clover is resistant to many diseases, such as bacterial wilt, bacterial blight, mildew, and northern anthracnose, which can cause major losses in other forage legumes. Annual herb from a taproot; stems 1 to several, erect, 20-80 cm tall, mostly unbranched, long-soft-hairy. Crimson clover is an annual in the legume family (Fabaceae). Plants are generally densely hairy with a rosette of upright, usually unbranched stems reaching 0.3–0.9 m tall supported by a central taproot and many fibrous roots. The trifoliate leaves growing along the stems have egg-to heart-shaped leaflets that are nearly ½ to 2.5 cm long and are distinguished from the leaves of red clover (T. pratense) by their rounded tips and absence of V-shaped leaf marks (Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture, 2012).

Naturalized populations of crimson clover can be found in moist to dry sites along roadsides, and in fields, pastures, and disturbed areas from lowlands to montane zones (Douglas et al., 1999). Crimson clover is native to southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia Minor, and was introduced to the United States as a cultivated crop in the 1800’s (Hollowell, 1951). It is now grown widely as a winter annual in the Southeast from Kentucky southward and from eastern Texas to the Atlantic Coast (USDA Hardiness Zones 6–9) (Ball and Lacefield, 2000).

In the Willamette Valley of Oregon, where much of the US crimson clover seed is produced, fields are planted in late September with the fall rains, flower in mid-May, and are harvested in late June to early July when about three-fourths of the pods have turned golden brown. Plants are swathed at night, when they are damp with dew, to reduce losses of the easily shattered seed. Seed is allowed to dry in the swath for about a week, and then harvested with a combine using a belt pick-up header.

If sowing in a location where crimson clover has not been grown in the last three years, seed should be inoculated (use inoculant type “R”, Rhizobium leguminosarum biovar trifolii) immediately before sowing for best stand establishment and root nodulation (Harper, 2004).

If sowing in a location where crimson clover has not been grown in the last three years, seed should be inoculated (use inoculant type “R”, Rhizobium leguminosarum biovar trifolii) immediately before sowing for best stand establishment and root nodulation. Soil testing prior to sowing is important, particularly for phosphorus and potassium levels, which may limit N fixation and stand productivity if they are too low.

Livestock/Grazing: If seeded with winter annual grasses, initial growth should be monitored closely and grazed appropriately to keep the grasses from shading out the clover. In general, crimson clover should not be grazed until the plants are 10.2–15.2 cm tall, and grazing should leave at least 7.6 cm of stubble. Leaving too much foliage may increase the occurrence of crown rot, so mowing or grazing prior to the coolest, wettest months is often necessary. Careful monitoring and grazing management is needed to prevent overgrazing crimson clover pasture, both alone and in mixtures.

The two most widespread, serious diseases of crimson clover are crown and stem rot (caused by Sclerotinia trifoliorum) and sooty blotch (caused by Cymadothea trifolii). Crown and stem rot is worst in the cool wet weather of fall, winter, and spring, and may completely destroy a stand. Stands that are overly thick or rank throughout the winter months may create conditions that promote this rot, but fall and winter grazing that removes excess foliage can reduce the spread of the disease. | Host insect damage: Strymon melinus: on flowers/fruits/leaves; Rachiplusia nu: on green parts

Red clover has approximately 275,000 seeds per pound. The full seeding rate is 6 pounds PLS per acre for a solid stand. The recommended seeding rate for a grass/legume pasture is approximately 25 percent or 1.5 pounds PLS per acre.

Some of the major cultivars for the western US are ‘Pennscott’, ‘Chesapeake’, ‘Kenland’, ‘Cumberland’, ‘Dollard’, ‘Midland’ and ‘Lakeland’. ‘Altaswede’, ‘Norlac’, and ‘Craig’ are mammoth red clovers. In the eastern US, varieties selected should be resistant to anthracnose and powdery mildew.

Graze or cut for hay when the red clover is ¼-½ bloom. A second cutting or successive grazing should occur when red clover is ¼ bloom. Leave at least 5.1 cm of growth after each harvest. Mammoth red clover does not produce flowers the first year.

Typha species may be planted from bare rootstock or seedlings from container stalk or directly seeded into the soil. Bare rootstock or seedlings are preferred revegetation methods where there is moving water.

Heavy grazing will eliminate Typha species, as well as other native species, from riparian corridors. Cattails are fairly resistant to moderate grazing, providing wet soils are not compacted. Field trials demonstrate that mowing cattails after the heads are well– formed, but not mature, then following up with another mowing about a month later (when new growth is two or three feet high) will kill at least 75% of the plants.
This species is readily available for native plant nurseries specializing in wetland plants.

All parts of the cattail are edible when gathered at the appropriate stage of growth. The young shoots are cut from the rhizomes (underground stems) in the spring when they are about 10.2–40.6 cm long. The base of the stem where it attaches to the rhizome can be boiled or roasted like potatoes.

Lengths of cattail were plied into rope or other size cordage, and cattail rope was used in some areas to bind bundles of tule into tule boats. Some tribes used the leaves and sheath bases as caulking materials. The fluff can also be used as tinder, insulation, or for lining baby cradleboards.
The Cahuilla Indians used the stalks for matting, bedding material, and ceremonial bundles. Apaches used the pollen in female puberty ceremonies.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

The Menomini used the inner bark in a tea and it was taken as a physic.

Slippery elm was also used extensively as a medicine. The inner bark was made into an eye wash for sore eyes. The inner bark was used by the Menomini and the Meskwaki in a poultice to heal sores on the body.

The inner bark was used for cordage by many tribes. The Menomini gathered the bark, boiled it, and used it for making fiber bags and large storage baskets. The Dakota, Omaha-Ponca, Winnebago, and Pawnee used the inner bark fiber for making ropes and cords.

Seeds or cuttings can propagate plants of highbush blueberry. Ideal soil for cultivation is moist, high in organic matter, highly acidic (4.5-5.5), and well drained. The plants grow in full sun to partial shade, but those in open sites produce more flowers and have brighter fall foliage color. Highbush blueberry (V. corymbosum) is self-fertile, but cross-pollination increases fruit set and results in larger, earlier berries with more seeds (see Agriculture Western Australia 2000).

Black huckleberry is a medium-sized shrub or subshrub (Ericaceae) with erect to spreading, densely branched stems up to 1.5 m tall (0.1-2 m tall); young twigs are somewhat angled, yellow-green, and smooth and hairless or slightly hairy, while older bark is greyish and shredding. Inhabiting dry to moist forests and openings in the montane and subalpine zones, this species is common throughout British Columbia except on the Queen Charlotte Islands, ranging north to southeastern Yukon Territory, east to Alberta, and south to Idaho, Montana, and northern California, with subalpine and subarctic distribution across western and eastern Canada and the northern and western USA.

Black huckleberry is a medium-sized shrub or subshrub (Ericaceae) with erect to spreading, densely branched stems up to 1.5 m tall (0.1-2 m tall); young twigs are somewhat angled, yellow-green, and glabrous or slightly hairy, while older bark is greyish and shredding. Leaves are alternate, deciduous, egg-shaped to elliptic-oblong (elliptical), 1.5-6 cm long (up to 5 cm long), (0.6) 1-3 cm wide, gradually narrowing to a pointed tip (long pointed tip), and rounded to tapered at the base, with margins finely nearly full length (finely serrated margin), obscurely veined and not lustrous, sparsely glandular, and somewhat paler on the lower surfaces. Flowers are bell-shaped and creamy-pink, found singly on the underside of the twigs. Berries are large, spherical, sweet, dark purple or black, with some forms covered with a waxy bloom and others having shiny dark berries.

Inhabiting bogs in the lowland and montane zones, this species is frequent throughout British Columbia with a circumboreal distribution ranging north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and south to Oregon, Idaho, and Minnesota, extending into Eurasia. The small cranberry occurs in wetlands including bogs, swamps, and muskegs, and along the marshy shores of ponds and lakes formed by glacial melting 10,000 to 18,000 years ago, often where there is no perched water table caused by a hardpan.

Small cranberry is a small, creeping, trailing, vine-like shrub (Ericaceae) with very slender stems 15-50 cm long, 0.2-1 mm thick, and glabrous to finely hairy, often creeping over Sphagnum moss. Leaves are evergreen, alternate, leathery, egg- to lance-shaped, tapering to the tip, 2-10 mm long, 1-5 mm wide, deep green and shining on the upper surface, greyish beneath, and with margins rolled under. The pale rose flowers feature petals bent backwards, 1-4 in number, appearing between May and August, resembling small shooting stars, forming a terminal cluster, and springing from the tips of stems. The red, sometimes off-white berry is small (10 mm wide), round, and slightly acid, ripening between August and October (Jacquemart 1997).

Birds such as wild geese, Hudsonian godwits, sharp-tailed grouse, and ring-necked pheasants also eat small cranberries.

The berries are eaten by many kinds of animals such as Roosevelt elk, black bears, black-tailed deer, foxes, squirrels, chipmunks, rabbits, and hares (Anderson 2009). Persistent cranberries provide high-energy forage for diverse mammals.

Small cranberry can be propagated by seeds or by cuttings or by severing sectors of rooted runners. Regenerates vegetatively from rhizomes and by layering. Cuttings should be taken during the dormant season, and treated with rooting hormone (Leopold 2005).
This plant is available from native plant nurseries.

Edible fruit. Food (edible bog cranberries harvested in mossy bogs). Fresh and preserved fruits stored in water or oulachen grease, widely traded along coast and interior. Early non-Indian descriptions of the small cranberry paint a picture of abundance. Albert Reagan reported in 1928 for the Bois Fort Ojibwa of Minnesota that: "Cranberries [both Vaccinium macrocarpon and V. oxycoccos] are very plentiful in the swampy regions and are quite an article of food. Many bushels of them are sold by the Indians each year." Part of the coast of Lake Superior was described as "flaming red with [Vaccinium oxycoccos] berries" in 1855 (Eastwood 1856).
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Host insect damage: Epidemia epixanthe: on leaves/shoots; Olethreutes schulziana: on leaves

Littleleaf huckleberry is a small, matted, broom-like native deciduous shrub (Ericaceae) <5 dm tall, with stems 10-25 cm tall, numerous, slender, broom-like, strongly angled, greenish or yellowish-green, and glabrous, along with strongly angled green twigs. Foliage is 8-15 mm, ovate, and serrate. Flowers are solitary, urn-shaped, pink blossoms in the axils of the lowest leaves and youngest shoots. The berry is bright red, tiny, and 3-6 mm in diameter.

Annual grass from fibrous roots, smooth to short-hairy, basally branched; stems mostly 30-70 cm tall. Grass Family (Poaceae). Ventenata is a winter annual that germinates in the fall when temperatures are moderate to high (18° - 28°C, or 18–28°C) (Northam & Callihan, 1986). Seed heads are produced May through June, about one month following annual Bromus species.
Annual grass from fibrous roots, smooth to short-hairy, basally branched; stems mostly 30-70 cm tall.

Due to the prostrate growth form, seed collection is best done by manually lifting and shearing the seed-bearing stems off the plant or by pulling the entire plant out by the taproot. Plants should be dried for several days to weeks. Seed is removed from the plant by vigorous shaking or with the aid of a hammer mill.

This species germinates readily in greenhouse conditions without pre-treatment or stratification. Seed should be sown on the soil surface or lightly covered. IDPMC has also germinated seed using an oxygenated water treatment following Tilley and Pickett (2021) and observed high rates of germination after 4 days.

Bigbract verbena is an early seral colonizer. It can be locally abundant on disturbed sites for the first few years following disturbance and then reduce in density making way for later seral, longer-lived species. Occasionally these species can form persistent stands, especially under management where succession is interrupted such as roadsides and field borders.

Bigbract verbena seed is currently difficult to obtain on the commercial market and wildland collection is often the only means of obtaining seed. Seed should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

Highbush cranberry is easy to grow, adaptable to a variety of soil and acidity, but it does best in consistently moist but well-drained soil. A yearly application of compost or well-rotted manure will maintain growth and fruit yields The plants are shade-tolerant, but flowering, fruiting, and foliage color will be best on plants in full sun. Plants may require occasional pruning to keep them from becoming leggy and to encourage the production of new shoots; prune immediately after flowering. Highbush cranberry can be propagated through hardwood and softwood cuttings, layering, crown division and by seed.

Thriving in moist to mesic meadows, thickets, and open forests throughout lowland, steppe, and montane zones, this plant is common in the southern two-thirds of British Columbia, becoming less frequent northward and absent from the Queen Charlotte Islands. Its range extends north to southeast Alaska and the Northwest Territories, east to Quebec and New Brunswick, and south to Ohio, Kansas, West Virginia, New Mexico, and California.

A perennial rhizomatous herb with mostly single, trailing or climbing stems nearly glabrous to densely hairy, measuring 15-100 cm long/tall. Leaves are alternate and pinnately compound, comprising 8 to 12 (18) linear to oval leaflets that are blunt, notched, pointed, or few-toothed at the tip, 1-3.5 cm long, glabrous to hairy, and thin to leathery with prominent parallel veins on the lower surface; tendrils are simple to branched and grasping; stipules are deeply toothed, 3-10 mm long, and crescent-shaped. American vetch is a native rhizomatous, single-stemmed, climbing perennial forb growing up to 40.6 cm tall with 8 to 16 broadly elliptical to linear leaflets measuring 1–3.8 cm in length. Lower stipules are deeply lacerated, frequently appearing star-like (Isley 1998).

American vetch is drought tolerant and has the ability to fix nitrogen into the soil (Stubbendiek and Conard, 1989). American vetch occurs frequently on slightly saline to moderately acidic soils of medium to coarse texture, but can also be found on clays. In western mountains, American vetch is usually more abundant in deep porous loams that are rich in organic matter.

Thriving in moist to mesic meadows, thickets, and open forests throughout lowland, steppe, and montane zones, this plant is common in the southern two-thirds of British Columbia, becoming less frequent northward and absent from the Queen Charlotte Islands. Its range extends north to southeast Alaska and the Northwest Territories, east to Quebec and New Brunswick, and south to Ohio, Kansas, West Virginia, New Mexico, and California. American vetch grows in a wide variety of habitats, typically found in moist areas including swampy woods, mixed forests, sheltered canyons, and clearings, though it also occurs in arid locations on hilltops or valley badlands (Cronquist et al, 1989). It is widely distributed west of the Mississippi River, in the northeastern United States, Alaska, and parts of Canada (Stubbendiek and Conard, 1989).

Restoration: Relatives of American vetch are often used as cover crops. Planting American vetch in disturbed sites can help remediate the habitat and restore disturbed rangelands by providing a natural source of nitrogen (Kirk, and Belt, 2010). American vetch has been successfully seeded in disturbed alpine rangelands (Brown et al, 1979). American vetch is one of the few non-toxic native legumes adapted to sites receiving less than 30.5 cm mean annual precipitation, making it a valuable option for native restoration seedings on arid rangeland (Tilley et al, 2013).
Not suited for heavy foot traffic; best planted in restoration beds, meadows, or borders.

Hand harvesting of wildland populations with clippers or shears is the most common means of seed collection. Due to its low and twining growth habit, mechanical and vacuum harvesting are ineffective. Seed production fields may be harvested mechanically.

The full stand seeding rate for approximately 25 seeds/ft² is 33 PLS lbs/ac (Tilley et al, 2013). American vetch should be seeded in the fall to a depth of 2.5–5.1 cm. Unscarified seed will germinate in approximately 14 days.
There are no recommended cultivars or selected materials for American vetch at this time.

American vetch could be used as a minor component of restoration seed mixtures. Management strategies should be based on the key species in the established plant community. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment.
Seed source should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.

Seeds, young shoots eaten. Indigenous peoples used the seed leaves and seeds of American vetch as a source of food.
A poultice of the leaves has been used to treat ailments such as spider bites, and an infusion of the plant was used as an eyewash.
American vetch has also been used as a panacea, an aphrodisiac, and a good luck charm.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Hookedspur violet was used in traditional medicine by the Blackfoot, Nuxalk (Bella Coola) and Tolowa tribes. Leaves and roots were used to treat stomach problems and asthma in children, and as a cataplasm to treat soreness and swelling. In addition, the Southern Dakelh (Carrier), and S'Klallam (Klallam) used the plant as an analgesic and gastrointestinal aid, and the Makah tribe used it as a gynecological aid.
The Blackfoot Indians used a blue dye obtained from hookedspur violet to dye arrows.
Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

There are no cultivars or improved materials of northern bog violet available from commercial sources.

Basal leaves are numerous in large clumps, rigid, wiry, narrowly linear and grass-like, evergreen, tough, 20-90 cm long, 1.5-6 mm wide, with harshly rough-margined tiny teeth capable of cutting unprotected hands; stem leaves are several to many, reduced upward and eventually bract-like. The finely toothed edges of the leaves can cut unprotected hands Beattie 1915:102.

Inhabiting dry to mesic coniferous forests, glades, meadows, and clearings in the montane and subalpine zones, this taxon is locally common in southeastern British Columbia, extending east to Alberta and south to Wyoming, Idaho, and California, ranging from western Canada to northern California. It is moderately shade tolerant and appears in clumps in clearings, prairies, bogs, ridge tops, rocky slopes, and open woods from sea level to 2300 m (Utech 2002). It grows in association with many kinds of conifers including Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), grand fir (Abies grandis), Pacific silver fir (Abies amabilis), subalpine fir (Abies lasiocarpa), mountain hemlock (Tsuga mertensiana), western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla), western white pine (Pinus monticola), and lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta). It can be found in all soil types, but prefers xeric to subxeric and submesic sites (Wick et al. 2008).

A native, evergreen, perennial shrub of the Agave Family (Agavaceae) with long, thick underground stems and rarely an above-ground stem. Grayish-green, stiff, sword-shaped leaves (30 to 76 cm long, 2.5 cm wide) emerge from a basal rosette, featuring sharp, pointed tips and long, curly, filamentous threads at the margins. Creamy white to pale yellow or greenish, bell-shaped flowers (5 to 8 cm wide) with broadly ovate petals (4-5 cm) bloom in late spring and summer, hanging loosely in clusters from a large central spike (1 to 4 m tall) emerging from the rosette. The fruits are capsules that contain 120 to 150, small black seeds that are dispersed by wind.

Gathered and cooked as a choice grain food. Annual wildrice, commonly referred to as “manomin” by Native Americans, was an important grain food used by multiple Native American tribes. It was a staple food and constituted an important element of the diets of the Chippewa, Dakota, Menominee, Meskwaki, Ojibwa, Omaha, Ponca, Nlaka'pamux (Thompson), and Winnebago Tribes.

Annual wildrice is well documented as a historically important species to many Native American tribes’ way of life as a form of subsistence and has been incorporated into religious ceremonies, social rituals, and oral traditions (MacCauley, 1884). The Dakota Tribe used an annual wildrice dish seasoned with dried blueberries and presented on birch bark dishes during ceremonial banquets.
